abstract: The complexity and computational capacity of multi-layered, feedforward neural networks is examined. Neural networks for special purpose (structured) functions are examined from the perspective of circuit complexity. Known re(cid:173) sults in complexity theory are applied to the special instance of neural network circuits, and in particular, classes of functions that can be implemented in shallow circuits characterised. Some conclusions are also drawn about learning complexity, and some open problems raised. The dual problem of determining the computational capacity of a class of multi-layered networks with dynamics regulated by an algebraic Hamiltonian is considered. Formal results are pre(cid:173) sented on the storage capacities of programmed higher-order structures, and a tradeoff between ease of programming and capacity is shown. A precise de(cid:173) termination is made of the static fixed point structure of random higher-order constructs, and phase-transitions (0-1 laws) are shown.

paragraphs: The paper investigates the computational complexity and capacity of neural networks from two theoretical perspectives. First, it treats multilayer feedforward networks as circuits and applies known complexity results to structured functions. This identifies classes of functions that shallow neural circuits can implement and leads to conclusions and open questions about learning complexity.

The second perspective concerns networks whose dynamics are governed by an algebraic Hamiltonian, a mathematical expression regulating their behavior. Here the question shifts toward the storage capacity of higher-order structures. The paper gives formal capacity results for programmed networks and shows a tradeoff between how easily a structure can be programmed and how much it can store.

For random higher-order constructions, the authors precisely determine the static fixed-point structure and establish phase transitions expressed as zero–one laws. Fixed points are states that remain unchanged under the dynamics. These results connect the mathematical organization of a network to its possible stable states, complementing the analysis of which functions a feedforward network can compute.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes neural circuit expressiveness, higher-order memory capacity, and fixed-point behavior, including a tradeoff between programmability and storage.

title: On Properties of Networks of Neuron-Like Elements

paragraphs: The paper considers when feedforward neural networks are appropriate classifiers, how their architectures should be selected, and how complexity and training-set size affect classification reliability. It focuses on settings where labeled examples are available but the process producing those examples is poorly understood. In that setting, reliable behavior on new inputs becomes a central design question.

The authors argue that pursuing an unspecified notion of optimality is unhelpful without a sufficiently detailed mathematical model of the pattern source. They also suggest that high input dimensionality can have a constructive side. A linear-threshold unit can express more divisions of a set of points as the number of input dimensions increases.

This observation concerns representational power, while the paper separately considers the statistical evidence needed to support reliable classification. It discusses improvements to bounds from Vapnik-Chervonenkis theory that could reduce the gap between theory and practice, while explicitly saying they cannot eliminate it. The overall contribution is a framework for reasoning jointly about architecture, available examples, and prediction reliability.
summary.tldr: The paper examines how classifier architecture, input dimensionality, and training-set size jointly shape representational power and statistical reliability.

title: Designing Linear Threshold Based Neural Network Pattern Classifiers

abstract: ALCOVE is a connectionist model of human category learning that fits a broad spectrum of human learning data. Its architecture is based on well(cid:173) established psychological theory, and is related to networks using radial basis functions. From the perspective of cognitive psychology, ALCOVE can be construed as a combination of exemplar-based representation and error(cid:173) driven learning. From the perspective of connectionism, it can be seen as incorporating constraints into back-propagation networks appropriate for modelling human learning.

paragraphs: ALCOVE is a neural network model intended to explain how people learn categories. Its architecture draws on established psychological theory and is related to radial basis function networks. The goal is to build a learning system whose organization reflects ideas about human categorization, so its behavior can be compared with human learning data.

From a psychological perspective, the model combines exemplar-based representation with error-driven learning. Exemplar-based representation organizes category knowledge around examples, while error-driven learning changes the model in response to mistakes. Combining these ideas connects what the system represents with how that representation contributes to learning category judgments.

From a neural network perspective, ALCOVE places psychologically motivated constraints on a backpropagation architecture. The abstract reports that it fits a broad range of human learning data. That finding supports the usefulness of building psychological commitments into the network's design: the resulting architecture serves as a computational account of category learning, linking an explicit representation of examples with a mechanism for learning from errors.
summary.tldr: ALCOVE combines exemplar-based representation and error-driven neural learning to account for a broad range of human category-learning data.

title: ALCOVE: A Connectionist Model of Human Category Learning

abstract: We introduce a novel algorithm, termed PPA (Performance Prediction Algorithm), that quantitatively measures the contributions of elements of a neural system to the tasks it performs. The algorithm identifies the neurons or areas which participate in a cognitive or behavioral task, given data about performance decrease in a small set of lesions. It also allows the accurate prediction of performances due to multi-element lesions. The effectiveness of the new algorithm is demonstrated in two models of recurrent neural networks with complex interactions among the ele(cid:173) ments. The algorithm is scalable and applicable to the analysis of large neural networks. Given the recent advances in reversible inactivation techniques, it has the potential to significantly contribute to the under(cid:173) standing of the organization of biological nervous systems, and to shed light on the long-lasting debate about local versus distributed computa(cid:173) tion in the brain.

paragraphs: Understanding a neural system requires identifying how its components contribute to behavior. The paper introduces the Performance Prediction Algorithm, or PPA, which uses decreases in task performance following lesions to quantify those contributions. Its input is performance information from a small set of lesions, and its targets are the neurons or areas participating in the task.

PPA also predicts performance after lesions affecting multiple elements. This matters for systems with complex interactions, where understanding individual components is only part of understanding the whole. The authors demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness in two recurrent neural-network models containing such interactions and describe it as scalable to large networks.

The abstract presents biological application as a potential next use, supported by advances in reversible inactivation techniques. Such techniques could provide the intervention data needed to investigate contributions in nervous systems. The demonstrated results concern neural-network models, while the broader promise is to clarify how biological functions are organized and inform the debate over localized versus distributed computation in the brain.
summary.tldr: PPA uses limited lesion-performance data to estimate neural components' task contributions and predict the effects of combined lesions.

title: Who Does What? A Novel Algorithm to Determine Function Localization

abstract: This study investigates a population decoding paradigm, in which the estimation of stimulus in the previous step is used as prior knowledge for consecutive decoding. We analyze the decoding accu(cid:173) racy of such a Bayesian decoder (Maximum a Posteriori Estimate), and show that it can be implemented by a biologically plausible recurrent network, where the prior knowledge of stimulus is con(cid:173) veyed by the change in recurrent interactions as a result of Hebbian learning.
originalAbstract: This study investigates a population decoding paradigm, in which the estimation of stimulus in the previous step is used as prior knowledge for consecutive decoding. We analyze the decoding accu(cid:173) racy of such a Bayesian decoder (Maximum a Posteriori Estimate), and show that it can be implemented by a biologically plausible recurrent network, where the prior knowledge of stimulus is con(cid:173) veyed by the change in recurrent interactions as a result of Hebbian learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a neural population can be decoded repeatedly while retaining information from an earlier estimate. At each step, the estimated stimulus from the previous step supplies prior knowledge for the next decoding operation. This makes the decoding process sequential, with earlier inference contributing to the interpretation of subsequent population activity.

The decoder uses maximum a posteriori estimation: it selects the stimulus estimate favored after combining current evidence with the prior. The authors analyze the accuracy of this Bayesian decoding scheme. The question is therefore both computational, concerning estimation accuracy, and biological, concerning how neural circuitry could perform the operation.

The proposed implementation is a biologically plausible recurrent network. Prior knowledge is conveyed through changes in recurrent interactions produced by Hebbian learning. This connects a probabilistic ingredient—the prior—to an adaptable property of the network itself. The result shows that the studied Bayesian decoder can be implemented through such recurrent interactions, providing a concrete link between sequential population decoding and a neural learning mechanism.
summary.tldr: A recurrent network can implement sequential Bayesian population decoding by encoding prior estimates through Hebbian changes in recurrent interactions.

title: Neural Implementation of Bayesian Inference in Population Codes

abstract: Most proposals for quantum neural networks have skipped over the prob- lem of how to train the networks. The mechanics of quantum computing are different enough from classical computing that the issue of training should be treated in detail. We propose a simple quantum neural network and a training method for it. It can be shown that this algorithm works in quantum systems. Results on several real-world data sets show that this algorithm can train the proposed quantum neural networks, and that it has some advantages over classical learning algorithms.
originalAbstract: Most proposals for quantum neural networks have skipped over the prob- lem of how to train the networks. The mechanics of quantum computing are different enough from classical computing that the issue of training should be treated in detail. We propose a simple quantum neural network and a training method for it. It can be shown that this algorithm works in quantum systems. Results on several real-world data sets show that this algorithm can train the proposed quantum neural networks, and that it has some advantages over classical learning algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to train a quantum neural network, an issue the authors argue has often been skipped in earlier proposals. Quantum computation follows mechanics sufficiently different from classical computation that a training procedure needs its own justification. The paper therefore treats learning as a central part of defining the network.

The authors propose both a simple quantum neural network and a method for training it. They state that the algorithm can be shown to work in quantum systems. This connects the proposed learning procedure to the computational setting in which the network is intended to operate.

Results on several real-world datasets show that the method can train the proposed networks and has some advantages over classical learning algorithms. Those findings support the particular network-and-training combination studied here. The contribution is a concrete treatment of quantum-network training, combining a procedure compatible with quantum systems and empirical evidence of learning, with advantages described as qualified rather than universal.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes a quantum neural network with a compatible training method and reports successful learning with some advantages over classical algorithms.

title: Training a Quantum Neural Network

abstract: Rao–Blackwellization is an approximation technique for probabilistic in- ference that ﬂexibly combines exact inference with sampling. It is useful in models where conditioning on some of the variables leaves a sim- pler inference problem that can be solved tractably. This paper presents Sample Propagation, an efﬁcient implementation of Rao–Blackwellized approximate inference for a large class of models. Sample Propagation tightly integrates sampling with message passing in a junction tree, and is named for its simple, appealing structure: it walks the clusters of a junction tree, sampling some of the current cluster’s variables and then passing a message to one of its neighbors. We discuss the application of Sample Propagation to conditional Gaussian inference problems such as switching linear dynamical systems.
originalAbstract: Rao–Blackwellization is an approximation technique for probabilistic in- ference that ﬂexibly combines exact inference with sampling. It is useful in models where conditioning on some of the variables leaves a sim- pler inference problem that can be solved tractably. This paper presents Sample Propagation, an efﬁcient implementation of Rao–Blackwellized approximate inference for a large class of models. Sample Propagation tightly integrates sampling with message passing in a junction tree, and is named for its simple, appealing structure: it walks the clusters of a junction tree, sampling some of the current cluster’s variables and then passing a message to one of its neighbors. We discuss the application of Sample Propagation to conditional Gaussian inference problems such as switching linear dynamical systems.

paragraphs: Probabilistic inference can become easier when some variables are fixed: the remaining problem may then admit a tractable exact solution. Rao–Blackwellization uses this structure by combining sampling with exact inference. This paper introduces Sample Propagation as an efficient implementation of that combination for a large class of probabilistic models.

The method integrates sampling directly with message passing in a junction tree. It moves among the tree’s clusters, samples some variables in the current cluster, and passes a message to a neighboring cluster. This gives the mixed inference procedure a local operational structure, with sampling and message passing carried out as parts of the same traversal.

The authors discuss conditional Gaussian inference problems, including switching linear dynamical systems, as applications. The method matters where conditioning on selected variables exposes an easier inference problem that can be solved exactly. Its contribution is an organized way to exploit that opportunity within a junction tree, preserving the combination of sampled and exact computation rather than requiring either one alone.
summary.tldr: Sample Propagation combines sampling and exact inference through local sampling and message passing in a junction tree.

title: Sample Propagation

abstract: Complex objects can often be conveniently represented by finite sets of simpler components, such as images by sets of patches or texts by bags of words. We study the class of positive definite (p.d.) kernels for two such objects that can be expressed as a function of the merger of their respective sets of components. We prove a general integral representa- tion of such kernels and present two particular examples. One of them leads to a kernel for sets of points living in a space endowed itself with a positive definite kernel. We provide experimental results on a benchmark experiment of handwritten digits image classification which illustrate the validity of the approach.
originalAbstract: Complex objects can often be conveniently represented by finite sets of simpler components, such as images by sets of patches or texts by bags of words. We study the class of positive definite (p.d.) kernels for two such objects that can be expressed as a function of the merger of their respective sets of components. We prove a general integral representa- tion of such kernels and present two particular examples. One of them leads to a kernel for sets of points living in a space endowed itself with a positive definite kernel. We provide experimental results on a benchmark experiment of handwritten digits image classification which illustrate the validity of the approach.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to compare complex objects represented as finite collections of simpler components. Examples include image patches and words in a text. The authors focus on positive-definite kernels whose value for two objects can be expressed through the merger of their respective component collections.

They prove a general integral representation for this class of kernels and give two particular constructions. The representation provides a mathematical description of the family under study. One construction handles sets of points whose underlying space already has a positive-definite kernel, connecting a comparison defined for individual points to one defined for entire sets.

The approach is evaluated on a handwritten-digit image-classification benchmark, where the experimental results illustrate its validity. The paper thus combines a theoretical characterization with concrete kernel examples and an application. Its broader relevance is to learning tasks in which objects are naturally described by their components and a suitable comparison is needed at the level of the complete object.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes positive-definite kernels based on merged component sets and demonstrates the approach on handwritten-digit classification.

title: Semigroup Kernels on Finite Sets

abstract: Recent work has led to the ability to perform space efﬁcient, approximate counting over large vocabularies in a streaming context. Motivated by the existence of data structures of this type, we explore the computation of associativity scores, other- wise known as pointwise mutual information (PMI), in a streaming context. We give theoretical bounds showing the impracticality of perfect online PMI compu- tation, and detail an algorithm with high expected accuracy. Experiments on news articles show our approach gives high accuracy on real world data.
originalAbstract: Recent work has led to the ability to perform space efﬁcient, approximate counting over large vocabularies in a streaming context. Motivated by the existence of data structures of this type, we explore the computation of associativity scores, other- wise known as pointwise mutual information (PMI), in a streaming context. We give theoretical bounds showing the impracticality of perfect online PMI compu- tation, and detail an algorithm with high expected accuracy. Experiments on news articles show our approach gives high accuracy on real world data.

paragraphs: Pointwise mutual information, or PMI, measures association by comparing how often items occur together with what their individual frequencies would suggest. This paper studies how to compute such scores when data arrive as a stream. The motivation comes from space-efficient approximate counting methods that can handle very large vocabularies without maintaining every count exactly.

Moving from counts to association scores raises a separate computational question: what accuracy is achievable online? The authors establish theoretical bounds showing that perfect online PMI computation is impractical. They then describe an algorithm with high expected accuracy, making approximation the basis of the proposed streaming solution.

Experiments on news articles show high accuracy on real-world data. That empirical result complements the theoretical argument: the bounds motivate giving up perfect computation, while the experiments indicate that the proposed approximation can still provide accurate association scores. The contribution is a treatment of PMI itself in the streaming setting, building on the availability of compact approximate counting structures.
summary.tldr: The paper shows why perfect streaming PMI is impractical and presents an approximation with high expected and observed accuracy.

title: Streaming Pointwise Mutual Information

abstract: We introduce the first temporal-difference learning algorithms that converge with smooth value function approximators, such as neural networks. Conventional temporal-difference (TD) methods, such as TD($\lambda$), Q-learning and Sarsa have been used successfully with function approximation in many applications. However, it is well known that off-policy sampling, as well as nonlinear function approximation, can cause these algorithms to become unstable (i.e., the parameters of the approximator may diverge). Sutton et al (2009a,b) solved the problem of off-policy learning with linear TD algorithms by introducing a new objective function, related to the Bellman-error, and algorithms that perform stochastic gradient-descent on this function. In this paper, we generalize their work to nonlinear function approximation. We present a Bellman error objective function and two gradient-descent TD algorithms that optimize it. We prove the asymptotic almost-sure convergence of both algorithms for any finite Markov decision process and any smooth value function approximator, under usual stochastic approximation conditions. The computational complexity per iteration scales linearly with the number of parameters of the approximator. The algorithms are incremental and are guaranteed to converge to locally optimal solutions.

We prove the asymptotic almost-sure convergence of both algorithms for any finite Markov decision process and any smooth value function approximator, under usual stochastic approximation conditions. The computational complexity per iteration scales linearly with the number of parameters of the approximator. The algorithms are incremental and are guaranteed to converge to locally optimal solutions.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning can become unstable when it uses nonlinear value approximators or learns from off-policy samples. Successful applications of conventional methods do not remove that possibility: their parameters may diverge. This paper extends an earlier gradient-based solution for linear approximation to smooth nonlinear approximators, including neural networks.

The authors introduce an objective related to Bellman error and two temporal-difference algorithms that optimize it through gradient descent. This provides a specific objective for the learning updates. The algorithms work incrementally, and their computational cost per iteration grows linearly with the number of parameters in the value approximator.

For finite Markov decision processes and smooth value approximators, the paper proves asymptotic almost-sure convergence under the usual stochastic approximation conditions. The algorithms are guaranteed to reach locally optimal solutions, so the result does not assert global optimality. The contribution is a conditional convergence foundation for nonlinear temporal-difference learning together with updates whose per-iteration cost scales directly with model size.
summary.tldr: Two gradient-based temporal-difference algorithms converge to local optima with smooth value approximators under stated stochastic approximation conditions.

title: Convergent Temporal-Difference Learning with Arbitrary Smooth Function Approximation

abstract: We pose transductive classification as a matrix completion problem. By assuming the underlying matrix has a low rank, our formulation is able to handle three problems simultaneously: i) multi-label learning, where each item has more than one label, ii) transduction, where most of these labels are unspecified, and iii) missing data, where a large number of features are missing. We obtained satisfactory results on several real-world tasks, suggesting that the low rank assumption may not be as restrictive as it seems. Our method allows for different loss functions to apply on the feature and label entries of the matrix. The resulting nuclear norm minimization problem is solved with a modified fixed-point continuation method that is guaranteed to find the global optimum.

paragraphs: This paper treats classification with incomplete information as a matrix completion problem. The matrix contains feature and label entries, some of which are missing. Assuming that the underlying matrix has low rank lets the method address multiple labels per item, unspecified labels in a transductive setting, and missing feature values within one formulation.

The low-rank assumption ties the completion of these different entries together. The method also permits different loss functions for features and labels, allowing the optimization to treat those two kinds of observations differently. It formulates the task through nuclear norm minimization and solves it using a modified fixed-point continuation method with a guarantee of reaching the global optimum.

Results on several real-world tasks are described as satisfactory, suggesting that the low-rank assumption may be useful beyond narrowly structured examples. That empirical conclusion remains qualified: the results suggest the assumption is less restrictive than it might appear. The main contribution is a common optimization framework for three forms of incomplete or multiple-output data.
summary.tldr: Low-rank matrix completion jointly handles multiple labels, unspecified labels, and missing features through an optimization method with a global-optimum guarantee.

title: Transduction with Matrix Completion: Three Birds with One Stone

abstract: Computing a {\em maximum a posteriori} (MAP) assignment in graphical models is a crucial inference problem for many practical applications. Several provably convergent approaches have been successfully developed using linear programming (LP) relaxation of the MAP problem. We present an alternative approach, which transforms the MAP problem into that of inference in a finite mixture of simple Bayes nets. We then derive the Expectation Maximization (EM) algorithm for this mixture that also monotonically increases a lower bound on the MAP assignment until convergence. The update equations for the EM algorithm are remarkably simple, both conceptually and computationally, and can be implemented using a graph-based message passing paradigm similar to max-product computation. We experiment on the real-world protein design dataset and show that EM's convergence rate is significantly higher than the previous LP relaxation based approach MPLP. EM achieves a solution quality within $95$\% of optimal for most instances and is often an order-of-magnitude faster than MPLP.

Several provably convergent approaches have been successfully developed using linear programming (LP) relaxation of the MAP problem. We present an alternative approach, which transforms the MAP problem into that of inference in a finite mixture of simple Bayes nets. We then derive the Expectation Maximization (EM) algorithm for this mixture that also monotonically increases a lower bound on the MAP assignment until convergence. The update equations for the EM algorithm are remarkably simple, both conceptually and computationally, and can be implemented using a graph-based message passing paradigm similar to max-product computation. We experiment on the real-world protein design dataset and show that EM's convergence rate is significantly higher than the previous LP relaxation based approach MPLP. EM achieves a solution quality within $95$\% of optimal for most instances and is often an order-of-magnitude faster than MPLP.

paragraphs: Maximum a posteriori estimation seeks the most probable joint assignment in a graphical model. This can be a difficult inference problem, and linear-programming relaxations provide one established route. The paper develops an alternative by transforming the MAP problem into inference in a finite mixture of simple Bayesian networks.

From this mixture formulation, the authors derive an Expectation Maximization algorithm. Its updates monotonically improve a lower bound associated with the MAP objective until convergence. The update equations are simple and can be implemented as messages passed through a graph, in a manner similar to max-product computation. This gives the reformulation a concrete computational procedure as well as a convergence property.

Experiments on a real-world protein design dataset compare the method with MPLP, an approach based on linear-programming relaxation. EM converges substantially faster, often by an order of magnitude, and reaches solution quality within 95 percent of optimal for most instances. These are empirical solution-quality results; the monotonic bound improvement itself does not establish exact optimality.
summary.tldr: Recasting MAP inference as mixture-model inference yields simple EM updates with monotonic bound improvement and fast empirical convergence.

title: MAP Estimation for Graphical Models by Likelihood Maximization

abstract: The use of machine learning algorithms frequently involves careful tuning of learning parameters and model hyperparameters. Unfortunately, this tuning is often a “black art” requiring expert experience, rules of thumb, or sometimes brute-force search. There is therefore great appeal for automatic approaches that can optimize the performance of any given learning algorithm to the problem at hand. In this work, we consider this problem through the framework of Bayesian optimization, in which a learning algorithm’s generalization performance is modeled as a sample from a Gaussian process (GP). We show that certain choices for the nature of the GP, such as the type of kernel and the treatment of its hyperparameters, can play a crucial role in obtaining a good optimizer that can achieve expert-level performance. We describe new algorithms that take into account the variable cost (duration) of learning algorithm experiments and that can leverage the presence of multiple cores for parallel experimentation. We show that these proposed algorithms improve on previous automatic procedures and can reach or surpass human expert-level optimization for many algorithms including Latent Dirichlet Allocation, Structured SVMs and convolutional neural networks.

paragraphs: Choosing learning parameters and model hyperparameters can require substantial expertise or repeated trial and error. This paper studies automated tuning through Bayesian optimization. It models a learning algorithm's generalization performance using a Gaussian process, providing a probabilistic representation of how performance changes across parameter choices.

The authors show that decisions within this performance model matter. In particular, the kernel and the treatment of the Gaussian process's own hyperparameters can play a crucial role in building an effective optimizer. They also develop algorithms that account for experiments taking different amounts of time and that use multiple cores to run experiments in parallel.

The reported results improve on previous automatic procedures and reach or exceed human-expert tuning performance for many algorithms, including latent Dirichlet allocation, structured support vector machines, and convolutional neural networks. These findings establish practical value across several model families. They also show why effective automatic tuning involves both statistical modeling choices and decisions about how to allocate experimental computation.
summary.tldr: Carefully designed Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization accounts for experiment duration and parallelism, reaching or exceeding expert tuning in reported applications.

title: Practical Bayesian Optimization of Machine Learning Algorithms

abstract: We develop a novel approach for supervised learning based on adaptively partitioning the feature space into different regions and learning local region-specific classifiers. We formulate an empirical risk minimization problem that incorporates both partitioning and classification in to a single global objective. We show that space partitioning can be equivalently reformulated as a supervised learning problem and consequently any discriminative learning method can be utilized in conjunction with our approach. Nevertheless, we consider locally linear schemes by learning linear partitions and linear region classifiers. Locally linear schemes can not only approximate complex decision boundaries and ensure low training error but also provide tight control on over-fitting and generalization error. We train locally linear classifiers by using LDA, logistic regression and perceptrons, and so our scheme is scalable to large data sizes and high-dimensions. We present experimental results demonstrating improved performance over state of the art classification techniques on benchmark datasets. We also show improved robustness to label noise.

Both the partition and the regional classifiers are learned through one global empirical-risk objective. This connects where the model makes distinctions with how it predicts within each resulting area.

The authors show that learning the partition can itself be reformulated as a supervised learning problem, allowing discriminative methods to be used within the framework. Their concrete focus is locally linear learning: linear partitions combined with linear classifiers. They use linear discriminant analysis, logistic regression, and perceptrons to train regional models.

Combining local linear rules can approximate complex decision boundaries while providing control over overfitting and generalization error. The paper also describes scalability to large datasets and high-dimensional inputs. Benchmark experiments report better performance than the compared classification techniques and improved robustness to label noise. The contribution is a unified way to adapt the regions and their predictors while retaining simple learning methods as building blocks.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning feature-space partitions and local classifiers yields flexible decision boundaries and reported robustness to label noise.

title: Local Supervised Learning through Space Partitioning

abstract: Selecting the right algorithm is an important problem in computer science, because the algorithm often has to exploit the structure of the input to be efficient. The human mind faces the same challenge. Therefore, solutions to the algorithm selection problem can inspire models of human strategy selection and vice versa. Here, we view the algorithm selection problem as a special case of metareasoning and derive a solution that outperforms existing methods in sorting algorithm selection. We apply our theory to model how people choose between cognitive strategies and test its prediction in a behavioral experiment. We find that people quickly learn to adaptively choose between cognitive strategies. People's choices in our experiment are consistent with our model but inconsistent with previous theories of human strategy selection. Rational metareasoning appears to be a promising framework for reverse-engineering how people choose among cognitive strategies and translating the results into better solutions to the algorithm selection problem.

paragraphs: Choosing an algorithm involves more than knowing which methods can solve a problem. An efficient choice can depend on the structure of the particular input. This paper connects that computational problem with a psychological one: how people select a cognitive strategy when several approaches are available.

The authors treat algorithm selection as metareasoning, meaning reasoning about which reasoning procedure to use. They derive a selection method from this perspective and report that it outperforms existing methods for choosing sorting algorithms. The contribution therefore includes a concrete computational application as well as a proposed explanation of human behavior.

summary.tldr: A metareasoning approach improves sorting-algorithm selection and matches adaptive human strategy choices in a behavioral experiment.

title: Algorithm selection by rational metareasoning as a model of human strategy selection

abstract: Precision-Recall analysis abounds in applications of binary classification where true negatives do not add value and hence should not affect assessment of the classifier's performance. Perhaps inspired by the many advantages of receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and the area under such curves for accuracy-based performance assessment, many researchers have taken to report Precision-Recall (PR) curves and associated areas as performance metric. We demonstrate in this paper that this practice is fraught with difficulties, mainly because of incoherent scale assumptions -- e.g., the area under a PR curve takes the arithmetic mean of precision values whereas the $F_{\beta}$ score applies the harmonic mean. We show how to fix this by plotting PR curves in a different coordinate system, and demonstrate that the new Precision-Recall-Gain curves inherit all key advantages of ROC curves. In particular, the area under Precision-Recall-Gain curves conveys an expected $F_1$ score on a harmonic scale, and the convex hull of a Precision-Recall-Gain curve allows us to calibrate the classifier's scores so as to determine, for each operating point on the convex hull, the interval of $\beta$ values for which the point optimises $F_{\beta}$. We demonstrate experimentally that the area under traditional PR curves can easily favour models with lower expected $F_1$ score than others, and so the use of Precision-Recall-Gain curves will result in better model selection.

The paper identifies a problem with summarizing these curves by their area: the calculation averages precision arithmetically, while F-scores combine quantities harmonically. The new representation addresses this concrete mismatch in model selection and operating-point choice.
summary.tldr: Precision-Recall-Gain curves align area-based assessment with a harmonic-scale expected F1 score and support Fβ-based operating-point selection.

title: Precision-Recall-Gain Curves: PR Analysis Done Right

abstract: Stochastic search algorithms are general black-box optimizers. Due to their ease of use and their generality, they have recently also gained a lot of attention in operations research, machine learning and policy search. Yet, these algorithms require a lot of evaluations of the objective, scale poorly with the problem dimension, are affected by highly noisy objective functions and may converge prematurely. To alleviate these problems, we introduce a new surrogate-based stochastic search approach. We learn simple, quadratic surrogate models of the objective function. As the quality of such a quadratic approximation is limited, we do not greedily exploit the learned models. The algorithm can be misled by an inaccurate optimum introduced by the surrogate. Instead, we use information theoretic constraints to bound the `distance' between the new and old data distribution while maximizing the objective function. Additionally the new method is able to sustain the exploration of the search distribution to avoid premature convergence. We compare our method with state of art black-box optimization methods on standard uni-modal and multi-modal optimization functions, on simulated planar robot tasks and a complex robot ball throwing task.The proposed method considerably outperforms the existing approaches.

paragraphs: Stochastic search can optimize objectives treated as black boxes, making it broadly useful. However, it may require many objective evaluations, struggle as dimension increases, react poorly to noise, or settle too early. This paper introduces a surrogate-based approach intended to alleviate these problems by learning simple quadratic approximations to the objective.

The method does not simply move toward the optimum predicted by its surrogate. Because a quadratic model can be inaccurate, that optimum may be misleading. Instead, information-theoretic constraints limit how far the new search distribution can move from the previous one while seeking improved objective values. The method also sustains exploration to counter premature convergence.

The authors compare the approach with existing black-box optimizers on standard functions with one or multiple modes, simulated planar robot tasks, and a complex robot ball-throwing task. They report considerable improvements over the compared methods. The contribution combines inexpensive model guidance with controlled distribution updates, so a learned approximation can guide search without being treated as a fully reliable description of the objective.
summary.tldr: Quadratic surrogate models guide stochastic search through constrained distribution updates that preserve exploration and improve performance in the reported comparisons.

title: Model-Based Relative Entropy Stochastic Search

abstract: We study the problem of multiclass classification with an extremely large number of classes (k), with the goal of obtaining train and test time complexity logarithmic in the number of classes. We develop top-down tree construction approaches for constructing logarithmic depth trees. On the theoretical front, we formulate a new objective function, which is optimized at each node of the tree and creates dynamic partitions of the data which are both pure (in terms of class labels) and balanced. We demonstrate that under favorable conditions, we can construct logarithmic depth trees that have leaves with low label entropy. However, the objective function at the nodes is challenging to optimize computationally. We address the empirical problem with a new online decision tree construction procedure. Experiments demonstrate that this online algorithm quickly achieves improvement in test error compared to more common logarithmic training time approaches, which makes it a plausible method in computationally constrained large-k applications.

paragraphs: Classification becomes computationally demanding when the number of possible classes is extremely large. This paper targets training and prediction costs that grow logarithmically with the class count. It approaches the problem through trees built from the top down, seeking shallow decision paths that still separate labels effectively.

The authors introduce an objective for each tree node that encourages partitions to be both balanced and pure in their class labels. Balance supports short paths, while purity means the resulting groups contain less label uncertainty. Under favorable conditions, they show that logarithmic-depth trees can have leaves with low label entropy. The node objective itself, however, is computationally difficult to optimize.

To address the practical optimization problem, the paper develops an online tree-construction procedure. Experiments show that it quickly improves test error relative to more common approaches with logarithmic training time. These findings make the method a plausible option for large-class applications with limited computation, while the theoretical construction guarantee remains conditional on favorable circumstances.
summary.tldr: An online tree-building method targets logarithmic multiclass prediction costs through balanced, label-pure partitions.

title: Logarithmic Time Online Multiclass prediction

abstract: The reparameterization gradient has become a widely used method to obtain Monte Carlo gradients to optimize the variational objective. However, this technique does not easily apply to commonly used distributions such as beta or gamma without further approximations, and most practical applications of the reparameterization gradient fit Gaussian distributions. In this paper, we introduce the generalized reparameterization gradient, a method that extends the reparameterization gradient to a wider class of variational distributions. Generalized reparameterizations use invertible transformations of the latent variables which lead to transformed distributions that weakly depend on the variational parameters. This results in new Monte Carlo gradients that combine reparameterization gradients and score function gradients. We demonstrate our approach on variational inference for two complex probabilistic models. The generalized reparameterization is effective: even a single sample from the variational distribution is enough to obtain a low-variance gradient.

paragraphs: Variational inference uses an adjustable probability distribution to approximate a probabilistic model's unknown quantities. Optimizing that approximation often requires gradients estimated from random samples. The reparameterization gradient is useful for this purpose, but the standard technique does not readily handle distributions such as beta and gamma without further approximations.

This paper extends the technique using invertible transformations of latent variables. After transformation, the resulting distribution is allowed to retain a weak dependence on the variational parameters. Accounting for that dependence produces a gradient estimator that combines reparameterization and score-function components. This construction broadens the class of variational distributions that the approach can accommodate.

The authors demonstrate the method on variational inference for two complex probabilistic models. They report low-variance gradients even when using only one sample from the variational distribution. This finding supports the method's effectiveness in the demonstrated settings; it does not establish a universal single-sample guarantee for every model. The contribution is a more flexible gradient construction that reduces the restriction imposed by conventional reparameterization methods.
summary.tldr: Generalized reparameterization combines pathwise and score-function gradients to support a wider range of variational distributions.

title: The Generalized Reparameterization Gradient

abstract: This paper explores image caption generation using conditional variational auto-encoders (CVAEs). Standard CVAEs with a fixed Gaussian prior yield descriptions with too little variability. Instead, we propose two models that explicitly structure the latent space around K components corresponding to different types of image content, and combine components to create priors for images that contain multiple types of content simultaneously (e.g., several kinds of objects). Our first model uses a Gaussian Mixture model (GMM) prior, while the second one defines a novel Additive Gaussian (AG) prior that linearly combines component means. We show that both models produce captions that are more diverse and more accurate than a strong LSTM baseline or a “vanilla” CVAE with a fixed Gaussian prior, with AG-CVAE showing particular promise.

paragraphs: An image can support several accurate descriptions, so a captioning system needs useful variation as well as correctness. This paper explores conditional variational autoencoders for that purpose. The authors identify a fixed Gaussian prior as a source of insufficient variation in the descriptions generated by standard versions of these models.

They propose two alternatives that organize the latent space around K components associated with different kinds of image content. Components can be combined to form priors for images containing several content types at once. One model uses a Gaussian mixture prior. The other introduces an Additive Gaussian prior, which combines component means linearly.

This construction gives the prior an explicit relationship to the mixture of content present in an image. In the reported comparisons, both models produce captions that are more varied and more accurate than a strong LSTM baseline and a standard conditional variational autoencoder with a fixed Gaussian prior. The Additive Gaussian version is especially promising, suggesting that compositional prior structure can improve both goals together.
summary.tldr: Content-structured Gaussian priors help variational image-captioning models produce descriptions that are both more diverse and more accurate in reported comparisons.

title: Diverse and Accurate Image Description Using a Variational Auto-Encoder with an Additive Gaussian Encoding Space

abstract: The variational autoencoder (VAE) is a popular model for density estimation and representation learning. Canonically, the variational principle suggests to prefer an expressive inference model so that the variational approximation is accurate. However, it is often overlooked that an overly-expressive inference model can be detrimental to the test set performance of both the amortized posterior approximator and, more importantly, the generative density estimator. In this paper, we leverage the fact that VAEs rely on amortized inference and propose techniques for amortized inference regularization (AIR) that control the smoothness of the inference model. We demonstrate that, by applying AIR, it is possible to improve VAE generalization on both inference and generative performance. Our paper challenges the belief that amortized inference is simply a mechanism for approximating maximum likelihood training and illustrates that regularization of the amortization family provides a new direction for understanding and improving generalization in VAEs.

paragraphs: A variational autoencoder learns both a generative model and an inference model that approximates hidden-variable distributions for observations. A common motivation for making the inference model more expressive is to improve that approximation. This paper points out that greater expressiveness can also hurt performance on unseen data, affecting both inference and the learned generative density estimator.

The proposed approach, amortized inference regularization, uses the fact that one learned inference mechanism is shared across observations. Its techniques control the smoothness of that mechanism. This makes the behavior of the inference model across inputs an explicit part of regularization, rather than treating approximation accuracy as its only desirable property.

The authors demonstrate that AIR can improve generalization in both posterior approximation and generative performance. The claim is that regularization can help, not that a less expressive inference model always wins. More broadly, the findings suggest that amortized inference influences how a VAE generalizes, giving researchers another component to shape when improving the model.
summary.tldr: Regularizing the smoothness of a VAE’s shared inference model can improve generalization in both inference and generation.

title: Amortized Inference Regularization

abstract: Language is dynamic, constantly evolving and adapting with respect to time, domain or topic. The adaptability of language is an active research area, where researchers discover social, cultural and domain-specific changes in language using distributional tools such as word embeddings. In this paper, we introduce the global anchor method for detecting corpus-level language shifts. We show both theoretically and empirically that the global anchor method is equivalent to the alignment method, a widely-used method for comparing word embeddings, in terms of detecting corpus-level language shifts. Despite their equivalence in terms of detection abilities, we demonstrate that the global anchor method is superior in terms of applicability as it can compare embeddings of different dimensionalities. Furthermore, the global anchor method has implementation and parallelization advantages. We show that the global anchor method reveals fine structures in the evolution of language and domain adaptation. When combined with the graph Laplacian technique, the global anchor method recovers the evolution trajectory and domain clustering of disparate text corpora.

paragraphs: Language changes across time, domains, and topics, and word embeddings offer a way to study those differences. This paper introduces the global anchor method for measuring shifts at the level of whole text collections. Its target is the relationship between corpora, including how language evolves and how domains differ.

The authors show theoretically and empirically that global anchors and the widely used embedding-alignment approach are equivalent in their ability to detect corpus-level shifts. Global anchors nevertheless offer broader applicability because they can compare embeddings with different numbers of dimensions. The abstract also identifies advantages for implementation and parallelization, making the equivalent detection capability available through a more flexible comparison method.

The method reveals fine structure in language evolution and domain adaptation. Combined with a graph Laplacian technique, it recovers evolutionary trajectories and domain clusters among disparate corpora. These findings show how pairwise linguistic comparisons can support a broader picture of relationships across collections. The claimed advantage over alignment concerns applicability and computation, alongside equivalent shift-detection ability.
summary.tldr: Global anchors detect corpus-level language shifts as effectively as alignment while accommodating embeddings of different dimensionalities.

title: The Global Anchor Method for Quantifying Linguistic Shifts and Domain Adaptation

abstract: Probability estimation is one of the fundamental tasks in statistics and machine learning. However, standard methods for probability estimation on discrete objects do not handle object structure in a satisfactory manner. In this paper, we derive a general Bayesian network formulation for probability estimation on leaf-labeled trees that enables flexible approximations which can generalize beyond observations. We show that efficient algorithms for learning Bayesian networks can be easily extended to probability estimation on this challenging structured space. Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our methods greatly outperform the current practice of using the empirical distribution, as well as a previous effort for probability estimation on trees.

However, standard methods for probability estimation on discrete objects do not handle object structure in a satisfactory manner. In this paper, we derive a general Bayesian network formulation for probability estimation on leaf-labeled trees that enables flexible approximations which can generalize beyond observations. We show that efficient algorithms for learning Bayesian networks can be easily extended to probability estimation on this challenging structured space. Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our methods greatly outperform the current practice of using the empirical distribution, as well as a previous effort for probability estimation on trees.

paragraphs: Estimating probabilities over structured objects requires more than counting how often each complete object appears. This paper focuses on trees whose leaves carry labels. An empirical distribution captures the observed trees, but does not itself provide a way to use their internal structure to generalize beyond those observations.

The authors derive a general Bayesian-network formulation for probability estimation on this space. The formulation supports flexible approximations that can assign probabilities beyond the specific trees seen in the data. Its central purpose is to make the structure of trees part of the probability model, rather than treating every complete tree as an unrelated discrete outcome.

A further contribution is showing that efficient Bayesian-network learning algorithms extend naturally to this structured estimation problem. Experiments using synthetic and real data report large improvements over the empirical distribution and an earlier tree-probability method. These results support the value of learning reusable structural relationships when estimating probabilities over trees, while the formulation connects the problem to an existing family of learning algorithms.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian-network formulation estimates probabilities over leaf-labeled trees and generalizes beyond the trees observed during training.

title: Generalizing Tree Probability Estimation via Bayesian Networks

abstract: Optimal transport (\OT) theory defines a powerful set of tools to compare probability distributions. \OT~suffers however from a few drawbacks, computational and statistical, which have encouraged the proposal of several regularized variants of OT in the recent literature, one of the most notable being the \textit{sliced} formulation, which exploits the closed-form formula between univariate distributions by projecting high-dimensional measures onto random lines. We consider in this work a more general family of ground metrics, namely \textit{tree metrics}, which also yield fast closed-form computations and negative definite, and of which the sliced-Wasserstein distance is a particular case (the tree is a chain). We propose the tree-sliced Wasserstein distance, computed by averaging the Wasserstein distance between these measures using random tree metrics, built adaptively in either low or high-dimensional spaces. Exploiting the negative definiteness of that distance, we also propose a positive definite kernel, and test it against other baselines on a few benchmark tasks.

We consider in this work a more general family of ground metrics, namely \textit{tree metrics}, which also yield fast closed-form computations and negative definite, and of which the sliced-Wasserstein distance is a particular case (the tree is a chain). Exploiting the negative definiteness of that distance, we also propose a positive definite kernel, and test it against other baselines on a few benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: Optimal transport provides ways to compare probability distributions, but its computational and statistical difficulties motivate simpler variants. Sliced Wasserstein distance takes advantage of easy one-dimensional calculations by projecting distributions onto random lines. This paper extends that strategy to a broader family of underlying distance structures based on trees.

Tree metrics also permit fast closed-form Wasserstein calculations. A line corresponds to a chain-shaped tree, so the familiar sliced construction fits within this broader perspective. The proposed tree-sliced distance averages Wasserstein comparisons across random tree metrics. These trees are built adaptively and can be used in either low-dimensional or high-dimensional spaces.

The authors also exploit the distance's negative definiteness to construct a positive definite kernel, connecting the distribution comparison to kernel-based methods. They test that kernel against baselines on several benchmark tasks. The central contribution is therefore a broader computationally convenient geometry for comparing distributions, together with a kernel construction. The abstract reports evaluation but does not state a particular benchmark advantage.
summary.tldr: Tree-sliced Wasserstein distances average efficient transport comparisons over random tree metrics and support a positive definite kernel.

title: Tree-Sliced Variants of Wasserstein Distances

abstract: Leveraging the wealth of unlabeled data produced in recent years provides great potential for improving supervised models. When the cost of acquiring labels is high, probabilistic active learning methods can be used to greedily select the most informative data points to be labeled. However, for many large-scale problems standard greedy procedures become computationally infeasible and suffer from negligible model change. In this paper, we introduce a novel Bayesian batch active learning approach that mitigates these issues. Our approach is motivated by approximating the complete data posterior of the model parameters. While naive batch construction methods result in correlated queries, our algorithm produces diverse batches that enable efficient active learning at scale. We derive interpretable closed-form solutions akin to existing active learning procedures for linear models, and generalize to arbitrary models using random projections. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach on several large-scale regression and classification tasks.

However, for many large-scale problems standard greedy procedures become computationally infeasible and suffer from negligible model change. In this paper, we introduce a novel Bayesian batch active learning approach that mitigates these issues. paragraphs: Active learning chooses which unlabeled examples should receive costly labels. Standard probabilistic methods often make these choices greedily, selecting individual examples judged informative. At large scale, the paper argues, this process can become computationally impractical while producing only small changes in the model. Simply collecting individually attractive choices into a batch can also produce correlated queries.

The authors instead formulate Bayesian batch selection around approximating the posterior distribution over model parameters that the complete data would provide. This gives batch construction a collective target: choose a subset whose information represents the larger collection. Their algorithm produces diverse batches, addressing redundancy among the requested labels while supporting efficient active learning at scale.

For linear models, the approach yields interpretable closed-form solutions related to existing active learning procedures. Random projections extend the approach to arbitrary models. Experiments on several large-scale regression and classification tasks demonstrate benefits, supporting the usefulness of selecting informative batches jointly through a posterior-approximation perspective.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian posterior-approximation approach selects diverse batches of examples for efficient active learning at scale.

title: Bayesian Batch Active Learning as Sparse Subset Approximation

abstract: Lipschitz continuity is a central requirement for achieving the optimal O(1/T) rate of convergence in monotone, deterministic variational inequalities (a setting that includes convex minimization, convex-concave optimization, nonatomic games, and many other problems). However, in many cases of practical interest, the operator defining the variational inequality may become singular at the boundary of the feasible region, precluding in this way the use of fast gradient methods that attain this rate (such as Nemirovski's mirror-prox algorithm and its variants). To address this issue, we propose a novel smoothness condition which we call Bregman smoothness, and which relates the variation of the operator to that of a suitably chosen Bregman function. Leveraging this condition, we derive an adaptive mirror prox algorithm which attains an O(1/T) rate of convergence in problems with possibly singular operators, without any prior knowledge of the problem's Bregman constant (the Bregman analogue of the Lipschitz constant). We also present an extension of our algorithm to stochastic variational inequalities where the algorithm achieves a $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ convergence rate.

Fast methods for monotone deterministic problems typically rely on Lipschitz continuity, which controls how quickly the defining operator changes. Operators that become singular near the feasible region's boundary can violate this requirement.

The paper introduces Bregman smoothness as an alternative way to control operator variation. Instead of measuring that variation through the usual Lipschitz condition, it relates it to a suitably chosen Bregman function. This allows the analysis to reflect a geometry that can accommodate some boundary singularities.

The method does not require advance knowledge of the corresponding Bregman constant. The guarantee applies to problems satisfying the proposed condition, including possibly singular operators. A stochastic extension achieves O(1/√T), extending the framework to settings with randomness while providing a different convergence guarantee.
summary.tldr: Bregman smoothness enables adaptive Mirror-Prox convergence guarantees for problems whose operators may be singular at the boundary.

title: An adaptive Mirror-Prox method for variational inequalities with singular operators

abstract: With the rapid developments of deep neural networks, numerous deep cross-modal analysis methods have been presented and are being applied in widespread real-world applications, including healthcare and safety-critical environments. However, the recent studies on robustness and stability of deep neural networks show that a microscopic modification, known as adversarial sample, which is even imperceptible to humans, can easily fool a well-performed deep neural network and brings a new obstacle to deep cross-modal correlation exploring. In this paper, we propose a novel Cross-Modal correlation Learning with Adversarial samples, namely CMLA, which for the first time presents the existence of adversarial samples in cross-modal data. Moreover, we provide a simple yet effective adversarial sample learning method, where inter- and intra- modality similarity regularizations across different modalities are simultaneously integrated into the learning of adversarial samples. Finally, our proposed CMLA is demonstrated to be highly effective in cross-modal hashing based retrieval. Extensive experiments on two cross-modal benchmark datasets show that the adversarial examples produced by our CMLA are efficient in fooling a target deep cross-modal hashing network. On the other hand, such adversarial examples can significantly strengthen the robustness of the target network by conducting an adversarial training.

paragraphs: Cross-modal learning connects information across different forms of data. The paper examines whether networks learning these connections can be fooled by tiny input changes, extending the concern about adversarial examples to cross-modal analysis. Its focus is retrieval using cross-modal hashing, where learned representations support finding related items across modalities.

The proposed method, CMLA, learns adversarial samples while incorporating two kinds of similarity constraints. One concerns relationships within a modality, and the other concerns relationships across modalities. Bringing both into adversarial sample learning ties the perturbations to the relationships that the target system is meant to capture.

The same examples also have a defensive use: incorporating them into adversarial training substantially improves the target network's robustness. The contribution therefore links a demonstrated vulnerability with a training method that strengthens the evaluated system against adversarial samples, rather than treating attack generation as an end in itself.
summary.tldr: CMLA generates effective adversarial examples for cross-modal retrieval and uses them in training to improve the target network's robustness.

title: Cross-Modal Learning with Adversarial Samples

abstract: Several recent publications report advances in training optimal decision trees (ODTs) using mixed-integer programs (MIPs), due to algorithmic advances in integer programming and a growing interest in addressing the inherent suboptimality of heuristic approaches such as CART. In this paper, we propose a novel MIP formulation, based on 1-norm support vector machine model, to train a binary oblique ODT for classification problems. We further present techniques, such as cutting planes, to tighten its linear relaxation, to improve run times to reach optimality. Using 36 datasets from the University of California Irvine Machine Learning Repository, we demonstrate that our training approach outperforms its counterparts from literature in terms of out-of-sample performance (around 10% improvement in mean out-of-sample testing accuracy). Towards our goal of developing a scalable framework to train multivariate ODT on large datasets, we propose a new linear programming based data selection method to choose a subset of the data, and use it to train a decision tree through our proposed MIP model. We conclude this paper with extensive numerical testing results, that showcase the generalization performance of our new MIP formulation, and the improvement in mean out-of-sample accuracy on large datasets.

paragraphs: Decision trees are often trained using rules that make convenient choices along the way, which can leave the final tree short of the best solution. This paper instead formulates training as a mixed-integer optimization problem. It targets binary classification trees whose splits can combine several input features, allowing more flexible decision boundaries.

The proposed formulation builds on a support vector machine model using a 1-norm. The authors also introduce techniques, including cutting planes, that strengthen the relaxed optimization problem and shorten the time needed to reach optimality. This matters because the usefulness of explicitly optimizing an entire tree depends partly on whether the resulting computation is manageable.

Across 36 datasets from the UCI repository, the authors report around a 10% improvement in mean testing accuracy over methods from the literature. For larger datasets, they additionally use linear programming to select a training subset. Their numerical results support both the formulation's generalization performance and the usefulness of this data-selection approach for improving mean accuracy at larger scales.
summary.tldr: A mixed-integer formulation and data-selection method make optimal multivariate decision-tree training more scalable while improving reported testing accuracy.

title: A Scalable MIP-based Method for Learning Optimal Multivariate Decision Trees

abstract: We consider the problem of robust and adaptive model predictive control (MPC) of a linear system, with unknown parameters that are learned along the way (adaptive), in a critical setting where failures must be prevented (robust). This problem has been studied from different perspectives by different communities. However, the existing theory deals only with the case of quadratic costs (the LQ problem), which limits applications to stabilisation and tracking tasks only. In order to handle more general (non-convex) costs that naturally arise in many practical problems, we carefully select and bring together several tools from different communities, namely non-asymptotic linear regression, recent results in interval prediction, and tree-based planning. Combining and adapting the theoretical guarantees at each layer is non trivial, and we provide the first end-to-end suboptimality analysis for this setting. Interestingly, our analysis naturally adapts to handle many models and combines with a data-driven robust model selection strategy, which enables to relax the modelling assumptions. Last, we strive to preserve tractability at any stage of the method, that we illustrate on two challenging simulated environments.

paragraphs: The paper studies model predictive control for a linear system whose parameters are initially unknown and learned during operation. The authors seek to extend theory beyond quadratic costs to more general, potentially nonconvex objectives arising in practical control problems.

Their method combines non-asymptotic linear regression, interval prediction, and tree-based planning. These components address learning the system, describing uncertain predictions, and selecting actions. The main theoretical challenge is making their guarantees work together. The authors provide an end-to-end suboptimality analysis for this setting, linking the different layers to a bound on the quality of the resulting control.

The analysis also accommodates multiple models and combines with data-driven robust model selection, allowing the modeling assumptions to be relaxed. Throughout, the authors aim to keep computation tractable and illustrate the method in two challenging simulated environments. The contribution brings learning, uncertainty handling, and planning into a shared analysis for control objectives beyond the quadratic case.
summary.tldr: A combined learning-and-planning approach provides end-to-end suboptimality analysis for robust adaptive linear control with general, potentially nonconvex costs.

title: Robust-Adaptive Control of Linear Systems: beyond Quadratic Costs

abstract: Ensembles over neural network weights trained from different random initialization, known as deep ensembles, achieve state-of-the-art accuracy and calibration. The recently introduced batch ensembles provide a drop-in replacement that is more parameter efficient. In this paper, we design ensembles not only over weights, but over hyperparameters to improve the state of the art in both settings. For best performance independent of budget, we propose hyper-deep ensembles, a simple procedure that involves a random search over different hyperparameters, themselves stratified across multiple random initializations. Its strong performance highlights the benefit of combining models with both weight and hyperparameter diversity. We further propose a parameter efficient version, hyper-batch ensembles, which builds on the layer structure of batch ensembles and self-tuning networks. The computational and memory costs of our method are notably lower than typical ensembles. On image classification tasks, with MLP, LeNet, ResNet 20 and Wide ResNet 28-10 architectures, we improve upon both deep and batch ensembles.

paragraphs: Deep ensembles combine neural networks trained from different random initializations, providing strong accuracy and calibration. This paper asks whether ensemble members should also differ in their hyperparameters. Its central proposal is to combine diversity in learned weights with diversity in the settings used to train the models.

For performance without prioritizing a computational budget, the authors introduce hyper-deep ensembles. The procedure performs random hyperparameter search across multiple random initializations. For greater parameter efficiency, they introduce hyper-batch ensembles, which build on the layer structure of batch ensembles and self-tuning networks. This second version has notably lower computational and memory costs than typical ensembles.

summary.tldr: Combining hyperparameter diversity with weight diversity improves image-classification ensembles, with a parameter-efficient variant reducing resource costs.

title: Hyperparameter Ensembles for Robustness and Uncertainty Quantification

abstract: One of the main challenges in using deep learning-based methods for simulating physical systems and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) is formulating physics-based data in the desired structure for neural networks. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have gained popularity in this area since graphs offer a natural way of modeling particle interactions and provide a clear way of discretizing the continuum models. However, the graphs constructed for approximating such tasks usually ignore long-range interactions due to unfavorable scaling of the computational complexity with respect to the number of nodes. The errors due to these approximations scale with the discretization of the system, thereby not allowing for generalization under mesh-refinement. Inspired by the classical multipole methods, we purpose a novel multi-level graph neural network framework that captures interaction at all ranges with only linear complexity. Our multi-level formulation is equivalent to recursively adding inducing points to the kernel matrix, unifying GNNs with multi-resolution matrix factorization of the kernel. Experiments confirm our multi-graph network learns discretization-invariant solution operators to PDEs and can be evaluated in linear time.
