paragraphs: Graph neural networks offer a natural representation for physical interactions and discretized partial differential equations. However, including long-range interactions can be computationally expensive as the number of nodes grows. Omitting those interactions introduces errors that depend on discretization, making it difficult for a learned model to generalize when the mesh is refined.

Inspired by classical multipole methods, the paper proposes a multilevel graph network that captures interactions at all ranges with linear computational complexity. Its hierarchy connects the graph formulation to a matrix perspective: the construction is equivalent to recursively introducing inducing points into a kernel matrix. This links graph learning with multiresolution factorization.

Experiments show that the resulting network learns solution operators that are invariant to discretization and can be evaluated in linear time. The findings connect two goals that otherwise conflict: retaining interactions across distance and keeping computation manageable. In the reported experiments, the representation supports PDE solution prediction across discretizations rather than tying the learned operator to a particular mesh.
summary.tldr: A multilevel graph network captures short- and long-range physical interactions in linear time and empirically learns discretization-invariant PDE solution operators.

title: Multipole Graph Neural Operator for Parametric Partial Differential Equations

abstract: Motivated by pricing applications in online advertising, we study a variant of linear regression with a discontinuous loss function that we term Myersonian regression. In this variant, we wish to find a linear function $f : \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ that well approximates a set of points $(x_i, v_i) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times [0, 1]$ in the following sense: we receive a loss of $v_i$ when $f(x_i) > v_i$ and a loss of $v_i - f(x_i)$ when $f(x_i) \leq v_i$. This arises naturally in the economic application of designing a pricing policy for differentiated items (where the loss is the gap between the performance of our policy and the optimal Myerson prices). We show that Myersonian regression is NP-hard to solve exactly and furthermore that no fully polynomial-time approximation scheme exists for Myersonian regression conditioned on the Exponential Time Hypothesis being true. In contrast to this, we demonstrate a polynomial-time approximation scheme for Myersonian regression that obtains an $\epsilon m$ additive approximation to the optimal possible revenue and can be computed in time $O(\exp(\mathrm{poly}(1/\epsilon))\poly(m, n))$. We show that this algorithm is stable and generalizes well over distributions of samples.

paragraphs: Pricing errors are asymmetric: a price above a buyer’s value can lose the entire opportunity, while a lower price leaves some revenue uncollected. Motivated by online-advertising pricing, this paper studies linear regression with a discontinuous loss reflecting that distinction.

For an example with value v, the loss is v if the prediction exceeds v, and otherwise v minus the prediction. The authors prove exact optimization is NP-hard and, assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis, rule out a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme.

They nevertheless obtain a polynomial-time approximation scheme with additive error epsilon times the number of examples in revenue. Its dependence on inverse accuracy is exponential in a polynomial, while its dependence on input size is polynomial. The algorithm is also shown to be stable and to generalize over sample distributions. These results characterize an accuracy-computation tradeoff, rather than promising efficient exact optimization.
summary.tldr: Myersonian regression formalizes pricing-sensitive linear prediction and gives approximation and hardness results.

title: Myersonian Regression

abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) enables researchers to automatically explore broad design spaces in order to improve efficiency of neural networks. This efficiency is especially important in the case of on-device deployment, where improvements in accuracy should be balanced out with computational demands of a model. In practice, performance metrics of model are computationally expensive to obtain. Previous work uses a proxy (e.g., number of operations) or a layer-wise measurement of neural network layers to estimate end-to-end hardware performance but the imprecise prediction diminishes the quality of NAS. To address this problem, we propose BRP-NAS, an efficient hardware-aware NAS enabled by an accurate performance predictor-based on graph convolutional network (GCN). What is more, we investigate prediction quality on different metrics and show that sample efficiency of the predictor-based NAS can be improved by considering binary relations of models and an iterative data selection strategy. We show that our proposed method outperforms all prior methods on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201, and that our predictor can consistently learn to extract useful features from the DARTS search space, improving upon the second-order baseline. Finally, to raise awareness of the fact that accurate latency estimation is not a trivial task, we release LatBench -- a latency dataset of NAS-Bench-201 models running on a broad range of devices.

paragraphs: BRP-NAS addresses a practical difficulty in automated neural network design: evaluating candidate architectures is expensive, and simple estimates of hardware performance can be inaccurate. For deployment on a device, accuracy must be balanced against computational demands. Counting operations or adding measurements from individual layers can give an imperfect picture of how the whole network performs.

The method uses a graph convolutional network to predict architecture performance and guide hardware-aware search. It also investigates prediction across different metrics. To make better use of evaluated candidates, it considers binary relationships between models and an iterative strategy for selecting data. The aim is to improve search efficiency by learning useful comparisons and choosing informative evaluations.

The authors report outperforming prior methods on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201. They also find that the predictor learns useful features in the DARTS search space and improves upon its second-order baseline. Alongside the method, they release LatBench, containing latency measurements across a broad range of devices, emphasizing that accurate hardware prediction is itself an important part of architecture search.
summary.tldr: BRP-NAS uses graph-based performance prediction, model comparisons, and iterative data selection to improve hardware-aware neural architecture search.

title: BRP-NAS: Prediction-based NAS using GCNs

abstract: Causal discovery aims to recover causal structures or models underlying the observed data. Despite its success in certain domains, most existing methods focus on causal relations between observed variables, while in many scenarios the observed ones may not be the underlying causal variables (e.g., image pixels), but are generated by latent causal variables or confounders that are causally related. To this end, in this paper, we consider Linear, Non-Gaussian Latent variable Models (LiNGLaMs), in which latent confounders are also causally related, and propose a Generalized Independent Noise (GIN) condition to estimate such latent variable graphs. Specifically, for two observed random vectors $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$, GIN holds if and only if $\omega^{\intercal}\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ are statistically independent, where $\omega$ is a parameter vector characterized from the cross-covariance between $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$. From the graphical view, roughly speaking, GIN implies that causally earlier latent common causes of variables in $\mathbf{Y}$ d-separate $\mathbf{Y}$ from $\mathbf{Z}$. Interestingly, we find that the independent noise condition, i.e., if there is no confounder, causes are independent from the error of regressing the effect on the causes, can be seen as a special case of GIN. Moreover, we show that GIN helps locate latent variables and identify their causal structure, including causal directions. We further develop a recursive learning algorithm to achieve these goals. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Observed measurements may be effects of hidden causal variables rather than the variables whose relationships we want to discover. This paper studies linear, non-Gaussian latent variable models in which hidden confounders can themselves be causally related. Its goal is to locate those latent variables and recover their causal structure, including directions.

The proposed Generalized Independent Noise condition examines two vectors of observed variables. It holds when a linear combination of one vector is statistically independent of the other, with the combination characterized using their cross-covariance. Roughly, the graphical interpretation connects this independence to earlier latent common causes separating the two observed groups.

The familiar independence between causes and regression errors in the absence of confounding appears as a special case. The authors use the generalized condition to develop a recursive learning algorithm and show its effectiveness on synthetic and real data. The contribution extends independence-based causal reasoning to related hidden causes within the stated linear, non-Gaussian model class.
summary.tldr: A generalized noise-independence condition supports discovery of hidden variables and causal directions in linear, non-Gaussian latent models.

title: Generalized Independent Noise Condition for Estimating Latent Variable Causal Graphs

abstract: Continual learning agents experience a stream of (related) tasks. The main challenge is that the agent must not forget previous tasks and also adapt to novel tasks in the stream. We are interested in the intersection of two recent continual-learning scenarios. In meta-continual learning, the model is pre-trained using meta-learning to minimize catastrophic forgetting of previous tasks. In continual-meta learning, the aim is to train agents for faster remembering of previous tasks through adaptation. In their original formulations, both methods have limitations. We stand on their shoulders to propose a more general scenario, OSAKA, where an agent must quickly solve new (out-of-distribution) tasks, while also requiring fast remembering. We show that current continual learning, meta-learning, meta-continual learning, and continual-meta learning techniques fail in this new scenario. We propose Continual-MAML, an online extension of the popular MAML algorithm as a strong baseline for this scenario. We show in an empirical study that Continual-MAML is better suited to the new scenario than the aforementioned methodologies including standard continual learning and meta-learning approaches.

paragraphs: A continual learner must adapt to new tasks while preserving access to earlier knowledge. OSAKA brings these demands together in a scenario requiring rapid learning of out-of-distribution tasks and rapid remembering of previous ones. It builds on two research directions that combine meta-learning with continual learning in different ways.

One direction uses meta-learning before continual learning to reduce forgetting. The other trains agents to recover previous tasks quickly through adaptation. The authors argue that their original formulations have limitations and propose OSAKA as a more general setting. In their study, existing continual learning, meta-learning, and combined approaches fail to meet the demands of this scenario.

The paper introduces Continual-MAML, an online extension of MAML, as a strong baseline. Empirical comparisons find it better suited to OSAKA than the evaluated alternatives. The contribution therefore includes both a setting that tests adaptation and remembering together and an algorithm designed for those combined demands. The reported advantage establishes empirical suitability for this scenario rather than a universal solution to continual learning.
summary.tldr: OSAKA tests rapid adaptation and remembering together, with Continual-MAML providing a stronger empirical baseline than the evaluated alternatives.

title: Online Fast Adaptation and Knowledge Accumulation (OSAKA): a New Approach to Continual Learning

abstract: We reformulate the Wasserstein Discriminant Analysis (WDA) as a ratio trace problem and present an eigensolver-based algorithm to compute the discriminative subspace of WDA. This new formulation, along with the proposed algorithm, can be served as an efficient and more stable alternative to the original trace ratio formulation and its gradient-based algorithm. We provide a rigorous convergence analysis for the proposed algorithm under the self-consistent field framework, which is crucial but missing in the literature. As an application, we combine WDA with low-dimensional clustering techniques, such as K-means, to perform subspace clustering. Numerical experiments on real datasets show promising results of the ratio trace formulation of WDA in both classification and clustering tasks.

paragraphs: Wasserstein Discriminant Analysis seeks a discriminative subspace for representing data. This paper changes the mathematical formulation used to compute that subspace, replacing the original trace-ratio problem with a ratio-trace problem. The closely related names conceal a consequential change: the reformulation supports a different approach to optimization.

The proposed algorithm uses an eigensolver and is presented as an efficient, more stable alternative to the original gradient-based method. The authors also supply a rigorous convergence analysis within the self-consistent field framework. This adds theoretical support for the computation, addressing a convergence-analysis gap identified in the earlier literature.

The paper applies the learned representation to subspace clustering by combining WDA with low-dimensional clustering methods such as K-means. Numerical experiments on real datasets show promising results for both classification and clustering. Together, these contributions connect a reformulated objective, an analyzed numerical algorithm, and downstream uses of the resulting subspace, while keeping the empirical claim at the level of promising observed performance.
summary.tldr: A ratio-trace reformulation gives Wasserstein Discriminant Analysis an eigensolver-based algorithm with convergence analysis and promising classification and clustering results.

title: Ratio Trace Formulation of Wasserstein Discriminant Analysis

abstract: We study the statistical problem of estimating a rank-one sparse tensor corrupted by additive gaussian noise, a Gaussian additive model also known as sparse tensor PCA. We show that for Bernoulli and Bernoulli-Rademacher distributed signals and \emph{for all} sparsity levels which are sublinear in the dimension of the signal, the sparse tensor PCA model exhibits a phase transition called the \emph{all-or-nothing phenomenon}. This is the property that for some signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) $\mathrm{SNR_c}$ and any fixed $\epsilon>0$, if the SNR of the model is below $\left(1-\epsilon\right)\mathrm{SNR_c}$, then it is impossible to achieve any arbitrarily small constant correlation with the hidden signal, while if the SNR is above $\left(1+\epsilon \right)\mathrm{SNR_c}$, then it is possible to achieve almost perfect correlation with the hidden signal. The all-or-nothing phenomenon was initially established in the context of sparse linear regression, and over the last year also in the context of sparse 2-tensor (matrix) PCA and Bernoulli group testing. Our results follow from a more general result showing that for any Gaussian additive model with a discrete uniform prior, the all-or-nothing phenomenon follows as a direct outcome of an appropriately defined ``near-orthogonality" property of the support of the prior distribution.

paragraphs: Sparse tensor PCA seeks a hidden rank-one sparse tensor from observations corrupted by additive Gaussian noise. This paper studies how recoverability changes with the signal-to-noise ratio. It establishes an abrupt statistical transition for Bernoulli and Bernoulli–Rademacher signals across all sparsity levels that grow sublinearly with signal dimension.

Below a fixed relative margin from a critical signal-to-noise threshold, recovering even an arbitrarily small constant correlation with the hidden signal is impossible. Above a fixed relative margin, almost perfect correlation becomes possible. This is the all-or-nothing phenomenon: the stated asymptotic regimes separate essentially uninformative recovery from nearly complete recovery.

The tensor result follows from a more general theorem for Gaussian additive models with discrete uniform priors. An appropriately defined near-orthogonality property of the prior's support is sufficient to produce the transition. The contribution therefore identifies both a broad sparse-tensor recovery phenomenon and a geometric condition that can explain it in other models covered by the theorem. These are statistical possibility and impossibility results, with the signal assumptions and threshold margins forming part of their scope.
summary.tldr: Sparse tensor PCA has an all-or-nothing recovery threshold for specified signal distributions and sublinear sparsity, explained by a sufficient near-orthogonality condition.

title: The All-or-Nothing Phenomenon in Sparse Tensor PCA

abstract: In this paper, we propose an end-to-end graph learning framework, namely \textbf{I}terative \textbf{D}eep \textbf{G}raph \textbf{L}earning (\alg), for jointly and iteratively learning graph structure and graph embedding. The key rationale of \alg is to learn a better graph structure based on better node embeddings, and vice versa (i.e., better node embeddings based on a better graph structure). Our iterative method dynamically stops when the learned graph structure approaches close enough to the graph optimized for the downstream prediction task. In addition, we cast the graph learning problem as a similarity metric learning problem and leverage adaptive graph regularization for controlling the quality of the learned graph. Finally, combining the anchor-based approximation technique, we further propose a scalable version of \alg, namely \salg, which significantly reduces the time and space complexity of \alg without compromising the performance. Our extensive experiments on nine benchmarks show that our proposed \alg models can consistently outperform or match the state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, \alg can be more robust to adversarial graphs and cope with both transductive and inductive learning.

Furthermore, \alg can be more robust to adversarial graphs and cope with both transductive and inductive learning.

paragraphs: Iterative Deep Graph Learning jointly learns a graph's structure and representations of its nodes. Its guiding idea is reciprocal improvement: more useful node representations can reveal better connections, and better connections can support more useful representations. This makes the graph itself part of the learning process for the downstream prediction task.

The method repeatedly updates structure and embeddings, stopping dynamically when the learned structure is sufficiently close to the graph optimized for the task. It treats graph construction as learning a similarity metric and uses adaptive regularization to control the resulting graph's quality. An additional version uses anchor-based approximation to reduce both time and memory requirements without compromising reported performance.

Experiments across nine benchmarks show that the models consistently match or outperform state-of-the-art comparison methods. The paper also reports that the approach can be more robust to adversarial graphs and can handle both transductive and inductive learning. These findings support refining connectivity alongside representations rather than taking graph structure as a fixed input throughout training.
summary.tldr: Iteratively refining graph structure and node embeddings improves prediction, with a scalable approximation and reported robustness benefits.

title: Iterative Deep Graph Learning for Graph Neural Networks: Better and Robust Node Embeddings

abstract: Graphs have been widely adopted to denote structural connections between entities. The relations are in many cases heterogeneous, but entangled together and denoted merely as a single edge between a pair of nodes. For example, in a social network graph, users in different latent relationships like friends and colleagues, are usually connected via a bare edge that conceals such intrinsic connections. In this paper, we introduce a novel graph convolutional network (GCN), termed as factorizable graph convolutional network (FactorGCN), that explicitly disentangles such intertwined relations encoded in a graph. FactorGCN takes a simple graph as input, and disentangles it into several factorized graphs, each of which represents a latent and disentangled relation among nodes. The features of the nodes are then aggregated separately in each factorized latent space to produce disentangled features, which further leads to better performances for downstream tasks. We evaluate the proposed FactorGCN both qualitatively and quantitatively on the synthetic and real-world datasets, and demonstrate that it yields truly encouraging results in terms of both disentangling and feature aggregation. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/ihollywhy/FactorGCN.PyTorch.

paragraphs: A graph edge can hide several kinds of relationships between the same entities. In a social network, for example, a connection might represent friendship, a working relationship, or both. Treating every connection as a single undifferentiated relation leaves those underlying distinctions entangled when a graph neural network aggregates information.

FactorGCN takes a simple graph and separates it into several factorized graphs, each representing a latent relationship among nodes. It then aggregates node features separately within the corresponding latent spaces. The resulting features are intended to preserve distinctions between relationships rather than combining all connected information in one shared aggregation.

The authors evaluate the model qualitatively and quantitatively on synthetic and real-world datasets. They report encouraging results for separating relations and aggregating features, together with improved downstream performance. These findings support learning relational structure that is not explicitly labeled in the input graph. The method's central contribution is to make that inferred structure part of how node representations are constructed.
summary.tldr: FactorGCN separates graph connections into latent relation types and aggregates features within each to improve learned representations.

title: Factorizable Graph Convolutional Networks

abstract: Policy makers often need to estimate the long-term effects of novel treatments, while only having historical data of older treatment options. We propose a surrogate-based approach using a long-term dataset where only past treatments were administered and a short-term dataset where novel treatments have been administered. Our approach generalizes previous surrogate-style methods, allowing for continuous treatments and serially-correlated treatment policies while maintaining consistency and root-n asymptotically normal estimates under a Markovian assumption on the data and the observational policy. Using a semi-synthetic dataset on customer incentives from a major corporation, we evaluate the performance of our method and discuss solutions to practical challenges when deploying our methodology.

paragraphs: Estimating a new treatment’s long-term effect is difficult when only older treatments have long-term follow-up. This paper combines two complementary datasets: historical observations with long-term outcomes and observations of novel treatments with only short-term outcomes. Its surrogate-based approach uses short-term information to connect the evidence available in these two settings.

The method extends earlier surrogate approaches to allow continuous treatments and treatment policies that are correlated across time. These extensions broaden the kinds of treatment sequences the analysis can accommodate. Under a Markovian assumption on both the data and the observational policy, the authors establish consistency and root-n asymptotic normality for their estimates.

Consistency describes convergence toward the target effect as data increase, while the asymptotic result characterizes estimation uncertainty at the root-n scale. These are conditional statistical guarantees tied to the stated Markovian assumption. The authors evaluate the method on a semi-synthetic customer-incentive dataset from a major corporation and discuss deployment challenges. The contribution is a framework for using historical follow-up to inform estimates for treatments whose own long-term outcomes are not yet observed.
summary.tldr: A surrogate-based estimator combines historical long-term outcomes with new-treatment short-term data, with statistical guarantees under a Markovian assumption.

title: Estimating the Long-Term Effects of Novel Treatments

abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have attracted more and more attentions in recent years. A typical GCN layer consists of a linear feature propagation step and a nonlinear transformation step. Recent works show that a linear GCN can achieve comparable performance to the original non-linear GCN while being much more computationally efficient. In this paper, we dissect the feature propagation steps of linear GCNs from a perspective of continuous graph diffusion, and analyze why linear GCNs fail to benefit from more propagation steps. Following that, we propose Decoupled Graph Convolution (DGC) that decouples the terminal time and the feature propagation steps, making it more flexible and capable of exploiting a very large number of feature propagation steps. Experiments demonstrate that our proposed DGC improves linear GCNs by a large margin and makes them competitive with many modern variants of non-linear GCNs.

Following that, we propose Decoupled Graph Convolution (DGC) that decouples the terminal time and the feature propagation steps, making it more flexible and capable of exploiting a very large number of feature propagation steps. paragraphs: A graph convolutional network typically combines the propagation of features across a graph with nonlinear transformations. Earlier work showed that linear versions can deliver comparable performance with substantially less computation. This paper investigates a remaining difficulty: adding more propagation steps to a linear graph network does not necessarily improve its results.

The authors interpret feature propagation through continuous graph diffusion. This perspective distinguishes the terminal time of diffusion from the number of steps used to carry it out. Their proposed Decoupled Graph Convolution, or DGC, separates those two choices, giving the model more flexibility and allowing it to exploit a very large number of propagation steps.

Experiments show large improvements over the linear graph networks considered and competitive performance against many modern nonlinear variants. The significance is that propagation depth becomes a more useful design choice once it is separated from diffusion duration. The work therefore uses an analysis of the propagation process to improve a computationally efficient class of graph models.
summary.tldr: DGC improves linear graph networks by separating diffusion duration from the number of feature-propagation steps.

title: Dissecting the Diffusion Process in Linear Graph Convolutional Networks

abstract: Adder neural networks (AdderNets) have shown impressive performance on image classification with only addition operations, which are more energy efficient than traditional convolutional neural networks built with multiplications. Compared with classification, there is a strong demand on reducing the energy consumption of modern object detectors via AdderNets for real-world applications such as autonomous driving and face detection. In this paper, we present an empirical study of AdderNets for object detection. We first reveal that the batch normalization statistics in the pre-trained adder backbone should not be frozen, since the relatively large feature variance of AdderNets. Moreover, we insert more shortcut connections in the neck part and design a new feature fusion architecture for avoiding the sparse features of adder layers. We present extensive ablation studies to explore several design choices of adder detectors. Comparisons with state-of-the-arts are conducted on COCO and PASCAL VOC benchmarks. Specifically, the proposed Adder FCOS achieves a 37.8% AP on the COCO val set, demonstrating comparable performance to that of the convolutional counterpart with an about $1.4\times$ energy reduction.

paragraphs: Adder neural networks replace multiplication-based computations with additions, offering a route to lower energy consumption. This paper investigates whether their success in image classification can extend to object detection. Detection requires both recognizing objects and locating them, so the study examines how to adapt the network components used for that task.

The authors identify an important training choice: batch normalization statistics in the pretrained adder backbone should continue updating. These results support the practical potential of addition-based detection when its training and feature-processing architecture are adapted appropriately.
summary.tldr: Adapting normalization and feature fusion lets an addition-based object detector achieve comparable accuracy with lower energy consumption.

title: An Empirical Study of Adder Neural Networks for Object Detection

abstract: We study reinforcement learning (RL) with linear function approximation. Existing algorithms for this problem only have high-probability regret and/or Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) sample complexity guarantees, which cannot guarantee the convergence to the optimal policy. In this paper, in order to overcome the limitation of existing algorithms, we propose a new algorithm called FLUTE, which enjoys uniform-PAC convergence to the optimal policy with high probability. The uniform-PAC guarantee is the strongest possible guarantee for reinforcement learning in the literature, which can directly imply both PAC and high probability regret bounds, making our algorithm superior to all existing algorithms with linear function approximation. At the core of our algorithm is a novel minimax value function estimator and a multi-level partition scheme to select the training samples from historical observations. Both of these techniques are new and of independent interest.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning guarantees can describe accumulated regret or the amount of experience needed to reach a specified accuracy. The paper argues that the existing guarantees for linear function approximation do not by themselves ensure convergence to an optimal policy. It introduces FLUTE to obtain a stronger, uniform-PAC form of assurance.

FLUTE combines a minimax value-function estimator with a multilevel partition scheme that selects training samples from historical observations. These mechanisms address both how values are estimated and how past experience is organized for learning. The authors identify both techniques as contributions that may be useful independently of the complete algorithm.

The resulting uniform-PAC guarantee establishes convergence to the optimal policy with high probability and directly implies PAC and high-probability regret bounds. The improvement is therefore in the strength and coverage of the theoretical guarantee for reinforcement learning with linear function approximation. It connects eventual policy convergence with other familiar assurances, while retaining the probabilistic qualification rather than asserting success on every possible learning run.
summary.tldr: FLUTE provides uniform-PAC convergence to an optimal policy with high probability for reinforcement learning with linear function approximation.

title: Uniform-PAC Bounds for Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation

abstract: Efficiently approximating local curvature information of the loss function is a useful tool for the optimization and compression of deep neural networks. Yet, most existing methods to approximate second-order information have high computational or storage costs, limiting their practicality. In this work, we investigate matrix-free approaches for estimating Inverse-Hessian Vector Products (IHVPs) for the case when the Hessian can be approximated as a sum of rank-one matrices, as in the classic approximation of the Hessian by the empirical Fisher matrix. The first algorithm we propose is tailored towards network compression and can compute the IHVP for dimension $d$ given a fixed set of $m$ rank-one matrices using $O(dm^2)$ precomputation, $O(dm)$ cost for computing the IHVP and query cost $O(m)$ for computing any single element of the inverse Hessian approximation. The second algorithm targets an optimization setting, where we wish to compute the product between the inverse Hessian, estimated over a sliding window of optimization steps, and a given gradient direction. We give an algorithm with cost $O(dm + m^2)$ for computing the IHVP and $O(dm + m^3)$ for adding or removing any gradient from the sliding window. We show that both algorithms yield competitive results for network pruning and optimization, respectively, with significantly lower computational overhead relative to existing second-order methods.

paragraphs: Second-order information can improve neural-network optimization and pruning, but its storage and computation can be prohibitive. M-FAC studies matrix-free inverse-Hessian vector products when the Hessian is approximated by a sum of rank-one matrices, as in an empirical-Fisher approximation.

For compression with dimension d and m fixed rank-one terms, the first algorithm uses O(dm²) precomputation, O(dm) per vector product, and O(m) to query an individual inverse-matrix element. A second algorithm handles a sliding optimization window, with O(dm + m²) per product and O(dm + m³) to add or remove a gradient.

Experiments show competitive pruning and optimization results with substantially lower overhead than existing second-order methods. These costs apply to the specified approximation and data structures, not an arbitrary exact Hessian. The abstract does not give numerical accuracy or runtime comparisons, but clearly separates the compression and online-optimization use cases.
summary.tldr: M-FAC computes inverse-Hessian vector products without explicitly storing the full curvature matrix.

title: M-FAC: Efficient Matrix-Free Approximations of Second-Order Information

abstract: The worst-case training principle that minimizes the maximal adversarial loss, also known as adversarial training (AT), has shown to be a state-of-the-art approach for enhancing adversarial robustness. Nevertheless, min-max optimization beyond the purpose of AT has not been rigorously explored in the adversarial context. In this paper, we show how a general notion of min-max optimization over multiple domains can be leveraged to the design of different types of adversarial attacks. In particular, given a set of risk sources, minimizing the worst-case attack loss can be reformulated as a min-max problem by introducing domain weights that are maximized over the probability simplex of the domain set. We showcase this unified framework in three attack generation problems -- attacking model ensembles, devising universal perturbation under multiple inputs, and crafting attacks resilient to data transformations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach leads to substantial attack improvement over the existing heuristic strategies as well as robustness improvement over state-of-the-art defense methods against multiple perturbation types. Furthermore, we find that the self-adjusted domain weights learned from min-max optimization can provide a holistic tool to explain the difficulty level of attack across domains.

paragraphs: An adversarial attack may need to succeed across several conditions: different models, different inputs, or transformations of the same input. This paper asks how to handle these competing requirements within a shared optimization framework. It extends the use of min-max optimization beyond adversarial training to the construction of attacks themselves.

The method assigns weights to a collection of domains representing different sources of attack difficulty. These weights are nonnegative and sum to one. Maximizing over the weights expresses a worst-case attack loss, while minimizing that loss seeks an attack that addresses the difficult domains. The authors apply the framework to model ensembles, universal perturbations shared across inputs, and attacks designed to withstand data transformations.

Experiments report substantial attack improvements over existing heuristic approaches, alongside robustness improvements over leading defense methods against multiple perturbation types. The learned weights also offer information about which domains make an attack difficult. The framework therefore supplies both an optimization strategy and a way to interpret how attack difficulty is distributed across the conditions being considered.
summary.tldr: A unified min-max framework improves attacks across models, inputs, and transformations by automatically weighting difficult domains.

title: Adversarial Attack Generation Empowered by Min-Max Optimization

abstract: Lévy flights describe a special class of random walks whose step sizes satisfy a power-law tailed distribution. As being an efficientsearching strategy in unknown environments, Lévy flights are widely observed in animal foraging behaviors. Recent studies further showed that human cognitive functions also exhibit the characteristics of Lévy flights. Despite being a general phenomenon, the neural mechanism at the circuit level for generating Lévy flights remains unresolved. Here, we investigate how Lévy flights can be achieved in attractor neural networks. To elucidate the underlying mechanism clearly, we first study continuous attractor neural networks (CANNs), and find that noisy neural adaptation, exemplified by spike frequency adaptation (SFA) in this work, can generate Lévy flights representing transitions of the network state in the attractor space. Specifically, the strength of SFA defines a travelling wave boundary, below which the network state displays local Brownian motion, and above which the network state displays long-jump motion. Noises in neural adaptation causes the network state to intermittently switch between these two motion modes, manifesting the characteristics of Lévy flights. We further extend the study to a general attractor neural network, and demonstrate that our model can explain the Lévy-flight phenomenon observed during free memory retrieval of humans. We hope that this study will give us insight into understanding the neural mechanism for optimal information processing in the brain.

paragraphs: Lévy flights are random walks that combine many short movements with occasional large jumps through a heavy-tailed step-size distribution. Such patterns appear in animal search and human cognition, but their circuit-level origin remains unresolved. This paper investigates whether noisy adaptation within attractor neural networks can generate this kind of movement in the network’s internal state.

The authors first study continuous attractor networks with spike-frequency adaptation. Adaptation strength defines a boundary between local Brownian movement and long-jump movement. Noise in adaptation causes intermittent switching between these modes, producing Lévy-flight characteristics. The proposed mechanism therefore links a particular source of neural variability to the mixture of movement scales.

The study then extends the mechanism to a more general attractor network. The authors demonstrate that their model can explain Lévy-flight patterns observed during human free memory retrieval. This offers a possible neural account of those observations and connects circuit dynamics to cognitive search behavior. It does not establish that noisy adaptation is the unique mechanism underlying all Lévy-flight phenomena.
summary.tldr: Noisy neural adaptation can generate Lévy-flight-like state transitions by switching attractor networks between local motion and long jumps.

title: Noisy Adaptation Generates Lévy Flights in Attractor Neural Networks

abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have pushed the state-of-the-art for various visual recognition tasks by patch-wise image tokenization followed by self-attention. However, the employment of self-attention modules results in a quadratic complexity in both computation and memory usage. Various attempts on approximating the self-attention computation with linear complexity have been made in Natural Language Processing. However, an in-depth analysis in this work shows that they are either theoretically flawed or empirically ineffective for visual recognition. We further identify that their limitations are rooted in keeping the softmax self-attention during approximations. Specifically, conventional self-attention is computed by normalizing the scaled dot-product between token feature vectors. Keeping this softmax operation challenges any subsequent linearization efforts. Based on this insight, for the first time, a softmax-free transformer or SOFT is proposed. To remove softmax in self-attention, Gaussian kernel function is used to replace the dot-product similarity without further normalization. This enables a full self-attention matrix to be approximated via a low-rank matrix decomposition. The robustness of the approximation is achieved by calculating its Moore-Penrose inverse using a Newton-Raphson method. Extensive experiments on ImageNet show that our SOFT significantly improves the computational efficiency of existing ViT variants. Crucially, with a linear complexity, much longer token sequences are permitted in SOFT, resulting in superior trade-off between accuracy and complexity.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers use self-attention to relate image tokens, but conventional attention requires computation and memory that grow quadratically with sequence length. The contribution combines a change to attention's underlying similarity computation with an approximation strategy designed around that change, rather than treating the approximation independently of attention's normalization.
summary.tldr: SOFT replaces softmax attention with a Gaussian-kernel formulation that supports linear-complexity approximation and improved visual-recognition efficiency.

title: SOFT: Softmax-free Transformer with Linear Complexity

abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved human-level capabilities in various learning tasks. However, they generally lose performance in more realistic scenarios like learning in a continual manner. In contrast, humans can incorporate their prior knowledge to learn new concepts efficiently without forgetting older ones. In this work, we leverage meta-learning to encourage the model to learn how to learn continually. Inspired by human concept learning, we develop a generative classifier that efficiently uses data-driven experience to learn new concepts even from few samples while being immune to forgetting. Along with cognitive and theoretical insights, extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The ability to remember all previous concepts, with negligible computational and structural overheads, suggests that generative models provide a natural way for alleviating catastrophic forgetting, which is a major drawback of discriminative models.

paragraphs: Learning new concepts sequentially can cause a neural network to lose competence on concepts it learned earlier. This paper addresses that continual-learning problem through meta-learning: it trains a model to acquire a way of learning that supports continued adaptation. The aim is to use prior experience efficiently while preserving previously acquired concepts.

Inspired by human concept learning, the authors develop a generative classifier that uses data-driven experience to learn new concepts from few examples. They describe the proposed method as immune to forgetting and able to retain all previous concepts. The architectural choice places generative classification at the center of their approach to continual learning.

The paper supports the method with cognitive and theoretical insights alongside extensive experiments on standard benchmarks. It reports effective learning and retention with negligible computational and structural overhead. Together, these findings suggest that generative models offer a useful route for alleviating catastrophic forgetting. That broader implication is presented as a direction supported by the proposed method, rather than a guarantee about every generative model.
summary.tldr: A meta-learned generative classifier learns new concepts from few examples while retaining previous concepts with negligible overhead.

title: Generative vs. Discriminative: Rethinking The Meta-Continual Learning

abstract: Domain adaptation (DA) benefits from the rigorous theoretical works that study its insightful characteristics and various aspects, e.g., learning domain-invariant representations and its trade-off. However, it seems not the case for the multiple source DA and domain generalization (DG) settings which are remarkably more complicated and sophisticated due to the involvement of multiple source domains and potential unavailability of target domain during training. In this paper, we develop novel upper-bounds for the target general loss which appeal us to define two kinds of domain-invariant representations. We further study the pros and cons as well as the trade-offs of enforcing learning each domain-invariant representation. Finally, we conduct experiments to inspect the trade-off of these representations for offering practical hints regarding how to use them in practice and explore other interesting properties of our developed theory.

paragraphs: Learning from several source domains creates a transfer problem: a representation must support predictions in a target domain while handling differences among the sources. Domain generalization adds another complication because the target may be unavailable during training. This paper studies domain-invariant representations in these multiple-source settings, where the theoretical picture is more complicated than in simpler adaptation problems.

The authors derive new upper bounds on target generalization loss. These bounds motivate two kinds of domain-invariant representation and provide a basis for examining their advantages, disadvantages, and trade-offs. The central question is how enforcing each type of invariance affects the objective of transferring successfully to the target.

Experiments investigate the trade-offs identified by the theory and explore additional properties of the bounds. Their stated purpose is to provide practical guidance on using these representations. The contribution is therefore a framework for reasoning about different forms of invariance in multiple-source learning, together with empirical examination of their consequences, rather than a claim that enforcing invariance always improves transfer.
summary.tldr: New target-loss bounds reveal two forms of domain invariance and their trade-offs in transfer learning from multiple sources.

title: On Learning Domain-Invariant Representations for Transfer Learning with Multiple Sources

abstract: Learning with neural networks relies on the complexity of their representable functions, but more importantly, their particular assignment of typical parameters to functions of different complexity. Taking the number of activation regions as a complexity measure, recent works have shown that the practical complexity of deep ReLU networks is often far from the theoretical maximum. In this work, we show that this phenomenon also occurs in networks with maxout (multi-argument) activation functions and when considering the decision boundaries in classification tasks. We also show that the parameter space has a multitude of full-dimensional regions with widely different complexity, and obtain nontrivial lower bounds on the expected complexity. Finally, we investigate different parameter initialization procedures and show that they can increase the speed of convergence in training.

paragraphs: A neural network’s maximum expressive power does not tell us how complex its behavior will usually be. The paper studies this distinction for maxout networks, using the number of activation regions as a measure of complexity. Its focus is on how parameter choices distribute networks across functions of different complexity, rather than only on the most elaborate function an architecture can represent.

The authors show that practical complexity can fall far below theoretical maximum complexity, extending a phenomenon previously observed in deep ReLU networks. They also find this behavior when examining classification decision boundaries. In parameter space, many full-dimensional regions correspond to widely differing complexity levels, so this variation is not confined to isolated parameter choices.

The work also establishes nontrivial lower bounds on expected complexity, complementing the observation that maximum-based descriptions can be misleading. Finally, it investigates initialization procedures and shows that these can accelerate training convergence. Together, the findings connect representational complexity with the parameter choices that shape a network’s starting point and learning behavior.
summary.tldr: Maxout networks can have practical complexity far below their theoretical maximum, and initialization choices can speed training convergence.

title: On the Expected Complexity of Maxout Networks

abstract: A key challenge for reinforcement learning is solving long-horizon planning problems. Recent work has leveraged programs to guide reinforcement learning in these settings. However, these approaches impose a high manual burden on the user since they must provide a guiding program for every new task. Partially observed environments further complicate the programming task because the program must implement a strategy that correctly, and ideally optimally, handles every possible configuration of the hidden regions of the environment. We propose a new approach, model predictive program synthesis (MPPS), that uses program synthesis to automatically generate the guiding programs. It trains a generative model to predict the unobserved portions of the world, and then synthesizes a program based on samples from this model in a way that is robust to its uncertainty. In our experiments, we show that our approach significantly outperforms non-program-guided approaches on a set of challenging benchmarks, including a 2D Minecraft-inspired environment where the agent must complete a complex sequence of subtasks to achieve its goal, and achieves a similar performance as using handcrafted programs to guide the agent. Our results demonstrate that our approach can obtain the benefits of program-guided reinforcement learning without requiring the user to provide a new guiding program for every new task.

paragraphs: Long-horizon reinforcement learning often requires an agent to complete a sequence of subtasks before reaching its goal. Programs can provide useful guidance, but manually writing a new program for each task creates substantial work. Partial observability makes that work harder because a guiding strategy must account for parts of the environment that the agent cannot yet see.

Model predictive program synthesis automates the creation of those guiding programs. It trains a generative model to predict hidden portions of the world, samples possible configurations from that model, and synthesizes a program that is robust to the modeled uncertainty. The generated guidance therefore incorporates several possible hidden situations instead of relying on a single assumed configuration.

On challenging benchmarks, including a two-dimensional Minecraft-inspired environment with complex subtask sequences, the approach significantly outperforms methods without program guidance. It also performs similarly to guidance from handcrafted programs. These experiments show that automatically synthesized guidance can retain the practical benefits of program-guided learning while removing the need for a user to supply a fresh guiding program for each new task.
summary.tldr: Model predictive program synthesis automatically creates uncertainty-aware guidance that matches handcrafted-program performance in the reported reinforcement-learning benchmarks.

title: Program Synthesis Guided Reinforcement Learning for Partially Observed Environments

abstract: We present a new behavioural distance over the state space of a Markov decision process, and demonstrate the use of this distance as an effective means of shaping the learnt representations of deep reinforcement learning agents. While existing notions of state similarity are typically difficult to learn at scale due to high computational cost and lack of sample-based algorithms, our newly-proposed distance addresses both of these issues. In addition to providing detailed theoretical analyses, we provide empirical evidence that learning this distance alongside the value function yields structured and informative representations, including strong results on the Arcade Learning Environment benchmark.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent learns an internal representation of the states it encounters. This paper asks how a measure of behavioral similarity between states can help shape that representation. It introduces a new distance over the state space of a Markov decision process, with the goal of making state similarity useful in deep reinforcement learning.

Existing similarity measures can be costly to learn and may lack algorithms that work directly from samples. The proposed distance addresses both obstacles. The authors provide theoretical analysis and use the distance as a learning objective alongside the value function. This gives representation learning an additional signal about relationships between states, beyond the signal supplied by value estimation alone.

The empirical results indicate that jointly learning this distance and the value function produces structured, informative representations. The paper also reports strong results on the Arcade Learning Environment benchmark. Its contribution connects a behavioral notion of state similarity with a sample-based learning procedure, making that notion more practical to incorporate into the training of deep reinforcement learning agents.
summary.tldr: MICo introduces a sample-based behavioral distance that helps deep reinforcement learning agents learn more informative state representations.

title: MICo: Improved representations via sampling-based state similarity for Markov decision processes

abstract: Cancer patients experience high rates of chronic pain throughout the treatment process. Assessing pain for this patient population is a vital component of psychological and functional well-being, as it can cause a rapid deterioration of quality of life. Existing work in facial pain detection often have deficiencies in labeling or methodology that prevent them from being clinically relevant. This paper introduces the first chronic cancer pain dataset, collected as part of the Intelligent Sight and Sound (ISS) clinical trial, guided by clinicians to help ensure that model findings yield clinically relevant results. The data collected to date consists of 29 patients, 509 smartphone videos, 189,999 frames, and self-reported affective and activity pain scores adopted from the Brief Pain Inventory (BPI). Using static images and multi-modal data to predict self-reported pain levels, early models show significant gaps between current methods available to predict pain today, with room for improvement. Due to the especially sensitive nature of the inherent Personally Identifiable Information (PII) of facial images, the dataset will be released under the guidance and control of the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

paragraphs: The paper introduces a dataset for studying chronic pain in people receiving cancer treatment. summary.tldr: A clinician-guided cancer pain dataset pairs smartphone recordings with patient-reported pain scores and reveals room to improve automated prediction.

title: Intelligent Sight and Sound: A Chronic Cancer Facial Pain Dataset

abstract: Learned optimizers---neural networks that are trained to act as optimizers---have the potential to dramatically accelerate training of machine learning models. However, even when meta-trained across thousands of tasks at huge computational expense, blackbox learned optimizers often struggle with stability and generalization when applied to tasks unlike those in their meta-training set. In this paper, we use tools from dynamical systems to investigate the inductive biases and stability properties of optimization algorithms, and apply the resulting insights to designing inductive biases for blackbox optimizers. Our investigation begins with a noisy quadratic model, where we characterize conditions in which optimization is stable, in terms of eigenvalues of the training dynamics. We then introduce simple modifications to a learned optimizer's architecture and meta-training procedure which lead to improved stability, and improve the optimizer's inductive bias. We apply the resulting learned optimizer to a variety of neural network training tasks, where it outperforms the current state of the art learned optimizer---at matched optimizer computational overhead---with regard to optimization performance and meta-training speed, and is capable of generalization to tasks far different from those it was meta-trained on.

paragraphs: A learned optimizer is a neural network trained to update another model's parameters. Such optimizers could accelerate training, but learning from many tasks does not automatically make them reliable on unfamiliar ones. This paper investigates how their built-in preferences, or inductive biases, affect both stability and transfer to different training problems.

The authors examine optimization through dynamical systems: they study how repeated updates evolve over time. Starting with a noisy quadratic model, they characterize stability conditions using eigenvalues of the training dynamics. They then use those insights to introduce simple changes to a learned optimizer's architecture and the procedure used to train it across tasks.

Across the neural network training tasks studied, the resulting optimizer improves optimization performance and meta-training speed relative to the leading learned optimizer, with optimizer computational overhead matched. It also transfers to tasks substantially different from its meta-training tasks. The contribution connects analysis of a simplified optimization setting to practical design choices that improve the tested optimizer's behavior.
summary.tldr: Dynamical-systems analysis guides changes to a learned optimizer that improve its stability, training performance, and transfer to unfamiliar tasks.

title: A Closer Look at Learned Optimization: Stability, Robustness, and Inductive Biases

abstract: This work studies operators mapping vector and scalar fields defined over a manifold $\mathcal{M}$, and which commute with its group of diffeomorphisms $\text{Diff}(\mathcal{M})$. We prove that in the case of scalar fields $L^p_\omega(\mathcal{M,\mathbb{R}})$, those operators correspond to point-wise non-linearities, recovering and extending known results on $\mathbb{R}^d$. In the context of Neural Networks defined over $\mathcal{M}$, it indicates that point-wise non-linear operators are the only universal family that commutes with any group of symmetries, and justifies their systematic use in combination with dedicated linear operators commuting with specific symmetries. In the case of vector fields $L^p_\omega(\mathcal{M},T\mathcal{M})$, we show that those operators are solely the scalar multiplication. It indicates that $\text{Diff}(\mathcal{M})$ is too rich and that there is no universal class of non-linear operators to motivate the design of Neural Networks over the symmetries of $\mathcal{M}$.

paragraphs: This paper studies operations on scalar and vector fields defined over a manifold. It asks which operations commute with every diffeomorphism, meaning that transforming the field and then applying the operation gives the same result as performing those steps in reverse order. This is a demanding symmetry requirement with consequences for geometric neural-network design.

For the scalar-field spaces considered, the authors prove that the qualifying operations are pointwise nonlinearities. Each output value is determined at its own location. The result extends known findings in Euclidean space and explains why these nonlinearities form a universal family compatible with arbitrary symmetry groups. It supports combining them with linear operators tailored to particular symmetries.

The vector-field result is much more restrictive: only scalar multiplication survives the full diffeomorphism requirement. Consequently, this symmetry group does not yield a universal class of nonlinear vector-field operators for neural-network construction. The contrast shows how the type of field changes what is possible under the same broad symmetry demand.
summary.tldr: Commuting with all diffeomorphisms permits pointwise nonlinearities for scalar fields but restricts vector-field operators to scalar multiplication.

title: On Non-Linear operators for Geometric Deep Learning

abstract: There is a disconnect between how researchers and practitioners handle privacy-utility tradeoffs. Researchers primarily operate from a privacy first perspective, setting strict privacy requirements and minimizing risk subject to these constraints. Practitioners often desire an accuracy first perspective, possibly satisfied with the greatest privacy they can get subject to obtaining sufficiently small error. Ligett et al. have introduced a `"noise reduction" algorithm to address the latter perspective. The authors show that by adding correlated Laplace noise and progressively reducing it on demand, it is possible to produce a sequence of increasingly accurate estimates of a private parameter and only pay a privacy cost for the least noisy iterate released. In this work, we generalize noise reduction to the setting of Gaussian noise, introducing the Brownian mechanism. The Brownian mechanism works by first adding Gaussian noise of high variance corresponding to the final point of a simulated Brownian motion. Then, at the practitioner's discretion, noise is gradually decreased by tracing back along the Brownian path to an earlier time. Our mechanism is more naturally applicable to the common setting of bounded $\ell_2$-sensitivity, empirically outperforms existing work on common statistical tasks, and provides customizable control of privacy loss over the entire interaction with the practitioner. We complement our Brownian mechanism with ReducedAboveThreshold, a generalization of the classical AboveThreshold algorithm that provides adaptive privacy guarantees. Overall, our results demonstrate that one can meet utility constraints while still maintaining strong levels of privacy.

paragraphs: Privacy-preserving analysis often starts with a privacy budget and asks how accurate an answer can be. This paper studies the reverse priority: obtain sufficiently accurate results while retaining as much privacy as possible. It builds on noise reduction, where correlated noisy releases let a practitioner progressively improve an estimate instead of committing to its accuracy upfront.

The proposed Brownian mechanism extends this idea to Gaussian noise. It starts with a highly noisy estimate associated with the endpoint of a simulated Brownian motion. When greater accuracy is needed, it traces that same path backward to an earlier time, reducing the noise. Linking the releases through one path supports control of privacy loss across the interaction.

The mechanism fits settings with bounded sensitivity measured in the l2 norm and empirically outperforms existing work on common statistical tasks. The authors also introduce ReducedAboveThreshold, which supplies adaptive privacy guarantees. Together, these contributions support accuracy-driven analysis with customizable privacy accounting, and demonstrate that meeting utility requirements can remain compatible with strong privacy protection.
summary.tldr: The Brownian mechanism progressively reduces correlated Gaussian noise to support accuracy targets while controlling privacy loss.

title: Brownian Noise Reduction: Maximizing Privacy Subject to Accuracy Constraints

abstract: How many degrees of freedom are there in a dataset consisting of $M$ samples embedded in $\mathbb{R}^D$? This number, formally known as \textsl{intrinsic dimensionality}, can be estimated using nearest neighbor statistics. However, nearest neighbor statistics do not scale to large datasets as their complexity scales quadratically in $M$, $\mathcal{O}(M^2)$. Additionally, methods based on nearest neighbor statistics perform poorly on datasets embedded in high dimensions where $D\gg 1$. In this paper, we propose a novel method to estimate the intrinsic dimensionality using Normalizing Flows that scale to large datasets and high dimensions. The method is based on some simple back-of-the-envelope calculations predicting how the singular values of the flow's Jacobian change when inflating the dataset with different noise magnitudes. Singular values associated with directions normal to the manifold evolve differently than singular values associated with directions tangent to the manifold. We test our method on various datasets, including 64x64 RGB images, where we achieve state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: A dataset can contain many measured coordinates while varying along far fewer underlying degrees of freedom. Intrinsic dimensionality estimates that smaller number. This paper addresses difficulties with nearest-neighbor approaches, whose computational cost grows quadratically with the number of samples and whose performance suffers when the data have many coordinates.

The proposed method uses normalizing flows and studies what happens when data are inflated with different amounts of noise. It examines singular values of the flow's Jacobian, quantities describing how the learned transformation changes different directions. The guiding calculations predict different behavior for directions tangent to the data manifold and directions normal to it.

That difference supplies a signal for estimating how many directions belong to the underlying data structure. The authors present the approach as scaling to both large datasets and high-dimensional observations. Tests include 64-by-64 RGB images and yield state-of-the-art results on the evaluated datasets. The contribution is to infer dimensionality from how a learned transformation responds to noise across directions.
summary.tldr: The method estimates intrinsic dimensionality by measuring how normalizing-flow Jacobians respond to different amounts of added noise.

title: Intrinsic dimensionality estimation using Normalizing Flows

abstract: We introduce Logical Credal Networks (or LCNs for short) -- an expressive probabilistic logic that generalizes prior formalisms that combine logic and probability. Given imprecise information represented by probability bounds and conditional probability bounds on logic formulas, an LCN specifies a set of probability distributions over all its interpretations. Our approach allows propositional and first-order logic formulas with few restrictions, e.g., without requiring acyclicity. We also define a generalized Markov condition that allows us to identify implicit independence relations between atomic formulas. We evaluate our method on benchmark problems such as random networks, Mastermind games with uncertainty and credit card fraud detection. Our results show that the LCN outperforms existing approaches; its advantage lies in aggregating multiple sources of imprecise information.

paragraphs: Logical Credal Networks provide a way to combine logical statements with uncertain information expressed as probability bounds. Instead of requiring one exact probability distribution, an LCN describes a collection of distributions consistent with the supplied bounds. These constraints can concern both probabilities of logical formulas and conditional probabilities.

The formalism accommodates propositional and first-order logic with relatively few restrictions, including no requirement that the structure be acyclic. It also introduces a generalized Markov condition for identifying independence relationships between atomic formulas. This gives the framework both a language for expressing uncertain knowledge and a way to capture independence implicit in its structure.

The authors evaluate LCNs on random networks, uncertain Mastermind games, and credit card fraud detection. They report better performance than existing approaches and attribute the advantage to combining multiple sources of imprecise information. The contribution matters when available knowledge constrains probabilities without determining them exactly: the model preserves that imprecision while bringing the constraints together in a common probabilistic logic.
summary.tldr: Logical Credal Networks combine logical formulas and probability bounds to reason with multiple sources of imprecise information.

title: Logical Credal Networks

abstract: In this paper, we provide the first deterministic algorithm that achieves $1/2$-approximation for monotone submodular maximization subject to a knapsack constraint, while making a number of queries that scales only linearly with the size of the ground set $n$. Moreover, our result automatically paves the way for developing a linear-time deterministic algorithm that achieves the tight $1-1/e$ approximation guarantee for monotone submodular maximization under a cardinality (size) constraint. To complement our positive results, we also show strong information-theoretic lower bounds. More specifically, we show that when the maximum cardinality allowed for a solution is constant, no deterministic or randomized algorithm making a sub-linear number of function evaluations can guarantee any constant approximation ratio. Furthermore, when the constraint allows the selection of a constant fraction of the ground set, we show that any algorithm making fewer than $\Omega(n/\log(n))$ function evaluations cannot perform better than an algorithm that simply outputs a uniformly random subset of the ground set of the right size. We extend our results to the general case of maximizing a monotone submodular function subject to the intersection of a $p$-set system and multiple knapsack constraints. Finally, we evaluate the performance of our algorithms on multiple real-life applications, including movie recommendation, location summarization, Twitter text summarization, and video summarization.

paragraphs: Submodular maximization selects items under diminishing returns: adding an item contributes less as the selected set grows. This paper studies monotone objectives under resource constraints. It gives a deterministic algorithm that achieves at least half the optimal value under a knapsack constraint while using a number of function queries linear in the number of candidate items.

The result also enables a deterministic linear-time algorithm attaining the tight one-minus-one-over-e approximation under a size constraint. Complementary lower bounds explain why much smaller query budgets can be inadequate. When the allowed selection size is constant, sublinear function evaluations cannot guarantee any constant approximation, whether the algorithm is deterministic or randomized.

When the selection size is a constant fraction of all items, the authors establish a further threshold: below order n divided by log n evaluations, an algorithm cannot outperform a uniformly random subset of the required size. They extend their results to combinations of a p-set system and multiple knapsack constraints. Evaluations cover recommendation and several summarization applications, connecting the theoretical guarantees and query limits to practical selection problems.
summary.tldr: The paper gives deterministic linear-query submodular maximization guarantees and lower bounds showing when fewer evaluations cannot suffice.

title: Submodular Maximization in Clean Linear Time

abstract: We consider distributed stochastic variational inequalities (VIs) on unbounded domains with the problem data that is heterogeneous (non-IID) and distributed across many devices. We make a very general assumption on the computational network that, in particular, covers the settings of fully decentralized calculations with time-varying networks and centralized topologies commonly used in Federated Learning. Moreover, multiple local updates on the workers can be made for reducing the communication frequency between the workers.We extend the stochastic extragradient method to this very general setting and theoretically analyze its convergence rate in the strongly-monotone, monotone, and non-monotone (when a Minty solution exists) settings. The provided rates explicitly exhibit the dependence on network characteristics (e.g., mixing time), iteration counter, data heterogeneity, variance, number of devices, and other standard parameters. As a special case, our method and analysis apply to distributed stochastic saddle-point problems (SPP), e.g., to the training of Deep Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for which decentralized training has been reported to be extremely challenging. In experiments for the decentralized training of GANs we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

paragraphs: This paper studies stochastic variational inequalities when information is spread across many devices and differs between them. The setting permits unbounded domains and heterogeneous, non-identically distributed data. Its network assumptions accommodate both decentralized communication with changing connections and centralized arrangements used in federated learning.

The authors extend the stochastic extragradient method so workers can perform multiple local updates between communications. This provides a way to reduce communication frequency while retaining a framework for analyzing convergence. Their rates explicitly track network properties such as mixing time, as well as data heterogeneity, stochastic variance, the number of devices, and the number of iterations.

Experiments on decentralized GAN training demonstrate the proposed method’s effectiveness in a setting described as particularly challenging.
summary.tldr: An extended stochastic extragradient method supports heterogeneous distributed optimization with local updates and convergence guarantees for several problem classes.

title: Decentralized Local Stochastic Extra-Gradient for Variational Inequalities

abstract: In recent years, pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable efficiency in achieving an inference-time few-shot learning capability known as in-context learning. However, existing literature has highlighted the sensitivity of this capability to the selection of few-shot demonstrations. Current understandings of the underlying mechanisms by which this capability arises from regular language model pretraining objectives remain disconnected from the real-world LLMs. This study aims to examine the in-context learning phenomenon through a Bayesian lens, viewing real-world LLMs as latent variable models. On this premise, we propose an algorithm to select optimal demonstrations from a set of annotated data with a small LM, and then directly generalize the selected demonstrations to larger LMs. We demonstrate significant improvement over baselines, averaged over eight GPT models on eight real-world text classification datasets. We also demonstrate the real-world usefulness of our algorithm on GSM8K, a math word problem dataset. Our empirical findings support our hypothesis that LLMs implicitly infer a latent variable containing task information.
