paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model use examples in its prompt to perform a task without a new training phase. Its effectiveness can depend strongly on which demonstrations are chosen. This paper studies that sensitivity through a Bayesian interpretation in which language models implicitly infer a hidden variable carrying information about the task.

On this premise, the authors develop a demonstration-selection algorithm that uses a small language model to choose examples from annotated data. The selected demonstrations are then transferred directly to larger language models. This links a proposed explanation of in-context learning to a practical procedure for deciding what examples to place in the prompt.

The evaluation reports significant improvements over baselines when averaged across eight GPT models and eight text-classification datasets. The authors also demonstrate usefulness on the GSM8K math word-problem dataset. These results support the hypothesis that task information is implicitly represented through a latent variable. They provide empirical support for that interpretation alongside a useful selection method, rather than conclusively identifying the internal mechanism of every language model.
summary.tldr: A latent-variable view of in-context learning motivates selecting demonstrations with a small language model and transferring them to larger models.

title: Large Language Models Are Latent Variable Models: Explaining and Finding Good Demonstrations for In-Context Learning

abstract: Neural ordinary differential equation (Neural ODE) is an elegant yet powerful framework to learn the temporal dynamics for time series modeling.However, we observe that existing Neural ODE forecasting models suffer from two disadvantages:i) controlling the latent states only through the linear transformation over the local change of the observed signals may be inadequate;ii) lacking the ability to capture the inherent periodical property in time series forecasting tasks;To overcome the two issues, we introduce a new neural ODE framework called \textbf{Neural Lad}, a \textbf{Neural} \textbf{La}tent \textbf{d}ynamics model in which the latent representations evolve with an ODE enhanced by the change of observed signal and seasonality-trend characterization. We incorporate the local change of input signal into the latent dynamics in an attention-based manner and design a residual architecture over basis expansion to depict the periodicity in the underlying dynamics. To accommodate the multivariate time series forecasting, we extend the Neural Lad through learning an adaptive relationship between multiple time series. Experiments demonstrate that our model can achieve better or comparable performance against existing neural ODE families and transformer variants in various datasets. Remarkably, the empirical superiority of Neural Lad is consistent across short and long-horizon forecasting for both univariate, multivariate and even irregular sampled time series.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations model time series by learning how an internal state evolves over time. The authors identify two weaknesses in existing forecasting approaches: a linear treatment of local signal changes may be inadequate, and the models may not capture recurring patterns effectively. Neural Lad modifies the latent dynamics to address both.

Its evolving state incorporates changes in the observed signal through attention. A residual architecture built over a basis expansion represents periodic behavior, adding seasonality and trend characterization to the dynamics. For multivariate forecasting, the framework also learns adaptive relationships between different time series, allowing their connections to inform predictions.

Across the evaluated datasets, Neural Lad achieves better or comparable performance relative to existing neural ODE models and transformer variants. The authors report consistent empirical advantages across short and long forecasting horizons, including single-variable, multivariable, and irregularly sampled series. The findings support enriching continuous-time latent dynamics with both responsive input information and explicit modeling of temporal patterns.
summary.tldr: Neural Lad strengthens neural ODE forecasting with attention to signal changes, periodic structure, and adaptive relationships between time series.

title: Neural Lad: A Neural Latent Dynamics Framework for Times Series Modeling

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) has been widely applied in improving model generalization on unlabeled target data. However, accurately selecting the best UDA model for the target domain is challenging due to the absence of labeled target data and domain distribution shifts. Traditional model selection approaches involve training extra models with source data to estimate the target validation risk. Recent studies propose practical methods that are based on measuring various properties of model predictions on target data. Although effective for some UDA models, these methods often lack stability and may lead to poor selections for other UDA models.In this paper, we present MixVal, an innovative model selection method that operates solely with unlabeled target data during inference. MixVal leverages mixed target samples with pseudo labels to directly probe the learned target structure by each UDA model. Specifically, MixVal employs two distinct types of probes: the intra-cluster mixed samples for evaluating neighborhood density and the inter-cluster mixed samples for investigating the classification boundary. With this comprehensive probing strategy, MixVal elegantly combines the strengths of two state-of-the-art model selection methods, Entropy and SND. We extensively evaluate MixVal on 11 UDA methods across 4 adaptation settings, including classification and segmentation tasks. Experimental results consistently demonstrate that MixVal achieves state-of-the-art performance and maintains exceptional stability in model selection. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/LHXXHB/MixVal}.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation produces models for a target domain without labeled target examples. Choosing the best resulting model is difficult for the same reason: there are no target labels for ordinary validation. MixVal addresses this selection problem using only unlabeled target data during inference.

The method creates mixed target samples with pseudo labels and uses them to probe the structure learned by each candidate model. Mixing within a cluster tests neighborhood density, while mixing across clusters investigates the classification boundary. These two probes combine the strengths of the Entropy and SND selection methods, examining complementary aspects of how a model organizes target data.

The authors evaluate MixVal with 11 adaptation methods across four adaptation settings, covering classification and segmentation. They report state-of-the-art model selection performance and consistently strong stability in those evaluations. That stability matters because earlier prediction-based selection methods can work well for some adaptation models and poorly for others. MixVal's contribution is a way to assess candidate models through targeted probes of their behavior without requiring labeled target validation data.
summary.tldr: MixVal selects domain-adapted models using mixed unlabeled target samples to probe neighborhood density and classification boundaries.

title: Mixed Samples as Probes for Unsupervised Model Selection in Domain Adaptation

abstract: In this paper, we revisit the bilevel optimization problem, in which the upper-level objective function is generally nonconvex and the lower-level objective function is strongly convex. Although this type of problem has been studied extensively, it still remains an open question how to achieve an $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1.5})$ sample complexity in Hessian/Jacobian-free stochastic bilevel optimization without any second-order derivative computation. To fill this gap, we propose a novel Hessian/Jacobian-free bilevel optimizer named FdeHBO, which features a simple fully single-loop structure, a projection-aided finite-difference Hessian/Jacobian-vector approximation, and momentum-based updates. Theoretically, we show that FdeHBO requires $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1.5})$ iterations (each using $\mathcal{O}(1)$ samples and only first-order gradient information) to find an $\epsilon$-accurate stationary point. As far as we know, this is the first Hessian/Jacobian-free method with an $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1.5})$ sample complexity for nonconvex-strongly-convex stochastic bilevel optimization.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization links two optimization problems: an upper-level objective depends on the solution of a lower-level problem. This paper studies the stochastic setting where the upper objective can be nonconvex while the lower objective is strongly convex. Its question is whether a strong sample-complexity guarantee can be achieved without computing second-order derivatives.

The proposed optimizer, FdeHBO, combines a single-loop structure with momentum updates and finite-difference approximations of Hessian-vector and Jacobian-vector products. A projection step assists those approximations. This arrangement allows the method to use first-order gradient information while approximating derivative effects that arise from the interaction between the two optimization levels.

The authors prove that FdeHBO reaches an epsilon-accurate stationary point in O(epsilon^-1.5) iterations, using a constant-order number of samples per iteration. This also gives O(epsilon^-1.5) sample complexity. The result applies to the stated nonconvex, strongly convex setting and guarantees stationarity. The authors describe it as the first Hessian/Jacobian-free method attaining this sample complexity for that problem class.
summary.tldr: FdeHBO achieves O(epsilon^-1.5) sample complexity for a specified stochastic bilevel problem class using only first-order gradients.

title: Achieving $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-1.5})$ Complexity in Hessian/Jacobian-free Stochastic Bilevel Optimization

abstract: We introduce OpenShape, a method for learning multi-modal joint representations of text, image, and point clouds. We adopt the commonly used multi-modal contrastive learning framework for representation alignment, but with a specific focus on scaling up 3D representations to enable open-world 3D shape understanding. To achieve this, we scale up training data by ensembling multiple 3D datasets and propose several strategies to automatically filter and enrich noisy text descriptions. We also explore and compare strategies for scaling 3D backbone networks and introduce a novel hard negative mining module for more efficient training. We evaluate OpenShape on zero-shot 3D classification benchmarks and demonstrate its superior capabilities for open-world recognition. Specifically, OpenShape achieves a zero-shot accuracy of 46.8% on the 1,156-category Objaverse-LVIS benchmark, compared to less than 10% for existing methods. OpenShape also achieves an accuracy of 85.3% on ModelNet40, outperforming previous zero-shot baseline methods by 20% and performing on par with some fully-supervised methods. Furthermore, we show that our learned embeddings encode a wide range of visual and semantic concepts (e.g., subcategories, color, shape, style) and facilitate fine-grained text-3D and image-3D interactions. Due to their alignment with CLIP embeddings, our learned shape representations can also be integrated with off-the-shelf CLIP-based models for various applications, such as point cloud captioning and point cloud-conditioned image generation.

It uses contrastive learning to align these modalities. The paper focuses on scaling the 3D side through larger training collections, improved descriptions, and stronger representation networks.

The results show how scaling aligned 3D representations can support both broader recognition and richer cross-modal applications.
summary.tldr: OpenShape scales aligned text, image, and point-cloud representations to improve zero-shot 3D recognition and cross-modal applications.

title: OpenShape: Scaling Up 3D Shape Representation Towards Open-World Understanding

abstract: A privacy policy serves as an online internet protocol crafted by service providers, which details how service providers collect, process, store, manage, and use personal information when users engage with applications. However, these privacy policies are often filled with technobabble and legalese, making them "incomprehensible''. As a result, users often agree to all terms unknowingly, even some terms may conflict with the law, thereby posing a considerable risk to personal privacy information. One potential solution to alleviate this challenge is to automatically summarize privacy policies using NLP techniques. However, existing techniques primarily focus on extracting key sentences, resulting in comparatively shorter agreements, but failing to address the poor readability caused by the "incomprehensible'' of technobabble and legalese. Moreover, research on Chinese application privacy policy summarization is currently almost nonexistent, and there is a lack of a high-quality corpus suitable for addressing readability issues. To tackle these challenges, we introduce a fine-grained CAPP-130 corpus and a TCSI-pp framework. CAPP-130 contains 130 Chinese privacy policies from popular applications that have been carefully annotated and interpreted by legal experts, resulting in 52,489 annotations and 20,555 rewritten sentences. TCSI-pp first extracts sentences related to the topic specified by users and then uses a generative model to rewrite the sentences into comprehensible summarization. Built upon TSCI-pp, we construct a summarization tool TSCI-pp-zh by selecting RoBERTa from six classification models for sentence extraction and selecting mT5 from five generative models for sentence rewriting. Experimental results show that TCSI-pp-zh outperforms GPT-4 and other baselines in Chinese application privacy policy summarization, demonstrating exceptional readability and reliability. Our data, annotation guidelines, benchmark models, and source code are publicly available at https://github.com/EnlightenedAI/CAPP-130.

paragraphs: Shortening a privacy policy does not necessarily make it understandable. Extracting important sentences can preserve the same technical and legal language that confused readers in the original document. This paper addresses that readability problem for Chinese application privacy policies through both expert-annotated data and a system that rewrites relevant passages.

CAPP-130 contains 130 policies from popular applications, with 52,489 annotations and 20,555 rewritten sentences prepared through legal-expert annotation and interpretation. The accompanying framework first identifies sentences connected to a topic chosen by the user. A generative model then rewrites those sentences into a more comprehensible summary, separating topic selection from language simplification.

For the implemented summarization tool, the authors select RoBERTa for extraction after comparing six classification models and mT5 for rewriting after comparing five generative models. Their experiments report better Chinese privacy-policy summarization than GPT-4 and other baselines, including strong readability and reliability. The contribution connects the data needed to learn understandable explanations with a practical pipeline that addresses what a user wants to understand.
summary.tldr: CAPP-130 pairs expert-interpreted Chinese privacy policies with a system that extracts user-relevant passages and rewrites them into understandable summaries.

title: CAPP-130: A Corpus of Chinese Application Privacy Policy Summarization and Interpretation

abstract: Structured state space sequence (S4) models have recently achieved state-of-the-art performance on long-range sequence modeling tasks. These models also have fast inference speeds and parallelisable training, making them potentially useful in many reinforcement learning settings. We propose a modification to a variant of S4 that enables us to initialise and reset the hidden state in parallel, allowing us to tackle reinforcement learning tasks. We show that our modified architecture runs asymptotically faster than Transformers in sequence length and performs better than RNN's on a simple memory-based task. We evaluate our modified architecture on a set of partially-observable environments and find that, in practice, our model outperforms RNN's while also running over five times faster. Then, by leveraging the model’s ability to handle long-range sequences, we achieve strong performance on a challenging meta-learning task in which the agent is given a randomly-sampled continuous control environment, combined with a randomly-sampled linear projection of the environment's observations and actions. Furthermore, we show the resulting model can adapt to out-of-distribution held-out tasks. Overall, the results presented in this paper show that structured state space models are fast and performant for in-context reinforcement learning tasks. We provide code at https://github.com/luchris429/s5rl.
originalAbstract: Structured state space sequence (S4) models have recently achieved state-of-the-art performance on long-range sequence modeling tasks. These models also have fast inference speeds and parallelisable training, making them potentially useful in many reinforcement learning settings. We propose a modification to a variant of S4 that enables us to initialise and reset the hidden state in parallel, allowing us to tackle reinforcement learning tasks. We show that our modified architecture runs asymptotically faster than Transformers in sequence length and performs better than RNN's on a simple memory-based task. We evaluate our modified architecture on a set of partially-observable environments and find that, in practice, our model outperforms RNN's while also running over five times faster. Then, by leveraging the model’s ability to handle long-range sequences, we achieve strong performance on a challenging meta-learning task in which the agent is given a randomly-sampled continuous control environment, combined with a randomly-sampled linear projection of the environment's observations and actions. Furthermore, we show the resulting model can adapt to out-of-distribution held-out tasks. Overall, the results presented in this paper show that structured state space models are fast and performant for in-context reinforcement learning tasks. We provide code at https://github.com/luchris429/s5rl.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents may need to use long histories when their current observations reveal only part of the environment. Structured state space models offer long-sequence modeling, fast inference, and parallelizable training. This paper adapts a variant of S4 so that hidden states can be initialized and reset in parallel for reinforcement-learning tasks.

The modified architecture has better asymptotic scaling with sequence length than Transformers and outperforms recurrent neural networks on a simple memory task. Across the evaluated partially observable environments, it also performs better than recurrent networks while running more than five times faster. These findings connect its sequence-processing advantages with measured agent performance.

The authors further test a challenging meta-learning setting with randomly sampled continuous-control environments and randomly sampled linear projections of observations and actions. The model achieves strong performance and adapts to held-out tasks outside the training distribution. Together, the results support structured state space models as an effective architecture for the evaluated in-context reinforcement-learning problems, including tasks requiring memory and adaptation from extended interaction histories.
summary.tldr: A modified structured state space model delivers fast, effective reinforcement learning with memory and adaptation across the evaluated tasks.

title: Structured State Space Models for In-Context Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Decentralized learning enables the training of deep learning models over large distributed datasets generated at different locations, without the need for a central server. However, in practical scenarios, the data distribution across these devices can be significantly different, leading to a degradation in model performance. In this paper, we focus on designing a decentralized learning algorithm that is less susceptible to variations in data distribution across devices. We propose Global Update Tracking (GUT), a novel tracking-based method that aims to mitigate the impact of heterogeneous data in decentralized learning without introducing any communication overhead. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed technique through an exhaustive set of experiments on various Computer Vision datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Fashion MNIST, and ImageNette), model architectures, and network topologies. Our experiments show that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance for decentralized learning on heterogeneous data via a 1-6% improvement in test accuracy compared to other existing techniques.

paragraphs: Decentralized learning trains models across devices without requiring a central server. A practical difficulty is that devices may hold data from substantially different distributions. This heterogeneity can degrade the resulting model's performance, making it important to design learning procedures that remain effective when local datasets differ.

Global Update Tracking, or GUT, is a tracking-based algorithm designed to reduce this sensitivity. The method aims to mitigate the effect of heterogeneous data without adding communication overhead. That combination matters because the proposed improvement addresses the learning behavior while preserving the communication requirements, an important consideration for training across a distributed network of devices.

The authors evaluate GUT across multiple architectures, network topologies, and vision datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Fashion MNIST, and ImageNette. They report state-of-the-art results for decentralized learning with heterogeneous data, with test accuracy improvements of 1–6% over existing techniques. These are experimental findings across the tested configurations, supporting tracking as a useful approach to this distribution mismatch.
summary.tldr: GUT uses update tracking to improve decentralized learning on heterogeneous data without additional communication overhead.

title: Global Update Tracking: A Decentralized Learning Algorithm for Heterogeneous Data

abstract: While large-scale unsupervised language models (LMs) learn broad world knowledge and some reasoning skills, achieving precise control of their behavior is difficult due to the completely unsupervised nature of their training. Existing methods for gaining such steerability collect human labels of the relative quality of model generations and fine-tune the unsupervised LM to align with these preferences, often with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). However, RLHF is a complex and often unstable procedure, first fitting a reward model that reflects the human preferences, and then fine-tuning the large unsupervised LM using reinforcement learning to maximize this estimated reward without drifting too far from the original model. In this paper, we leverage a mapping between reward functions and optimal policies to show that this constrained reward maximization problem can be optimized exactly with a single stage of policy training, essentially solving a classification problem on the human preference data. The resulting algorithm, which we call Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), is stable, performant, and computationally lightweight, eliminating the need for fitting a reward model, sampling from the LM during fine-tuning, or performing significant hyperparameter tuning. Our experiments show that DPO can fine-tune LMs to align with human preferences as well as or better than existing methods. Notably, fine-tuning with DPO exceeds RLHF's ability to control sentiment of generations and improves response quality in summarization and single-turn dialogue while being substantially simpler to implement and train.

paragraphs: Human preference comparisons help steer language models toward desired behavior. A common approach first learns a reward model from those comparisons, then uses reinforcement learning to improve the language model while limiting its departure from the original model. This creates a complex training procedure whose separate stages can be difficult to manage.

Direct Preference Optimization uses a mapping between reward functions and optimal policies to reformulate that constrained reward-maximization problem. The resulting training objective works directly with preference comparisons and resembles a classification problem. It removes the need to fit a separate reward model or sample language-model outputs during fine-tuning, and the authors describe it as stable and computationally lightweight.

Reported results include stronger sentiment control than RLHF and better response quality for summarization and single-turn dialogue. The significance is a simpler route to the stated preference-learning objective, with empirical evidence that this simplification can retain or improve alignment performance.
summary.tldr: DPO trains language models directly on preference comparisons, simplifying preference alignment while matching or improving tested alternatives.

title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model

abstract: Neural networks have achieved remarkable empirical performance, while the current theoretical analysis is not adequate for understanding their success, e.g., the Neural Tangent Kernel approach fails to capture their key feature learning ability, while recent analyses on feature learning are typically problem-specific. This work proposes a unified analysis framework for two-layer networks trained by gradient descent. The framework is centered around the principle of feature learning from gradients, and its effectiveness is demonstrated by applications in several prototypical problems, such as mixtures of Gaussians and parity functions.The framework also sheds light on interesting network learning phenomena such as feature learning beyond kernels and the lottery ticket hypothesis.

The framework is centered around the principle of feature learning from gradients, and its effectiveness is demonstrated by applications in several prototypical problems, such as mixtures of Gaussians and parity functions.The framework also sheds light on interesting network learning phenomena such as feature learning beyond kernels and the lottery ticket hypothesis.

paragraphs: Neural networks learn useful features during training, but explaining that ability theoretically remains challenging. The paper argues that Neural Tangent Kernel analysis does not capture this key capability, while existing feature-learning analyses often depend closely on individual problems. It proposes a shared framework for studying two-layer networks trained through gradient descent.

The framework centers on learning features from gradients. This places the evolution of the network's representation within the analysis of its training process. Its purpose is to provide a common way to understand feature learning across problems, instead of requiring a separate theoretical approach tailored to each particular target.

The authors demonstrate the framework on prototypical problems that include mixtures of Gaussians and parity functions. They also use it to shed light on feature learning beyond kernels and the lottery ticket hypothesis. These applications support the framework's usefulness across several settings. Its stated scope is two-layer gradient-trained networks, so the contribution is a unified analysis within that setting rather than a complete theory of all neural-network architectures.
summary.tldr: A unified framework analyzes how two-layer networks trained by gradient descent learn features across several prototypical problems.

title: Provable Guarantees for Neural Networks via Gradient Feature Learning

abstract: As hyper-parameters are ubiquitous and can significantly affect the model performance, hyper-parameter optimization is extremely important in machine learning. In this paper, we consider a sub-class of hyper-parameter optimization problems, where the hyper-gradients are not available. Such problems frequently appear when the performance metric is non-differentiable or the hyper-parameter is not continuous. However, existing algorithms, like Bayesian optimization and reinforcement learning, often get trapped in local optimals with poor performance. To address the above limitations, we propose to use cubic regularization to accelerate convergence and avoid saddle points. First, we adopt stochastic relaxation, which allows obtaining gradient and Hessian information without hyper-gradients. Then, we exploit the rich curvature information by cubic regularization. Theoretically, we prove that the proposed method can converge to approximate second-order stationary points, and the convergence is also guaranteed when the lower-level problem is inexactly solved. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter choices can strongly affect a model’s performance, but optimizing them is difficult when hyper-gradients are unavailable. This situation can arise with discrete hyperparameters or nondifferentiable evaluation metrics. The paper studies this class of problems and proposes a method intended to improve convergence and avoid saddle points during the search.

The first step is stochastic relaxation, which makes gradient and Hessian information available without requiring the original hyper-gradients. The method then uses cubic regularization to exploit this curvature information. These two components work together: relaxation supplies information about how the optimization landscape changes, and cubic regularization uses it to guide the search beyond purely first-order behavior.

The authors prove convergence to approximate second-order stationary points, including when the lower-level optimization problem is solved inexactly. This is a stationarity guarantee rather than a guarantee of finding the global optimum. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution thus combines a way to obtain useful optimization information with a curvature-based procedure and a guarantee that accommodates imperfect inner solves.
summary.tldr: Stochastic relaxation and cubic regularization enable hyperparameter optimization with second-order convergence guarantees when hyper-gradients are unavailable.

title: Efficient Hyper-parameter Optimization with Cubic Regularization

abstract: Meta-learning has been proven an effective learning paradigm for training machine learning models with good generalization ability. Apart from the common practice of uniformly sampling the meta-training tasks, existing methods working on task scheduling strategies are mainly based on pre-defined sampling protocols or the assumed task-model correlations, and greedily make scheduling decisions, which can lead to sub-optimal performance bottlenecks of the meta-model. In this paper, we propose a novel task scheduling framework under Contextual Bandits settings, named BASS, which directly optimizes the task scheduling strategy based on the status of the meta-model. By balancing the exploitation and exploration in meta-learning task scheduling, BASS can help tackle the challenge of limited knowledge about the task distribution during the early stage of meta-training, while simultaneously exploring potential benefits for forthcoming meta-training iterations through an adaptive exploration strategy. Theoretical analysis and extensive experiments are presented to show the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

paragraphs: Meta-learning trains a model across tasks to improve its ability to generalize. The choice of which task to train on next can affect that process. Uniform sampling ignores the model's current state, while scheduling based on fixed rules or assumed task relationships can make shortsighted choices. This paper treats scheduling itself as an adaptive learning problem.

The proposed framework, BASS, uses contextual bandits to optimize task selection based on the meta-model's status. It balances exploitation, which uses current knowledge to select promising tasks, with exploration, which investigates tasks whose benefits remain uncertain. This balance addresses incomplete knowledge about the task distribution early in training.

BASS also adapts its exploration strategy to seek potential benefits for later training iterations. Task selection therefore responds to the evolving model rather than following a fixed sampling protocol. The authors provide theoretical analysis and extensive experiments supporting the framework's effectiveness. The contribution is a scheduling mechanism that connects present model status with uncertainty about which training tasks will be useful.
summary.tldr: BASS uses a contextual-bandit scheduler to adapt meta-training task selection while balancing exploration and exploitation.

title: Meta-Learning with Neural Bandit Scheduler

abstract: Long-tailed object detection (LTOD) aims to handle the extreme data imbalance in real-world datasets, where many tail classes have scarce instances. One popular strategy is to explore extra data with image-level labels, yet it produces limited results due to (1) semantic ambiguity---an image-level label only captures a salient part of the image, ignoring the remaining rich semantics within the image; and (2) location sensitivity---the label highly depends on the locations and crops of the original image, which may change after data transformations like random cropping.To remedy this, we propose RichSem, a simple but effective method, which is robust to learn rich semantics from coarse locations without the need of accurate bounding boxes. RichSem leverages rich semantics from images, which are then served as additional ``soft supervision'' for training detectors. Specifically, we add a semantic branch to our detector to learn these soft semantics and enhance feature representations for long-tailed object detection. The semantic branch is only used for training and is removed during inference. RichSem achieves consistent improvements on both overall and rare-category of LVIS under different backbones and detectors. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance without requiring complex training and testing procedures. Moreover, we show the effectiveness of our method on other long-tailed datasets with additional experiments.

paragraphs: Long-tailed object detection deals with datasets where many object categories have very few examples. Extra images with image-level labels can help, but such labels often describe only the most prominent content. They can also become misleading after cropping, because the content associated with a label may no longer be present in the transformed image.

RichSem addresses these problems by learning richer semantic information from coarse locations without requiring precise bounding boxes for that supervision. This information supplies additional soft supervision to the detector. A dedicated semantic branch learns it during training, improving the detector's feature representations. The branch is removed during inference, so the extra training component does not remain part of the deployed detector.

On LVIS, RichSem consistently improves overall performance and performance on rare categories across different backbones and detectors. The authors report state-of-the-art results without complex training or testing procedures, with further experiments supporting effectiveness on other long-tailed datasets. The findings indicate that richer supervision can make additional imagery more useful for learning scarce categories.
summary.tldr: RichSem uses a training-only semantic branch to improve long-tailed object detection with rich supervision from coarse locations.

title: Learning from Rich Semantics and Coarse Locations for Long-tailed Object Detection

abstract: Neural 3D scene representations have shown great potential for 3D reconstruction from 2D images. However, reconstructing real-world captures of complex scenes still remains a challenge. Existing generic 3D reconstruction methods often struggle to represent fine geometric details and do not adequately model reflective surfaces of large-scale scenes. Techniques that explicitly focus on reflective surfaces can model complex and detailed reflections by exploiting better reflection parameterizations. However, we observe that these methods are often not robust in real scenarios where non-reflective as well as reflective components are present. In this work, we propose UniSDF, a general purpose 3D reconstruction method that can reconstruct large complex scenes with reflections. We investigate both camera view as well as reflected view-based color parameterization techniques and find that explicitly blending these representations in 3D space enables reconstruction of surfaces that are more geometrically accurate, especially for reflective surfaces. We further combine this representation with a multi-resolution grid backbone that is trained in a coarse-to-fine manner, enabling faster reconstructions than prior methods. Extensive experiments on object-level datasets DTU, Shiny Blender as well as unbounded datasets Mip-NeRF 360 and Ref-NeRF real demonstrate that our method is able to robustly reconstruct complex large-scale scenes with fine details and reflective surfaces, leading to the best overall performance. Project page: https://fangjinhuawang.github.io/UniSDF.

paragraphs: UniSDF reconstructs three-dimensional scenes from two-dimensional images, with particular attention to scenes containing reflections. General reconstruction methods can miss fine geometry and reflective appearance, while methods specialized for reflections can struggle when reflective and non-reflective components coexist. The paper aims to handle these mixed, complex scenes within a general-purpose method.

The authors investigate color representations based on both the camera view and the reflected view. Explicitly blending those representations in three-dimensional space produces more geometrically accurate surfaces, especially reflective ones. They combine this representation with a multi-resolution grid trained from coarse to fine, enabling faster reconstruction than prior methods.

Evaluation covers the object-level DTU and Shiny Blender datasets and the unbounded Mip-NeRF 360 and Ref-NeRF real datasets. The authors report robust reconstruction of large, detailed scenes with reflective surfaces and the best overall performance in their experiments. The findings support coordinating complementary appearance representations to improve geometry while using the grid backbone to accelerate reconstruction.
summary.tldr: UniSDF blends camera-view and reflected-view representations to reconstruct detailed scenes with reflections more accurately and quickly.

title: UniSDF: Unifying Neural Representations for High-Fidelity 3D Reconstruction of Complex Scenes with Reflections

abstract: Current approximate posteriors in Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) exhibit a crucial limitation: they fail to maintain invariance under reparameterization, i.e. BNNs assign different posterior densities to different parametrizations of identical functions. This creates a fundamental flaw in the application of Bayesian principles as it breaks the correspondence between uncertainty over the parameters with uncertainty over the parametrized function. In this paper, we investigate this issue in the context of the increasingly popular linearized Laplace approximation. Specifically, it has been observed that linearized predictives alleviate the common underfitting problems of the Laplace approximation. We develop a new geometric view of reparametrizations from which we explain the success of linearization. Moreover, we demonstrate that these reparameterization invariance properties can be extended to the original neural network predictive using a Riemannian diffusion process giving a straightforward algorithm for approximate posterior sampling, which empirically improves posterior fit.

paragraphs: A neural network can represent the same function through different parameterizations. The paper argues that current approximate Bayesian posteriors can treat these equivalent representations differently, disrupting the intended relationship between uncertainty over parameters and uncertainty over the function. This makes the geometry of parameterization relevant to the quality of approximate inference.

The authors study the issue through the linearized Laplace approximation. Linearized predictions have been observed to reduce underfitting associated with the Laplace approximation, and the paper develops a geometric account of reparameterization that explains this behavior. The explanation connects the success of linearization with invariance properties of the approximation.

The authors then extend these invariance properties to predictions from the original neural network using a Riemannian diffusion process. This yields an algorithm for approximately sampling the posterior, with empirical improvements in posterior fit. The contribution combines an explanation of an existing approximation's behavior with a sampling approach designed to respect the geometry associated with equivalent network parameterizations.
summary.tldr: A geometric analysis explains benefits of linearized Bayesian predictions and motivates a diffusion-based posterior sampler with improved empirical fit.

title: Reparameterization invariance in approximate Bayesian inference

abstract: We study fairness in social influence maximization, whereby one seeks to selectseeds that spread a given information throughout a network, ensuring balancedoutreach among different communities (e.g. demographic groups). In the literature,fairness is often quantified in terms of the expected outreach within individualcommunities. In this paper, we demonstrate that such fairness metrics can bemisleading since they overlook the stochastic nature of information diffusionprocesses. When information diffusion occurs in a probabilistic manner, multipleoutreach scenarios can occur. As such, outcomes such as “In 50% of the cases, noone in group 1 gets the information, while everyone in group 2 does, and in theother 50%, it is the opposite”, which always results in largely unfair outcomes,are classified as fair by a variety of fairness metrics in the literature. We tacklethis problem by designing a new fairness metric, mutual fairness, that capturesvariability in outreach through optimal transport theory. We propose a new seed-selection algorithm that optimizes both outreach and mutual fairness, and we showits efficacy on several real datasets. We find that our algorithm increases fairnesswith only a minor decrease (and at times, even an increase) in efficiency.

paragraphs: Influence maximization chooses initial recipients of information so it spreads through a network. Fairness adds a requirement to reach different communities in a balanced way. The paper shows why comparing only expected outreach can be misleading: equal averages can conceal severe imbalances in every individual diffusion outcome.

For example, information might reach everyone in one group and nobody in another, with the favored group switching equally often. The expected outreach is balanced, yet each realized outcome is highly unequal. To capture this variability, the authors introduce mutual fairness, a metric built using optimal transport. It makes uncertainty in the diffusion process part of the fairness assessment.

The authors then develop a seed-selection algorithm that optimizes both overall outreach and mutual fairness. On several real datasets, it improves fairness with only a minor efficiency decrease, and sometimes with an efficiency increase. The results show that accounting for variation across possible outcomes can improve fairness without necessarily imposing a large loss in reach.
summary.tldr: An optimal-transport fairness metric accounts for uncertain information spread, enabling seed selection that improves fairness with small or sometimes favorable efficiency changes.

title: Fairness in Social Influence Maximization via Optimal Transport

abstract: Neuro-symbolic neural networks have been extensively studied to integrate symbolic operations with neural networks, thereby improving systematic generalization. Specifically, Tensor Product Representation (TPR) framework enables neural networks to perform differentiable symbolic operations by encoding the symbolic structure of data within vector spaces. However, TPR-based neural networks often struggle to decompose unseen data into structured TPR representations, undermining their symbolic operations. To address this decomposition problem, we propose a Discrete Dictionary-based Decomposition (D3) layer designed to enhance the decomposition capabilities of TPR-based models. D3 employs discrete, learnable key-value dictionaries trained to capture symbolic features essential for decomposition operations. It leverages the prior knowledge acquired during training to generate structured TPR representations by mapping input data to pre-learned symbolic features within these dictionaries. D3 is a straightforward drop-in layer that can be seamlessly integrated into any TPR-based model without modifications. Our experimental results demonstrate that D3 significantly improves the systematic generalization of various TPR-based models while requiring fewer additional parameters. Notably, D3 outperforms baseline models on the synthetic task that demands the systematic decomposition of unseen combinatorial data.

paragraphs: Tensor Product Representations encode symbolic structure in vectors so that neural networks can perform differentiable symbolic operations. Their usefulness depends on first decomposing an input into the right structured representation. The paper targets a weakness at this stage: models can struggle to decompose unfamiliar inputs, undermining the symbolic operations that follow.

The proposed Discrete Dictionary-based Decomposition layer, or D3, uses learnable discrete key-value dictionaries. During training, these dictionaries capture symbolic features needed for decomposition. For a new input, the layer maps the data to those previously learned features to construct a structured representation. The authors describe D3 as a drop-in component that can be integrated into TPR-based models without modifying them.

Experiments show significant improvements in systematic generalization across several TPR-based models while requiring fewer additional parameters. D3 also outperforms baseline models on a synthetic task involving decomposition of unseen combinations. The results support the idea that reusable learned symbolic features can help a model handle unfamiliar combinations, improving the initial representation on which later symbolic processing depends.
summary.tldr: D3 uses learned discrete dictionaries to help neural-symbolic models decompose unfamiliar combinations into structured representations.

title: Discrete Dictionary-based Decomposition Layer for Structured Representation Learning

abstract: Estimating the out-of-distribution performance in regimes where labels are scarce is critical to safely deploy foundation models. Recently, it was shown that ensembles of neural networks observe the phenomena "agreement-on-the-line", which can be leveraged to reliably predict OOD performance without labels. However, in contrast to classical neural networks that are trained on in-distribution data from scratch for numerous epochs, foundation models undergo minimal finetuning from heavily pretrained weights, which may reduce the ensemble diversity needed to observe agreement-on-the-line. In our work, we demonstrate that when lightly finetuning multiple runs from a $\textit{single}$ foundation model, the choice of randomness during training (linear head initialization, data ordering, and data subsetting) can lead to drastically different levels of agreement-on-the-line in the resulting ensemble. Surprisingly, only random head initialization is able to reliably induce agreement-on-the-line in finetuned foundation models across vision and language benchmarks. Second, we demonstrate that ensembles of $\textit{multiple}$ foundation models pretrained on different datasets but finetuned on the same task can also show agreement-on-the-line. In total, by careful construction of a diverse ensemble, we can utilize agreement-on-the-line-based methods to predict the OOD performance of foundation models with high precision.

paragraphs: Estimating performance on unfamiliar data is difficult when its labels are unavailable. Agreement-on-the-line offers an approach based on how predictions from an ensemble relate to one another. This paper asks whether that relationship remains useful for foundation models, whose lightly fine-tuned copies may have less diversity than networks trained independently from scratch.

For multiple fine-tuning runs of one foundation model, the authors compare randomness from linear-head initialization, data order, and data subsets. These choices produce markedly different levels of agreement-on-the-line. Across the vision and language benchmarks studied, only random head initialization reliably induces the relationship among those tested sources of randomness.

The authors also find that ensembles of different foundation models, pretrained on different datasets and then fine-tuned on the same task, can exhibit the relationship. With carefully constructed diversity, agreement-based methods predict out-of-distribution performance with high precision in their evaluations. The practical lesson is that ensemble construction is central to making this form of prediction work; simply repeating fine-tuning does not reliably produce the needed behavior.
summary.tldr: Carefully chosen ensemble diversity enables agreement-based prediction of foundation-model performance on unlabeled out-of-distribution data.

title: Predicting the Performance of Foundation Models via Agreement-on-the-Line

abstract: As new machine learning methods demand larger training datasets, researchers and developers face significant challenges in dataset management. Although ethics reviews, documentation, and checklists have been established, it remains uncertain whether consistent dataset management practices exist across the community. This lack of a comprehensive overview hinders our ability to diagnose and address fundamental tensions and ethical issues related to managing large datasets. We present a systematic review of datasets published at the NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks track, focusing on four key aspects: provenance, distribution, ethical disclosure, and licensing. Our findings reveal that dataset provenance is often unclear due to ambiguous filtering and curation processes. Additionally, a variety of sites are used for dataset hosting, but only a few offer structured metadata and version control. These inconsistencies underscore the urgent need for standardized data infrastructures for the publication and management of datasets.

paragraphs: This paper examines how datasets are documented, distributed, and maintained within the NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks track. Its starting point is that larger datasets create management problems that ethics reviews and publication checklists alone may not resolve. Without a systematic overview, it is difficult to identify recurring weaknesses or understand the ethical tensions surrounding dataset management.

The review organizes its analysis around four aspects: provenance, distribution, ethical disclosure, and licensing. Provenance concerns how data reached its published form, including the filtering and curation decisions made along the way. The authors find that these processes are often described ambiguously, leaving dataset origins and construction unclear.

The review also finds that datasets are hosted across many sites, with relatively few providing structured metadata and version control. These findings point to inconsistent infrastructure as well as inconsistent documentation. The paper argues for standardized systems for publishing and managing datasets, so that information about their construction and changes can be handled more consistently.
summary.tldr: A review of NeurIPS datasets finds unclear provenance and inconsistent hosting practices, motivating standardized dataset management infrastructure.

title: A Systematic Review of NeurIPS Dataset Management Practices

abstract: Humans can picture a sound scene given an imprecise natural language description. For example, it is easy to imagine an acoustic environment given a phrase like "the lion roar came from right behind me!". For a machine to have the same degree of comprehension, the machine must know what a lion is (semantic attribute), what the concept of "behind" is (spatial attribute) and how these pieces of linguistic information align with the semantic and spatial attributes of the sound (what a roar sounds like when its coming from behind). State-of-the-art audio foundation models, such as CLAP, which learn to map between audio scenes and natural textual descriptions, are trained on non-spatial audio and text pairs, and hence lack spatial awareness. In contrast, sound event localization and detection models are limited to recognizing sounds from a fixed number of classes, and they localize the source to absolute position (e.g., 0.2m) rather than a position described using natural language (e.g., "next to me"). To address these gaps, we present ELSA (Embeddings for Language and Spatial Audio), a spatially aware-audio and text embedding model trained using multimodal contrastive learning. ELSA supports non-spatial audio, spatial audio, and open vocabulary text captions describing both the spatial and semantic components of sound. To train ELSA: (a) we spatially augment the audio and captions of three open-source audio datasets totaling 4,738 hours and 890,038 samples of audio comprised from 8,972 simulated spatial configurations, and (b) we design an encoder to capture the semantics of non-spatial audio, and the semantics and spatial attributes of spatial audio using contrastive learning. ELSA is a single model that is competitive with state-of-the-art for both semantic retrieval and 3D source localization. In particular, ELSA achieves +2.8\% mean audio-to-text and text-to-audio R@1 above the LAION-CLAP baseline, and outperforms by -11.6° mean-absolute-error in 3D source localization over the SeldNET baseline on the TUT Sound Events 2018 benchmark. Moreover, we show that the representation-space of ELSA is structured, enabling swapping of direction of audio via vector arithmetic of two directional text embeddings.

These findings show that spatial relationships can become part of the same learned representation used for semantic matching, with competitive results on both retrieval and localization.
summary.tldr: ELSA jointly represents sound identity and spatial location, supporting audio-text retrieval, source localization, and direction changes through embedding arithmetic.

title: Learning Spatially-Aware Language and Audio Embeddings

abstract: Prediction is a fundamental capability of all living organisms, and has been proposed as an objective for learning sensory representations. Recent work demonstrates that in primate visual systems, prediction is facilitated by neural representations that follow straighter temporal trajectories than their initial photoreceptor encoding, which allows for prediction by linear extrapolation. Inspired by these experimental findings, we develop a self-supervised learning (SSL) objective that explicitly quantifies and promotes straightening. We demonstrate the power of this objective in training deep feedforward neural networks on smoothly-rendered synthetic image sequences that mimic commonly-occurring properties of natural videos. The learned model contains neural embeddings that are predictive, but also factorize the geometric, photometric, and semantic attributes of objects. The representations also prove more robust to noise and adversarial attacks compared to previous SSL methods that optimize for invariance to random augmentations. Moreover, these beneficial properties can be transferred to other training procedures by using the straightening objective as a regularizer, suggesting a broader utility for straightening as a principle for robust unsupervised learning.

paragraphs: Predicting the next visual state becomes easier when a sequence follows a relatively straight path in its internal representation. Inspired by observations of primate vision, this paper develops a self-supervised objective that directly measures and encourages this straightening. A straighter trajectory can support prediction by continuing its current direction through linear extrapolation.

The researchers train deep feedforward networks on smoothly rendered synthetic image sequences designed to reproduce common properties of natural videos. The resulting representations are predictive and also separate geometric, photometric, and semantic object attributes. Thus, the training objective affects both how representations evolve over time and how they organize different aspects of an image.

Compared with earlier self-supervised methods based on invariance to random augmentations, the learned representations show greater robustness to noise and adversarial attacks. Adding straightening as a regularizer also transfers beneficial properties to other training procedures. These results support its potential as a broader learning principle, with the main demonstrations grounded in the synthetic sequence setting.
summary.tldr: Encouraging straight trajectories through representation space produces predictive, factorized, and more robust visual embeddings in the studied setting.

title: Learning predictable and robust neural representations by straightening image sequences

abstract: Believable agents can empower interactive applications ranging from immersive environments to rehearsal spaces for interpersonal communication. Recently, generative agents have been proposed to simulate believable human behavior by using Large Language Models. However, the existing method heavily relies on human-annotated agent profiles (e.g., name, age, personality, relationships with others, and so on) for the initialization of each agent, which cannot be scaled up easily. In this paper, we propose a scalable RoleAgent framework to generate high-quality role-playing agents from raw scripts, which includes building and interacting stages. Specifically, in the building stage, we use a hierarchical memory system to extract and summarize the structure and high-level information of each agent for the raw script. In the interacting stage, we propose a novel innovative mechanism with four steps to achieve a high-quality interaction between agents. Finally, we introduce a systematic and comprehensive evaluation benchmark called RoleAgentBench to evaluate the effectiveness of our RoleAgent, which includes 100 and 28 roles for 20 English and 5 Chinese scripts, respectively. Extensive experimental results on RoleAgentBench demonstrate the effectiveness of RoleAgent.

paragraphs: Role-playing agents can support immersive experiences and spaces for practicing interpersonal communication. Building them often requires people to annotate profiles containing personality, relationships, and other character details. RoleAgent aims to make this process more scalable by generating agents directly from raw scripts, using the source material to establish their roles.

The framework separates agent construction from interaction. During construction, a hierarchical memory system extracts and summarizes each character’s structure and high-level information from the script. During interaction, a four-step mechanism supports exchanges between agents. This organization connects information gathered from the script to the subsequent role-playing process.

The paper also introduces RoleAgentBench to evaluate the framework systematically. It includes 100 roles from 20 English scripts and 28 roles from five Chinese scripts. Extensive experiments on this benchmark demonstrate the reported effectiveness of RoleAgent. The combined contribution is a script-based agent-building pipeline and a shared evaluation resource, addressing both the effort required to initialize characters and the need to assess the resulting interactions.
summary.tldr: RoleAgent builds role-playing agents from raw scripts using hierarchical memory and evaluates them with a benchmark covering English and Chinese characters.

title: RoleAgent: Building, Interacting, and Benchmarking High-quality Role-Playing Agents from Scripts

abstract: Chat-based language models are designed to be helpful, yet they should not comply with every user request. While most existing work primarily focuses on refusal of ``unsafe'' queries, we posit that the scope of noncompliance should be broadened. We introduce a comprehensive taxonomy of contextual noncompliance describing when and how models should *not* comply with user requests. Our taxonomy spans a wide range of categories including *incomplete*, *unsupported*, *indeterminate*, and *humanizing* requests (in addition to *unsafe* requests). To test noncompliance capabilities of language models, we use this taxonomy to develop a new evaluation suite of 1000 noncompliance prompts. We find that most existing models show significantly high compliance rates in certain previously understudied categories with models like GPT-4 incorrectly complying with as many as 30\% of requests.To address these gaps, we explore different training strategies using a synthetically-generated training set of requests and expected noncompliant responses. Our experiments demonstrate that while direct finetuning of instruction-tuned models can lead to both over-refusal and a decline in general capabilities, using parameter efficient methods like low rank adapters helps to strike a good balance between appropriate noncompliance and other capabilities.

paragraphs: A helpful language model sometimes needs to decline or otherwise avoid fulfilling a request for reasons beyond safety. This paper develops a taxonomy of contextual noncompliance that includes incomplete, unsupported, indeterminate, and humanizing requests alongside unsafe ones. The taxonomy broadens the situations in which straightforward compliance can be inappropriate.

The authors build an evaluation suite of 1,000 prompts based on these categories. They find high rates of inappropriate compliance in some previously understudied areas, with models such as GPT-4 incorrectly complying with as many as 30% of requests. The evaluation exposes gaps that a focus on unsafe queries alone would not adequately capture.

To improve behavior, the paper explores training strategies using synthetic requests paired with expected noncompliant responses. Direct fine-tuning can cause excessive refusal and reduce general capabilities. Parameter-efficient approaches such as low-rank adapters achieve a better balance in the experiments. The findings make appropriate noncompliance a broader training and evaluation problem, where declining unsuitable requests must be balanced with preserving useful model behavior.
summary.tldr: A broader taxonomy reveals inappropriate compliance beyond unsafe requests, while low-rank adapter training better balances noncompliance with general capabilities.

title: The Art of Saying No: Contextual Noncompliance in Language Models

abstract: We study learning in a dynamically evolving environment modeled as a Markov game between a learner and a strategic opponent that can adapt to the learner's strategies. While most existing works in Markov games focus on external regret as the learning objective, external regret becomes inadequate when the adversaries are adaptive. In this work, we focus on \emph{policy regret} -- a counterfactual notion that aims to compete with the return that would have been attained if the learner had followed the best fixed sequence of policy, in hindsight. We show that if the opponent has unbounded memory or if it is non-stationary, then sample-efficient learning is not possible. For memory-bounded and stationary, we show that learning is still statistically hard if the set of feasible strategies for the learner is exponentially large. To guarantee learnability, we introduce a new notion of \emph{consistent} adaptive adversaries, wherein, the adversary responds similarly to similar strategies of the learner. We provide algorithms that achieve $\sqrt{T}$ policy regret against memory-bounded, stationary, and consistent adversaries.

paragraphs: When an opponent adapts to a learner’s behavior, assessing the learner requires accounting for how different choices would have changed the opponent’s responses. This paper studies Markov games using policy regret, a counterfactual comparison with the return obtainable by following the best fixed policy sequence in hindsight. It argues that conventional external regret is inadequate in this adaptive setting.

The authors establish barriers to sample-efficient learning. Such learning is impossible when the opponent has unbounded memory or is non-stationary. Even an opponent with bounded memory and stationary behavior leaves a statistically hard problem when the learner’s feasible strategy set is exponentially large. These results identify distinct sources of difficulty rather than treating all adaptation alike.

To obtain a learnable setting, the paper introduces consistent adaptive adversaries, which respond similarly to similar learner strategies. It provides algorithms with policy regret scaling as √T against adversaries that are simultaneously memory-bounded, stationary, and consistent. The positive guarantee therefore depends on these restrictions, showing how structure in an opponent’s reactions can make counterfactual performance guarantees attainable.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies barriers to learning against adaptive opponents and achieves √T policy regret under bounded-memory, stationary, consistent responses.

title: Learning in Markov Games with Adaptive Adversaries: Policy Regret, Fundamental Barriers, and Efficient Algorithms

abstract: The machine learning community has witnessed impressive advancements since large language models (LLMs) first appeared. Yet, their massive memory consumption has become a significant roadblock to large-scale training. For instance, a 7B model typically requires at least 60 GB of GPU memory with full parameter training, which presents challenges for researchers without access to high-resource environments. Parameter Efficient Fine-Tuning techniques such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) have been proposed to alleviate this problem. However, in most large-scale fine-tuning settings, their performance does not reach the level of full parameter training because they confine the parameter search to a low-rank subspace. Attempting to complement this deficiency, we investigate the layerwise properties of LoRA on fine-tuning tasks and observe an unexpected but consistent skewness of weight norms across different layers. Utilizing this key observation, a surprisingly simple training strategy is discovered, which outperforms both LoRA and full parameter training in a wide range of settings with memory costs as low as LoRA. We name it Layerwise Importance Sampled AdamW (LISA), a promising alternative for LoRA, which applies the idea of importance sampling to different layers in LLMs and randomly freeze most middle layers during optimization. Experimental results show that with similar or less GPU memory consumption, LISA surpasses LoRA or even full parameter tuning in downstream fine-tuning tasks, where LISA consistently outperforms LoRA by over 10%-35% in terms of MT-Bench score while achieving on-par or better performance in MMLU, AGIEval and WinoGrande. On large models, specifically LLaMA-2-70B, LISA surpasses LoRA on MT-Bench, GSM8K, and PubMedQA, demonstrating its effectiveness across different domains.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning all parameters of a large language model requires substantial GPU memory. Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, reduces that burden but restricts the parameter search to a low-rank subspace. This paper explores another route after observing a consistent imbalance in weight norms across layers during LoRA fine-tuning.

The resulting method, Layerwise Importance Sampled AdamW, or LISA, applies importance sampling across model layers and randomly freezes most middle layers during optimization. This changes which parts of the model are updated while keeping memory costs low. The approach makes the layer-level allocation of training updates the main mechanism for balancing adaptation and resource use.

Across the reported settings, LISA uses similar or less GPU memory than LoRA and can outperform both LoRA and full parameter training. The authors report MT-Bench improvements over LoRA of more than 10%–35%, with comparable or better results on MMLU, AGIEval, and WinoGrande. Results on LLaMA-2-70B also favor LISA over LoRA on MT-Bench, GSM8K, and PubMedQA, supporting its usefulness across the tested domains.
summary.tldr: LISA reduces fine-tuning memory by sampling layer updates and freezing most middle layers, with strong reported performance relative to LoRA.

title: LISA: Layerwise Importance Sampling for Memory-Efficient Large Language Model Fine-Tuning

abstract: The commercial text-to-image deep generation models (e.g. DALL·E) can produce high-quality images based on input language descriptions. These models incorporate a black-box safety filter to prevent the generation of unsafe or unethical content, such as violent, criminal, or hateful imagery. Recent jailbreaking methods generate adversarial prompts capable of bypassing safety filters and producing unsafe content, exposing vulnerabilities in influential commercial models. However, once these adversarial prompts are identified, the safety filter can be updated to prevent the generation of unsafe images. In this work, we propose an effective, simple, and difficult-to-detect jailbreaking solution: generating safe content initially with normal text prompts and then editing the generations to embed unsafe content. The intuition behind this idea is that the deep generation model cannot reject safe generation with normal text prompts, while the editing models focus on modifying the local regions of images and do not involve a safety strategy. However, implementing such a solution is non-trivial, and we need to overcome several challenges: how to automatically confirm the normal prompt to replace the unsafe prompts, and how to effectively perform editable replacement and naturally generate unsafe content. In this work, we propose the collaborative generation and editing for jailbreaking text-to-image deep generation (ColJailBreak), which comprises three key components: adaptive normal safe substitution, inpainting-driven injection of unsafe content, and contrastive language-image-guided collaborative optimization. We validate our method on three datasets and compare it to two baseline methods. Our method could generate unsafe content through two commercial deep generation models including GPT-4 and DALL·E 2.

paragraphs: ColJailBreak studies a safety vulnerability that spans image generation and editing. Existing adversarial prompts can be blocked once identified, motivating the authors to examine a different route: begin with an acceptable generated image and subsequently alter it to introduce unsafe content. The concern is whether protection at the initial generation stage covers the complete workflow.

The proposed system coordinates safe prompt substitution, image inpainting, and optimization guided by relationships between text and images. At a conceptual level, these components connect the initial acceptable output with a later edited result. The approach relies on the described gap between safety filtering in generation and the absence of a corresponding safety strategy in the editing models considered.

The authors evaluate their method on three datasets against two baselines and report generating unsafe content through systems involving GPT-4 and DALL·E 2. These findings expose a vulnerability in the evaluated generation-and-editing combinations. The paper's significance is its demonstration that the safety behavior of individual stages does not by itself establish the safety of their combined use.
summary.tldr: ColJailBreak demonstrates a safety gap in evaluated image workflows by combining initially acceptable generation with subsequent unsafe editing.

title: ColJailBreak: Collaborative Generation and Editing for Jailbreaking Text-to-Image Deep Generation

abstract: General Value Functions (GVFs) (Sutton et al., 2011) represent predictive knowledge in reinforcement learning. Each GVF computes the expected return for a given policy, based on a unique reward. Existing methods relying on fixed behavior policies or pre-collected data often face data efficiency issues when learning multiple GVFs in parallel using off-policy methods. To address this, we introduce *GVFExplorer*, which adaptively learns a single behavior policy that efficiently collects data for evaluating multiple GVFs in parallel. Our method optimizes the behavior policy by minimizing the total variance in return across GVFs, thereby reducing the required environmental interactions. We use an existing temporal-difference-style variance estimator to approximate the return variance. We prove that each behavior policy update decreases the overall mean squared error in GVF predictions. We empirically show our method's performance in tabular and nonlinear function approximation settings, including Mujoco environments, with stationary and non-stationary reward signals, optimizing data usage and reducing prediction errors across multiple GVFs.

We use an existing temporal-difference-style variance estimator to approximate the return variance. abstract: The Procrustes-Wasserstein problem consists in matching two high-dimensional point clouds in an unsupervised setting, and has many applications in natural language processing and computer vision. We consider a planted model with two datasets $X,Y$ that consist of $n$ datapoints in $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $Y$ is a noisy version of $X$, up to an orthogonal transformation and a relabeling of the data points. This setting is related to the graph alignment problem in geometric models.In this work, we focus on the euclidean transport cost between the point clouds as a measure of performance for the alignment. We first establish information-theoretic results, in the high ($d \gg \log n$) and low ($d \ll \log n$) dimensional regimes. We then study computational aspects and propose the ‘Ping-Pong algorithm', alternatively estimating the orthogonal transformation and the relabeling, initialized via a Franke-Wolfe convex relaxation. We give sufficient conditions for the method to retrieve the planted signal after one single step. We provide experimental results to compare the proposed approach with the state-of-the-art method of Grave et al. (2019).

paragraphs: The paper studies how to align two point clouds when neither the correspondence between points nor their relative orientation is known. Its planted model assumes that one dataset is a noisy version of the other, with an orthogonal transformation and a relabeling applied. Alignment quality is measured through Euclidean transport cost between the clouds.

The theoretical analysis examines what information permits in two regimes: dimension much larger than the logarithm of the number of points, and dimension much smaller than that quantity. This separates questions about the information available in the observations from questions about how an algorithm can use it. The setting also connects to aligning graphs generated from geometric data.

For computation, the authors introduce Ping-Pong, which alternates between estimating the transformation and estimating point correspondences, starting from a convex relaxation. They give sufficient conditions for recovering the planted signal after one step; this is a conditional result. Experiments compare the method with an existing approach, without the abstract specifying the comparison's outcome.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes when noisy point clouds can be aligned and proposes an alternating algorithm with conditional one-step recovery guarantees.

title: Aligning Embeddings and Geometric Random Graphs: Informational Results and Computational Approaches for the Procrustes-Wasserstein Problem

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a novel variation of multi-armed bandits called bandits with ranking feedback. Unlike traditional bandits, this variation provides feedback to the learner that allows them to rank the arms based on previous pulls, without quantifying numerically the difference in performance. This type of feedback is well-suited for scenarios where the arms' values cannot be precisely measured using metrics such as monetary scores, probabilities, or occurrences. Common examples include human preferences in matchmaking problems. Furthermore, its investigation answers the theoretical question on how numerical rewards are crucial in bandit settings. In particular, we study the problem of designing no-regret algorithms with ranking feedback both in the stochastic and adversarial settings. We show that, with stochastic rewards, differently from what happens with non-ranking feedback, no algorithm can suffer a logarithmic regret in the time horizon $T$ in the instance-dependent case. Furthermore, we provide two algorithms. The first, namely DREE, guarantees a superlogarithmic regret in $T$ in the instance-dependent case thus matching our lower bound, while the second, namely R-LPE, guarantees a regret of $\mathcal{\widetilde O}(\sqrt{T})$ in the instance-independent case. Remarkably, we show that no algorithm can have an optimal regret bound in both instance-dependent and instance-independent cases. Finally, we prove that no algorithm can achieve a sublinear regret when the rewards are adversarial.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a bandit problem in which a learner receives rankings of choices based on previous selections, without numerical information about performance differences. This matches situations where preferences can be ordered more readily than measured. It also isolates what is lost when a learning algorithm has relative feedback but no reward magnitudes.

For stochastic rewards, the authors prove that instance-dependent regret cannot grow only logarithmically with the time horizon.
