paragraphs: Learning how partial differential equations map inputs to solutions is difficult when the physical domain can take many shapes. The model must accommodate both geometric variation and the underlying physics. RIGNO addresses this problem with a graph neural network that learns solution operators from data represented as point clouds on arbitrary domains.

Its multi-scale architecture transfers information between input and output point clouds through a downsampled regional mesh. This intermediate representation provides a coarser structure through which the model processes the data. The design also includes components aimed at preserving behavior when spatial or temporal resolution changes, so the learned mapping can be applied beyond the sampling resolutions encountered during training.

The authors evaluate RIGNO on benchmarks containing both time-dependent and steady equations across diverse domains. They report significantly better accuracy than neural operator baselines and robust generalization to unseen resolutions in space and time. These findings support the combination of point-cloud inputs, regional processing, and resolution-aware design for learning PDE solution mappings across the tested geometries and physical problems.
summary.tldr: RIGNO learns PDE solution operators through point clouds and a regional mesh, with strong accuracy and generalization to unseen resolutions.

title: RIGNO: A Graph-based Framework For Robust And Accurate Operator Learning For PDEs On Arbitrary Domains

abstract: Speculative decoding is an effective and lossless method for Large Language Model (LLM) inference acceleration. It employs a smaller model to generate a draft token sequence, which is then verified by the original base model. In multi-GPU systems, inference latency can be further reduced through tensor parallelism (TP), while the optimal TP size of the draft model is typically smaller than that of the base model, leading to GPU idling during the drafting stage. We observe that such inefficiency stems from the sequential execution of layers, which is seemingly natural but actually unnecessary. Therefore, we propose EasySpec, a layer-parallel speculation strategy that optimizes the efficiency of multi-GPU utilization. EasySpec breaks the inter-layer data dependencies in the draft model, enabling multiple layers to run simultaneously across multiple devices as ``fuzzy'' speculation. After each drafting-and-verification iteration, the draft model’s key-value cache is calibrated in a single forward pass, preventing long-term fuzzy-error accumulation at minimal additional latency. EasySpec is a training-free and plug-in method. We evaluated EasySpec on several mainstream open-source LLMs, using smaller versions of models from the same series as drafters. The results demonstrate that EasySpec can achieve a peak speedup of 4.17x compared to vanilla decoding, while preserving the original distributions of the base LLMs. Specifically, the drafting stage can be accelerated by up to 1.62x with a maximum speculation accuracy drop of only 7\%. The code is available at https://github.com/Yize-Wu/EasySpec.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding speeds up language generation by asking a smaller model to draft tokens that the original model then verifies. On systems with multiple GPUs, the smaller model often benefits from fewer devices than the original model, leaving hardware idle during drafting. EasySpec targets this imbalance by changing how the draft model’s layers execute.

The method breaks dependencies between draft-model layers so that multiple layers can run simultaneously across devices. This produces approximate, or fuzzy, drafts. After each drafting and verification cycle, a single forward pass recalibrates the draft model’s key-value cache, preventing approximation errors from accumulating over time. The method requires no training and can be added to an existing decoding setup.

Evaluations use several open-source language models with smaller models from the same families as drafters. EasySpec reaches a peak speedup of 4.17 times over ordinary decoding while preserving the base model’s output distribution. Drafting accelerates by up to 1.62 times, with a maximum reported speculation-accuracy drop of 7%. These results show how faster approximate drafting can improve overall generation without changing the verified distribution.
summary.tldr: EasySpec runs draft-model layers in parallel to accelerate speculative decoding while preserving the original language model’s output distribution.

title: EasySpec: Layer-Parallel Speculative Decoding for Efficient Multi-GPU Utilization

abstract: Motivated by applications of large-scale graph clustering, we study random-walk-based LOCAL algorithms whose running times depend only on the size of the output cluster, rather than the entire graph. In particular, we develop a method with better theoretical guarantee compared to all previous work, both in terms of the clustering accuracy and the conductance of the output set. We also prove that our analysis is tight, and perform empirical evaluation to support our theory on both synthetic and real data. More specifically, our method outperforms prior work when the cluster is WELL-CONNECTED. In fact, the better it is well-connected inside, the more significant improvement we can obtain. Our results shed light on why in practice some random-walk-based algorithms perform better than its previous theory, and help guide future research about local clustering.

paragraphs: Finding a useful cluster in a huge graph need not require processing the entire graph. This paper studies local algorithms based on random walks, with running time tied to the size of the cluster they return. That computational goal makes the approach relevant when the desired output is small relative to the surrounding network.

The authors develop a method with stronger theoretical guarantees for both clustering accuracy and the conductance of the returned set. Conductance describes how strongly a set connects outward relative to its size in the graph. The improvement is especially associated with clusters that are well connected internally: stronger internal connectivity leads to a more substantial advantage over previous work.

The paper also proves that its analysis is tight and evaluates the method on synthetic and real data. These results help explain why some random-walk methods can work better in practice than earlier theory suggested. The central insight is that internal connectivity provides useful structure for analyzing local clustering, beyond simply asking whether a cluster has few outward connections.
summary.tldr: A local random-walk clustering method gains stronger guarantees when the desired cluster is well connected internally.

title: A Local Algorithm for Finding Well-Connected Clusters

abstract: We compare the plug-in rule approach for optimizing the F-measure in multi-label classification with an approach based on structured loss minimization, such as the structured support vector machine (SSVM). Whereas the former derives an optimal prediction from a probabilistic model in a separate inference step, the latter seeks to optimize the F-measure directly during the training phase. We introduce a novel plug-in rule algorithm that estimates all parameters required for a Bayes-optimal prediction via a set of multinomial regression models, and we compare this algorithm with SSVMs in terms of computational complexity and statistical consistency. As a main theoretical result, we show that our plug-in rule algorithm is consistent, whereas the SSVM approaches are not. Finally, we present results of a large experimental study showing the benefits of the introduced algorithm.

paragraphs: In multi-label classification, a prediction can assign several labels to one example. This paper compares two ways to optimize the F-measure for that task. A plug-in approach first learns a probabilistic model and then derives a prediction through a separate inference step. Structured loss minimization instead targets the measure during training.

The authors introduce a plug-in algorithm that uses a collection of multinomial regression models to estimate all parameters needed for a Bayes-optimal prediction. This separates learning the relevant probabilities from deciding which labels to output. They compare the method with structured support vector machines in both computational complexity and statistical consistency.

The main theoretical finding is that the proposed plug-in algorithm is consistent, whereas the SSVM approaches studied are not. This distinguishes their long-run statistical behavior, beyond whether their training objectives appear directly aligned with the evaluation measure. A large experimental study also reports benefits for the proposed algorithm, supporting its practical value alongside the consistency result.
summary.tldr: A multinomial-regression plug-in method for multi-label F-measure optimization is consistent, unlike the structured SVM approaches examined.

title: Optimizing the F-Measure in Multi-Label Classification: Plug-in Rule Approach versus Structured Loss Minimization

abstract: Much natural data is hierarchical in nature. Moreover, this hierarchy is often shared between different instances. We introduce the nested Chinese Restaurant Franchise Process as a means to obtain both hierarchical tree-structured representations for objects, akin to (but more general than) the nested Chinese Restaurant Process while sharing their structure akin to the Hierarchical Dirichlet Process. Moreover, by decoupling the \emphstructure generating part of the process from the components responsible for the observations, we are able to apply the same statistical approach to a variety of user generated data. In particular, we model the joint distribution of microblogs and locations for Twitter for users. This leads to a 40% reduction in location uncertainty relative to the best previously published results. Moreover, we model documents from the NIPS papers dataset, obtaining excellent perplexity relative to (hierarchical) Pachinko allocation and LDA.

paragraphs: Many datasets contain hierarchical structure, and different objects may share parts of that hierarchy. The paper introduces the nested Chinese Restaurant Franchise Process to represent both properties together. It supports tree-structured object representations while allowing their structure to be shared across instances.

The model combines ideas associated with nested Chinese Restaurant Processes and Hierarchical Dirichlet Processes, while offering a more general hierarchical representation than the former. It also separates the process that generates structure from the components that generate observations. This separation lets the same statistical framework be applied to different types of user-generated data.

One application jointly models Twitter users' microblogs and locations, reducing location uncertainty by 40% relative to the best previously published results cited in the abstract. Another models documents in the NIPS papers dataset and reports strong perplexity relative to hierarchical Pachinko allocation and LDA. These results demonstrate the framework in two settings where shared latent structure can help account for observed data.
summary.tldr: A shared hierarchical probabilistic model improves reported user-location uncertainty and gives strong document-modeling results.

title: Nested Chinese Restaurant Franchise Process: Applications to User Tracking and Document Modeling

abstract: A fundamental class of matrix optimization problems that arise in many areas of science and engineering is that of quadratic optimization with orthogonality constraints. Such problems can be solved using line-search methods on the Stiefel manifold, which are known to converge globally under mild conditions. To determine the convergence rates of these methods, we give an explicit estimate of the exponent in a Lojasiewicz inequality for the (non-convex) set of critical points of the aforementioned class of problems. This not only allows us to establish the linear convergence of a large class of line-search methods but also answers an important and intriguing problem in mathematical analysis and numerical optimization. A key step in our proof is to establish a local error bound for the set of critical points, which may be of independent interest.

Such problems can be solved using line-search methods on the Stiefel manifold, which are known to converge globally under mild conditions. To determine the convergence rates of these methods, we give an explicit estimate of the exponent in a Lojasiewicz inequality for the (non-convex) set of critical points of the aforementioned class of problems. This not only allows us to establish the linear convergence of a large class of line-search methods but also answers an important and intriguing problem in mathematical analysis and numerical optimization. paragraphs: The paper studies quadratic matrix optimization subject to orthogonality constraints. These constraints place the variables on a Stiefel manifold, and line-search algorithms on that manifold were already known to converge under mild conditions. The question addressed here is how quickly such methods converge for this class of problems.

The authors obtain an explicit estimate of the exponent in a Lojasiewicz inequality associated with the nonconvex set of critical points. This inequality provides the mathematical link needed to turn convergence information into a rate. Using the estimate, they establish linear convergence for a large class of line-search methods.

A central proof ingredient is a local error bound for the set of critical points, which the authors identify as potentially useful beyond this analysis. The result strengthens understanding of existing optimization methods by supplying a rate guarantee for the problem class. Its focus is convergence around critical points; linear convergence describes the rate of progress and should not be read as a statement that every method finds a global optimum.
summary.tldr: An explicit Lojasiewicz exponent establishes linear convergence for a broad class of orthogonality-constrained quadratic optimization methods.

title: Quadratic Optimization with Orthogonality Constraints: Explicit Lojasiewicz Exponent and Linear Convergence of Line-Search Methods

abstract: We propose an approximate strategy to efficiently train neural network based language models over very large vocabularies. Our approach, called adaptive softmax, circumvents the linear dependency on the vocabulary size by exploiting the unbalanced word distribution to form clusters that explicitly minimize the expectation of computation time. Our approach further reduces the computational cost by exploiting the specificities of modern architectures and matrix-matrix vector operations, making it particularly suited for graphical processing units. Our experiments carried out on standard benchmarks, such as EuroParl and One Billion Word, show that our approach brings a large gain in efficiency over standard approximations while achieving an accuracy close to that of the full softmax. The code of our method is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/adaptive-softmax.

paragraphs: The paper targets the computational expense of training neural language models with very large vocabularies. When computation grows linearly with vocabulary size, enlarging the set of possible words increases the training burden. Adaptive softmax uses the uneven distribution of word frequencies to reorganize this work.

The method forms word clusters with the explicit objective of minimizing expected computation time. Because words occur at different rates, the clustering can account for how often different computations will be needed. The approach also incorporates characteristics of modern computing architectures and matrix operations, making the resulting approximation especially suitable for GPUs.

Experiments on standard language-modeling benchmarks, including EuroParl and One Billion Word, show large efficiency gains over standard approximations. Prediction accuracy remains close to that of full softmax in those experiments. The significance is a demonstrated balance between computation and accuracy: the approximation uses both word-frequency structure and hardware characteristics to reduce training cost while retaining much of the full model’s accuracy.
summary.tldr: Adaptive softmax uses word-frequency-aware clustering and GPU-friendly computation to accelerate language-model training while approaching full-softmax accuracy.

title: Efficient softmax approximation for GPUs

abstract: In many sequential planning applications a natural approach to generating high quality plans is to maximize an information reward such as mutual information (MI). Unfortunately, MI lacks a closed form in all but trivial models, and so must be estimated. In applications where the cost of plan execution is expensive, one desires planning estimates which admit theoretical guarantees. Through the use of robust M-estimators we obtain bounds on absolute deviation of estimated MI. Moreover, we propose a sequential algorithm which integrates inference and planning by maximally reusing particles in each stage. We validate the utility of using robust estimators in the sequential approach on a Gaussian Markov Random Field wherein information measures have a closed form. Lastly, we demonstrate the benefits of our integrated approach in the context of sequential experiment design for inferring causal regulatory networks from gene expression levels. Our method shows improvements over a recent method which selects intervention experiments based on the same MI objective.

We validate the utility of using robust estimators in the sequential approach on a Gaussian Markov Random Field wherein information measures have a closed form. Our method shows improvements over a recent method which selects intervention experiments based on the same MI objective.

paragraphs: Sequential information gathering chooses actions according to how much they are expected to teach us. Mutual information provides a natural score for this purpose, but it usually cannot be calculated exactly. When executing a plan is expensive, inaccurate information estimates can undermine the value of the resulting decisions.

The paper uses robust M-estimators to estimate mutual information and derives bounds on the estimates’ absolute error. These bounds give theoretical support for the information scores used in planning. The authors also introduce a sequential algorithm that connects inference with planning by reusing particles as extensively as possible at each stage.

The evaluation first uses a Gaussian Markov Random Field, where information quantities can be calculated exactly, to assess the usefulness of robust estimation. The method is then applied to choosing intervention experiments for learning causal regulatory networks from gene expression. In that setting, the integrated approach improves over a recent method using the same mutual-information objective, supporting the value of how that objective is estimated and incorporated into sequential decisions.
summary.tldr: Robust mutual-information estimates and particle reuse improve sequential information gathering while providing bounds on estimation error.

title: A Robust Approach to Sequential Information Theoretic Planning

abstract: Predictive performance of machine learning algorithms on related problems can be improved using multitask learning approaches. Rather than performing survival analysis on each data set to predict survival times of cancer patients, we developed a novel multitask approach based on multiple kernel learning (MKL). Our multitask MKL algorithm both works on multiple cancer data sets and integrates cancer-related pathways/gene sets into survival analysis. We tested our algorithm, which is named as Path2MSurv, on the Cancer Genome Atlas data sets analyzing gene expression profiles of 7,655 patients from 20 cancer types together with cancer-specific pathway/gene set collections. Path2MSurv obtained better or comparable predictive performance when benchmarked against random survival forest, survival support vector machine, and single-task variant of our algorithm. Path2MSurv has the ability to identify key pathways/gene sets in predicting survival times of patients from different cancer types.

The motivation is that related prediction problems can benefit from being analyzed together, allowing the learning process to use information shared across tasks.

Path2MSurv uses multiple kernel learning and incorporates cancer-related pathways and gene sets into survival analysis. Its design therefore combines two kinds of structure: relationships among cancer datasets and biological groupings of genes. The method can also identify pathways or gene sets that are useful for predicting survival in different cancer types, connecting its predictions to these biological groupings.

The evaluation uses Cancer Genome Atlas gene expression profiles from 7,655 patients across 20 cancer types. Path2MSurv delivers better or comparable predictive performance against random survival forests, survival support vector machines, and its single-task variant. These findings support the usefulness of the combined approach without implying that it outperforms every comparator on every cancer type.
summary.tldr: Path2MSurv combines learning across cancer types with pathway information to achieve better or comparable survival prediction against the tested alternatives.

title: A Multitask Multiple Kernel Learning Algorithm for Survival Analysis with Application to Cancer Biology

abstract: Weak supervision is a popular method for building machine learning models without relying on ground truth annotations. Instead, it generates probabilistic training labels by estimating the accuracies of multiple noisy labeling sources (e.g., heuristics, crowd workers). Existing approaches use latent variable estimation to model the noisy sources, but these methods can be computationally expensive, scaling superlinearly in the data. In this work, we show that, for a class of latent variable models highly applicable to weak supervision, we can find a closed-form solution to model parameters, obviating the need for iterative solutions like stochastic gradient descent (SGD). We use this insight to build FlyingSquid, a weak supervision framework that runs orders of magnitude faster than previous weak supervision approaches and requires fewer assumptions. In particular, we prove bounds on generalization error without assuming that the latent variable model can exactly parameterize the underlying data distribution. Empirically, we validate FlyingSquid on benchmark weak supervision datasets and find that it achieves the same or higher quality compared to previous approaches without the need to tune an SGD procedure, recovers model parameters 170 times faster on average, and enables new video analysis and online learning applications.

A central task is estimating how accurate those sources are so their outputs can be combined into probabilistic labels. Existing latent-variable estimation approaches can make this step expensive, with computational costs growing superlinearly in the data.

The authors identify a class of latent-variable models for which the parameters have a closed-form solution. This removes the need for iterative fitting procedures such as stochastic gradient descent. They use the result to build FlyingSquid, a weak-supervision framework that also requires fewer assumptions. The reported speed improvements enable video-analysis and online-learning applications, showing why simplifying label-model estimation can expand where weak supervision is practical.
summary.tldr: FlyingSquid uses closed-form label-model estimation to accelerate weak supervision while maintaining or improving benchmark quality.

title: Fast and Three-rious: Speeding Up Weak Supervision with Triplet Methods

abstract: We demonstrate two new important properties of the 1-path-norm of shallow neural networks. First, despite its non-smoothness and non-convexity it allows a closed form proximal operator which can be efficiently computed, allowing the use of stochastic proximal-gradient-type methods for regularized empirical risk minimization. Second, when the activation functions is differentiable, it provides an upper bound on the Lipschitz constant of the network. Such bound is tighter than the trivial layer-wise product of Lipschitz constants, motivating its use for training networks robust to adversarial perturbations. In practical experiments we illustrate the advantages of using the proximal mapping and we compare the robustness-accuracy trade-off induced by the 1-path-norm, L1-norm and layer-wise constraints on the Lipschitz constant (Parseval networks).

paragraphs: The paper establishes two useful properties of the 1-path-norm for shallow neural networks. The first concerns optimization: despite being non-smooth and non-convex, this regularizer has a closed-form proximal operator that can be computed efficiently. That operator provides a way to incorporate the regularizer into a learning update.

This result enables stochastic proximal-gradient-type methods for regularized empirical risk minimization. The second property concerns sensitivity to input changes. When the network's activation function is differentiable, the 1-path-norm bounds the network's Lipschitz constant. The authors show that this bound is tighter than the straightforward product of layer-level Lipschitz bounds, motivating its use in training against adversarial perturbations.

Experiments illustrate the advantages of the proximal mapping and compare the robustness–accuracy tradeoff from three approaches: the 1-path-norm, L1 regularization, and layer-wise Lipschitz constraints used in Parseval networks. The contribution therefore joins an efficient optimization tool with a theoretical reason to study the same regularizer for robustness; the abstract does not declare a universal winner in the empirical comparison.
summary.tldr: The 1-path-norm admits an efficient proximal operator and, with differentiable activations, a tighter network sensitivity bound that motivates robustness applications.

title: Efficient Proximal Mapping of the 1-path-norm of Shallow Networks

abstract: When quantizing neural networks, assigning each floating-point weight to its nearest fixed-point value is the predominant approach. We find that, perhaps surprisingly, this is not the best we can do. In this paper, we propose AdaRound, a better weight-rounding mechanism for post-training quantization that adapts to the data and the task loss. AdaRound is fast, does not require fine-tuning of the network, and only uses a small amount of unlabelled data. We start by theoretically analyzing the rounding problem for a pre-trained neural network. By approximating the task loss with a Taylor series expansion, the rounding task is posed as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization problem. We simplify this to a layer-wise local loss and propose to optimize this loss with a soft relaxation. AdaRound not only outperforms rounding-to-nearest by a significant margin but also establishes a new state-of-the-art for post-training quantization on several networks and tasks. Without fine-tuning, we can quantize the weights of Resnet18 and Resnet50 to 4 bits while staying within an accuracy loss of 1%.

paragraphs: Quantization replaces floating-point neural-network weights with values that use fewer bits. The usual rule rounds each weight to its nearest representable value. This paper shows that choosing rounding directions with awareness of the data and task loss can preserve performance better than treating each weight’s numerical distance as the deciding factor.

The authors introduce AdaRound, a fast post-training rounding method requiring only a small amount of unlabeled data and no network fine-tuning. A Taylor approximation of the task loss leads to a binary optimization problem over rounding choices. They simplify that problem into a layer-wise local objective and optimize a soft relaxation, making the rounding decisions practical to learn.

AdaRound substantially outperforms nearest-value rounding and achieves leading post-training quantization results across several evaluated networks and tasks. For ResNet18 and ResNet50, the authors report four-bit weights with accuracy loss within 1%, without fine-tuning. These findings show that the rounding decision itself is a consequential part of preserving a trained network’s performance.
summary.tldr: AdaRound learns data-aware rounding choices, enabling reported four-bit ResNet quantization with accuracy loss within 1% and no fine-tuning.

title: Up or Down? Adaptive Rounding for Post-Training Quantization

abstract: Explaining how overparametrized neural networks simultaneously achieve low risk and zero empirical risk on benchmark datasets is an open problem. PAC-Bayes bounds optimized using variational inference (VI) have been recently proposed as a promising direction in obtaining non-vacuous bounds. We show empirically that this approach gives negligible gains when modelling the posterior as a Gaussian with diagonal covariance—known as the mean-field approximation. We investigate common explanations, such as the failure of VI due to problems in optimization or choosing a suboptimal prior. Our results suggest that investigating richer posteriors is the most promising direction forward.

We show empirically that this approach gives negligible gains when modelling the posterior as a Gaussian with diagonal covariance—known as the mean-field approximation. We investigate common explanations, such as the failure of VI due to problems in optimization or choosing a suboptimal prior. Our results suggest that investigating richer posteriors is the most promising direction forward.

paragraphs: Overparameterized neural networks can fit their training data perfectly while still making relatively few errors on new examples. Explaining this combination remains difficult. One proposed route uses PAC-Bayes bounds, which relate predictive performance to distributions over models, and optimizes those bounds using variational inference.

This paper examines the mean-field version of that approach. Here, the posterior distribution is represented by a Gaussian with diagonal covariance, so it does not represent correlations between model parameters. The authors empirically find that optimizing PAC-Bayes bounds within this restricted family produces negligible gains. Their investigation concerns how useful this particular approximation is for obtaining informative generalization guarantees.

The authors also examine possible explanations involving optimization difficulties in variational inference and a poorly chosen prior. Their results suggest that richer posterior distributions are the most promising direction for further progress. This is an empirical diagnosis and a research recommendation: the findings motivate reconsidering the distributional approximation used to describe trained networks, rather than establishing that every mean-field method must fail.
summary.tldr: An empirical study finds negligible gains from mean-field variational PAC-Bayes bounds and points toward richer posterior distributions.

title: Dissecting Non-Vacuous Generalization Bounds based on the Mean-Field Approximation

abstract: The success of GANs is usually attributed to properties of the divergence obtained by an optimal discriminator. In this work we show that this approach has a fundamental flaw:\\{If} we do not impose regularity of the discriminator, it can exploit visually imperceptible errors of the generator to always achieve the maximal generator loss. In practice, gradient penalties are used to regularize the discriminator. However, this needs a metric on the space of images that captures visual similarity. Such a metric is not known, which explains the limited success of gradient penalties in stabilizing GANs.\\{Instead}, we argue that the implicit competitive regularization (ICR) arising from the simultaneous optimization of generator and discriminator enables GANs performance. We show that opponent-aware modelling of generator and discriminator, as present in competitive gradient descent (CGD), can significantly strengthen ICR and thus stabilize GAN training without explicit regularization. In our experiments, we use an existing implementation of WGAN-GP and show that by training it with CGD without any explicit regularization, we can improve the inception score (IS) on CIFAR10, without any hyperparameter tuning.

paragraphs: GAN performance is often explained through the divergence defined by an optimal discriminator. This paper challenges that account: without restrictions on discriminator regularity, visually imperceptible generator errors can allow the discriminator to produce maximal generator loss. The authors also argue that gradient penalties face a difficulty because they need an image-space metric that captures visual similarity, which is not known.

Their alternative explanation emphasizes implicit competitive regularization arising as generator and discriminator are optimized together. The interaction between the two learning processes can itself provide regularization. The paper argues that opponent-aware updates, specifically competitive gradient descent, can strengthen this effect and stabilize training without adding explicit regularization.

In experiments, the authors take an existing WGAN-GP implementation and train it using competitive gradient descent with no explicit regularization. They report an improved inception score on CIFAR10 without hyperparameter tuning. This result supports the proposed role of competitive training dynamics and demonstrates a concrete setting where strengthening those dynamics improves the reported GAN outcome.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that competitive training dynamics implicitly regularize GANs and shows that opponent-aware updates can improve training without explicit regularization.

title: Implicit competitive regularization in GANs

abstract: Traditional differential privacy is independent of the data distribution. However, this is not well-matched with the modern machine learning context, where models are trained on specific data. As a result, achieving meaningful privacy guarantees in ML often excessively reduces accuracy. We propose Bayesian differential privacy (BDP), which takes into account the data distribution to provide more practical privacy guarantees. We also derive a general privacy accounting method under BDP, building upon the well-known moments accountant. Our experiments demonstrate that in-distribution samples in classic machine learning datasets, such as MNIST and CIFAR-10, enjoy significantly stronger privacy guarantees than postulated by DP, while models maintain high classification accuracy.

We also derive a general privacy accounting method under BDP, building upon the well-known moments accountant. paragraphs: Traditional differential privacy provides guarantees that do not depend on the data distribution. The authors argue that this can be a poor fit for machine learning, where a model is trained on a particular kind of data. Obtaining useful guarantees under the traditional formulation can substantially reduce prediction accuracy.

The paper introduces Bayesian differential privacy, which incorporates the data distribution into its privacy definition. It also develops a general method for accounting for privacy under this definition, building on the moments accountant. Together, the definition and accounting method provide a way to assess privacy while explicitly considering the distribution relevant to learning.

Experiments on datasets including MNIST and CIFAR-10 report substantially stronger guarantees for samples from the data distribution than traditional differential privacy would indicate, while classification accuracy remains high. The scope of that result matters: the improved guarantees concern in-distribution samples under the proposed formulation. The contribution is a distribution-aware approach to the privacy–accuracy tradeoff, supported by both accounting theory and empirical evaluation.
summary.tldr: Bayesian differential privacy incorporates the data distribution to obtain stronger in-distribution privacy guarantees while maintaining high classification accuracy.

title: Bayesian Differential Privacy for Machine Learning

abstract: Recent work has shown that topological enhancements to recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can increase their expressiveness and representational capacity. Two popular enhancements are stacked RNNs, which increases the capacity for learning non-linear functions, and bidirectional processing, which exploits acausal information in a sequence. In this work, we explore the delayed-RNN, which is a single-layer RNN that has a delay between the input and output. We prove that a weight-constrained version of the delayed-RNN is equivalent to a stacked-RNN. We also show that the delay gives rise to partial acausality, much like bidirectional networks. Synthetic experiments confirm that the delayed-RNN can mimic bidirectional networks, solving some acausal tasks similarly, and outperforming them in others. Moreover, we show similar performance to bidirectional networks in a real-world natural language processing task. These results suggest that delayed-RNNs can approximate topologies including stacked RNNs, bidirectional RNNs, and stacked bidirectional RNNs – but with equivalent or faster runtimes for the delayed-RNNs.

paragraphs: Recurrent networks often gain expressive power by stacking layers or processing a sequence in both directions. Stacking supports more complex nonlinear computations, while bidirectional processing lets predictions use information occurring later in the sequence. This paper examines whether delaying a single-layer network’s outputs can reproduce some of those benefits.

The proposed delayed-RNN leaves a gap between receiving an input and producing its corresponding output. The authors prove that a version with constrained weights is equivalent to a stacked recurrent network. Delaying outputs also permits partial access to later information, creating a form of the future context used by bidirectional networks.

In synthetic experiments, delayed-RNNs match bidirectional networks on some tasks requiring future information and outperform them on others. A natural language processing experiment also shows similar performance. Together, the results suggest that delayed networks can approximate stacked, bidirectional, and combined architectures with comparable or faster runtimes. The exact equivalence result applies to the weight-constrained construction; the broader architectural comparisons are supported by experiments.
summary.tldr: Delaying a single-layer recurrent network’s outputs can reproduce stacking and approximate bidirectional processing with competitive performance and runtime.

title: Approximating Stacked and Bidirectional Recurrent Architectures with the Delayed Recurrent Neural Network

abstract: Training machine learning models that are robust against adversarial inputs poses seemingly insurmountable challenges. To better understand adversarial robustness, we consider the underlying problem of learning robust representations. We develop a notion of representation vulnerability that captures the maximum change of mutual information between the input and output distributions, under the worst-case input perturbation. Then, we prove a theorem that establishes a lower bound on the minimum adversarial risk that can be achieved for any downstream classifier based on its representation vulnerability. We propose an unsupervised learning method for obtaining intrinsically robust representations by maximizing the worst-case mutual information between the input and output distributions. Experiments on downstream classification tasks support the robustness of the representations found using unsupervised learning with our training principle.
originalAbstract: Training machine learning models that are robust against adversarial inputs poses seemingly insurmountable challenges. To better understand adversarial robustness, we consider the underlying problem of learning robust representations. We develop a notion of representation vulnerability that captures the maximum change of mutual information between the input and output distributions, under the worst-case input perturbation. Then, we prove a theorem that establishes a lower bound on the minimum adversarial risk that can be achieved for any downstream classifier based on its representation vulnerability. We propose an unsupervised learning method for obtaining intrinsically robust representations by maximizing the worst-case mutual information between the input and output distributions. Experiments on downstream classification tasks support the robustness of the representations found using unsupervised learning with our training principle.

paragraphs: This paper examines adversarial robustness through the representations that a classifier uses. It asks how changes to the input can affect the information preserved by those representations. The authors define representation vulnerability through the largest change in mutual information between input and output distributions under a worst-case input perturbation.

They then prove a theorem connecting that vulnerability to a lower bound on the minimum adversarial risk attainable by any downstream classifier using the representation. This makes representation quality relevant to what later classifiers can achieve. A lower bound identifies a limit on attainable risk; it does not by itself guarantee that a particular classifier reaches that limit.

Guided by this analysis, the authors propose unsupervised learning that maximizes mutual information under worst-case perturbations. The training objective seeks representations that preserve information even when inputs are adversarially changed. Experiments on downstream classification tasks support the robustness of representations learned with this principle. The paper thus links a theoretical characterization of vulnerability to a representation-learning objective and empirical downstream evidence.
summary.tldr: Maximizing worst-case mutual information provides an unsupervised training principle for representations with empirically supported adversarial robustness.

title: Learning Adversarially Robust Representations via Worst-Case Mutual Information Maximization

abstract: We study the emergence of chaotic behavior of Follow-the-Regularized Leader (FoReL) dynamics in games. We focus on the effects of increasing the population size or the scale of costs in congestion games, and generalize recent results on unstable, chaotic behaviors in the Multiplicative Weights Update dynamics to a much larger class of FoReL dynamics. We establish that, even in simple linear non-atomic congestion games with two parallel links and \emph{any} fixed learning rate, unless the game is fully symmetric, increasing the population size or the scale of costs causes learning dynamics to becomes unstable and eventually chaotic, in the sense of Li-Yorke and positive topological entropy. Furthermore, we prove the existence of novel non-standard phenomena such as the coexistence of stable Nash equilibria and chaos in the same game. We also observe the simultaneous creation of a chaotic attractor as another chaotic attractor gets destroyed. Lastly, although FoReL dynamics can be strange and non-equilibrating, we prove that the time average still converges to an \emph{exact} equilibrium for any choice of learning rate and any scale of costs.

We establish that, even in simple linear non-atomic congestion games with two parallel links and \emph{any} fixed learning rate, unless the game is fully symmetric, increasing the population size or the scale of costs causes learning dynamics to becomes unstable and eventually chaotic, in the sense of Li-Yorke and positive topological entropy. We also observe the simultaneous creation of a chaotic attractor as another chaotic attractor gets destroyed. Lastly, although FoReL dynamics can be strange and non-equilibrating, we prove that the time average still converges to an \emph{exact} equilibrium for any choice of learning rate and any scale of costs.

paragraphs: When many users repeatedly choose routes, each user's learning changes the congestion experienced by everyone else. This paper studies that feedback under Follow-the-Regularized-Leader learning dynamics. It asks how increasing the population or scaling up costs affects stability, extending earlier results about Multiplicative Weights Update to a much broader family of learning rules.

Even a game with two parallel links and linear congestion costs can become unstable and eventually chaotic. For the non-atomic games studied, this happens as population size or cost scale increases at any fixed learning rate, unless the game is fully symmetric. The authors establish chaos in formal mathematical senses and prove that stable Nash equilibria and chaos can coexist within one game.

They also observe one chaotic attractor appearing while another disappears. Despite this complicated behavior, the time average converges to an exact equilibrium for every learning rate and cost scale in the studied setting. The result separates two notions of success: individual learning trajectories may remain erratic even while their long-run averages settle at equilibrium.
summary.tldr: Routing-game learning can become chaotic as demand or costs grow, while its time average still converges to an exact equilibrium.

title: Follow-the-Regularized-Leader Routes to Chaos in Routing Games

abstract: We develop and analyze MARINA: a new communication efficient method for non-convex distributed learning over heterogeneous datasets. MARINA employs a novel communication compression strategy based on the compression of gradient differences that is reminiscent of but different from the strategy employed in the DIANA method of Mishchenko et al. (2019). Unlike virtually all competing distributed first-order methods, including DIANA, ours is based on a carefully designed biased gradient estimator, which is the key to its superior theoretical and practical performance. The communication complexity bounds we prove for MARINA are evidently better than those of all previous first-order methods. Further, we develop and analyze two variants of MARINA: VR-MARINA and PP-MARINA. The first method is designed for the case when the local loss functions owned by clients are either of a finite sum or of an expectation form, and the second method allows for a partial participation of clients {–} a feature important in federated learning. All our methods are superior to previous state-of-the-art methods in terms of oracle/communication complexity. Finally, we provide a convergence analysis of all methods for problems satisfying the Polyak-{Ł}ojasiewicz condition.

(2019). paragraphs: Distributed learning must coordinate optimization across clients whose datasets can differ. Communication becomes part of the computational cost, especially when clients repeatedly exchange gradient information. MARINA addresses non-convex learning in this heterogeneous setting with a compression strategy built around differences between gradients.

A distinctive feature is its deliberately biased gradient estimator. The authors identify this carefully designed bias as central to the method’s theoretical and practical advantages. They prove communication complexity bounds that improve on previous first-order methods. The compression strategy resembles the idea used in DIANA but differs in its construction and in the estimator it supports.

The paper also develops VR-MARINA for local objectives expressed as finite sums or expectations, and PP-MARINA for settings where only some clients participate. These variants extend the approach to different local computation structures and participation patterns relevant to federated learning. The authors report improved oracle and communication complexity across their methods, and additionally analyze convergence for problems satisfying the Polyak-Łojasiewicz condition. That final analysis applies to a specified class of optimization problems.
summary.tldr: MARINA uses compressed gradient differences and a carefully biased estimator to improve distributed optimization complexity, with variants for different objectives and partial participation.

title: MARINA: Faster Non-Convex Distributed Learning with Compression

abstract: Hindsight rationality is an approach to playing general-sum games that prescribes no-regret learning dynamics for individual agents with respect to a set of deviations, and further describes jointly rational behavior among multiple agents with mediated equilibria. To develop hindsight rational learning in sequential decision-making settings, we formalize behavioral deviations as a general class of deviations that respect the structure of extensive-form games. Integrating the idea of time selection into counterfactual regret minimization (CFR), we introduce the extensive-form regret minimization (EFR) algorithm that achieves hindsight rationality for any given set of behavioral deviations with computation that scales closely with the complexity of the set. We identify behavioral deviation subsets, the partial sequence deviation types, that subsume previously studied types and lead to efficient EFR instances in games with moderate lengths. In addition, we present a thorough empirical analysis of EFR instantiated with different deviation types in benchmark games, where we find that stronger types typically induce better performance.

paragraphs: Hindsight rationality evaluates a player's behavior against a specified collection of alternative behaviors, called deviations. Learning should avoid accumulating regret relative to those alternatives. This paper develops that idea for sequential games, where decisions occur within a structured sequence, and where the players' interests need not be directly opposed to one another.

The authors formalize behavioral deviations that respect the structure of extensive-form games. They then introduce extensive-form regret minimization, or EFR, by combining time selection with counterfactual regret minimization. EFR achieves hindsight rationality for a chosen set of behavioral deviations, with computation scaling closely with the complexity of that set. The comparison standard and computational burden are consequently linked.

A family called partial sequence deviations includes previously studied deviation types and yields efficient EFR instances for games of moderate length. Benchmark experiments compare different choices and find that stronger deviation types typically improve performance. The result offers both a general learning framework and useful intermediate choices for balancing richer hindsight comparisons against their computational cost.
summary.tldr: EFR learns against structured alternatives in sequential games, with computational cost tied to the richness of those alternatives.

title: Efficient Deviation Types and Learning for Hindsight Rationality in Extensive-Form Games

abstract: We provide a unifying view of a large family of previous imitation learning algorithms through the lens of moment matching. At its core, our classification scheme is based on whether the learner attempts to match (1) reward or (2) action-value moments of the expert’s behavior, with each option leading to differing algorithmic approaches. By considering adversarially chosen divergences between learner and expert behavior, we are able to derive bounds on policy performance that apply for all algorithms in each of these classes, the first to our knowledge. We also introduce the notion of moment recoverability, implicit in many previous analyses of imitation learning, which allows us to cleanly delineate how well each algorithmic family is able to mitigate compounding errors. We derive three novel algorithm templates (AdVIL, AdRIL, and DAeQuIL) with strong guarantees, simple implementation, and competitive empirical performance.

paragraphs: Imitation learning seeks policies that reproduce useful aspects of an expert’s behavior. This paper organizes a large family of existing algorithms around moment matching: matching selected summaries of learner and expert behavior. Its main division is between methods that match reward moments and those that match action-value moments, leading to different algorithmic approaches.

The authors analyze these families by allowing the discrepancy between learner and expert to be chosen adversarially. This yields policy-performance bounds that apply across algorithms within each class. They also make explicit a concept called moment recoverability, which had been implicit in earlier analyses. It helps distinguish how effectively different families can mitigate errors that compound over a sequence of decisions.

The framework produces three new algorithm templates: AdVIL, AdRIL, and DAeQuIL. The authors report strong guarantees, simple implementations, and competitive empirical performance for these templates. The contribution therefore provides both a shared language for comparing existing approaches and a route to new methods, with recoverability clarifying why different forms of matching offer different protection against accumulating mistakes.
summary.tldr: A moment-matching framework unifies imitation-learning methods, bounds their performance, and produces three new algorithm templates.

title: Of Moments and Matching: A Game-Theoretic Framework for Closing the Imitation Gap

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of exact community recovery in the symmetric stochastic block model, where a graph of $n$ vertices is randomly generated by partitioning the vertices into $K \ge 2$ equal-sized communities and then connecting each pair of vertices with probability that depends on their community memberships. Although the maximum-likelihood formulation of this problem is discrete and non-convex, we propose to tackle it directly using projected power iterations with an initialization that satisfies a partial recovery condition. Such an initialization can be obtained by a host of existing methods. We show that in the logarithmic degree regime of the considered problem, the proposed method can exactly recover the underlying communities at the information-theoretic limit. Moreover, with a qualified initialization, it runs in $\mO(n\log^2n/\log\log n)$ time, which is competitive with existing state-of-the-art methods. We also present numerical results of the proposed method to support and complement our theoretical development.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovering every community membership in a symmetric stochastic block model. The graph is generated from at least two equally sized communities, with connection probabilities determined by whether vertices belong to the same or different communities. The maximum-likelihood formulation is discrete and non-convex, which makes direct optimization a challenging starting point.

The authors tackle that formulation using projected power iterations. Their method needs an initial assignment satisfying a partial-recovery condition, and existing methods can supply such an initialization. In the logarithmic-degree regime, they prove that the iterations can recover the communities exactly at the information-theoretic limit, reaching the statistical threshold identified for the problem.

With a qualified initialization, the stated running time is O(n log² n / log log n), competitive with existing state-of-the-art methods. Numerical results support and complement the theoretical analysis. The result shows that direct non-convex optimization can combine strong recovery guarantees with efficient computation in this model, provided the algorithm starts from a sufficiently informative initial community assignment.
summary.tldr: With suitable initialization, projected power iterations achieve information-theoretically optimal exact community recovery in the studied stochastic block model.

title: Optimal Non-Convex Exact Recovery in Stochastic Block Model via Projected Power Method

abstract: Due to the computational cost of running inference for a neural network, the need to deploy the inferential steps on a third party’s compute environment or hardware is common. If the third party is not fully trusted, it is desirable to obfuscate the nature of the inputs and outputs, so that the third party can not easily determine what specific task is being performed. Provably secure protocols for leveraging an untrusted party exist but are too computational demanding to run in practice. We instead explore a different strategy of fast, heuristic security that we call Connectionist Symbolic Pseudo Secrets . By leveraging Holographic Reduced Representations (HRRs), we create a neural network with a pseudo-encryption style defense that empirically shows robustness to attack, even under threat models that unrealistically favor the adversary.

paragraphs: Running neural-network predictions can require more computing power than is available locally, motivating deployment on a third party’s hardware. When that party is not fully trusted, the inputs and outputs can reveal the nature of the task being performed. This paper investigates a computationally practical way to obscure that information during outsourced inference.

The proposed strategy, called Connectionist Symbolic Pseudo Secrets, uses Holographic Reduced Representations to create a pseudo-encryption-style defense for a neural network. Its objective is to make the underlying task harder for the third party to determine. The paper frames this as fast, heuristic protection, motivated by the computational demands of protocols that provide provable security.

The reported experiments show robustness against attacks, including threat models that give the adversary unusually favorable conditions. Those findings provide empirical evidence for the defense in the evaluated settings. The distinction between experimental robustness and a security proof is central to the contribution: the method explores what protection a fast representation-based mechanism can provide when the computational cost of provably secure approaches is a barrier.
summary.tldr: A defense based on Holographic Reduced Representations empirically obscures neural-network inference on untrusted platforms using fast, heuristic protection.

title: Deploying Convolutional Networks on Untrusted Platforms Using 2D Holographic Reduced Representations

abstract: In label-noise learning, estimating the transition matrix is a hot topic as the matrix plays an important role in building statistically consistent classifiers. Traditionally, the transition from clean labels to noisy labels (i.e., clean-label transition matrix (CLTM)) has been widely exploited to learn a clean label classifier by employing the noisy data. Motivated by that classifiers mostly output Bayes optimal labels for prediction, in this paper, we study to directly model the transition from Bayes optimal labels to noisy labels (i.e., Bayes-label transition matrix (BLTM)) and learn a classifier to predict Bayes optimal labels. Note that given only noisy data, it is ill-posed to estimate either the CLTM or the BLTM. But favorably, Bayes optimal labels have less uncertainty compared with the clean labels, i.e., the class posteriors of Bayes optimal labels are one-hot vectors while those of clean labels are not. This enables two advantages to estimate the BLTM, i.e., (a) a set of examples with theoretically guaranteed Bayes optimal labels can be collected out of noisy data; (b) the feasible solution space is much smaller. By exploiting the advantages, we estimate the BLTM parametrically by employing a deep neural network, leading to better generalization and superior classification performance.

paragraphs: Learning from incorrect labels often involves estimating a transition matrix that describes how clean labels become noisy observations. This paper changes the starting point of that transition. It models how Bayes optimal labels, the labels an optimal classifier would predict, relate to noisy labels, and trains a classifier to predict those optimal decisions.

The distinction matters because clean-label class probabilities can express uncertainty, whereas the Bayes optimal labels considered here have one-hot class probabilities. The authors use this lower uncertainty in two ways: they can collect examples whose Bayes optimal labels have theoretical guarantees, and they can restrict the space of feasible transition matrices. They estimate the resulting Bayes-label transition matrix using a deep neural network.

The paper reports better generalization and superior classification performance from exploiting these advantages. However, it explicitly recognizes that estimating either kind of transition matrix from noisy data alone is ill-posed. Its contribution is therefore an approach that exploits the structure of Bayes optimal labels to constrain estimation, rather than a claim that arbitrary label corruption becomes uniquely recoverable.
summary.tldr: Modeling transitions from Bayes optimal labels to noisy labels provides structure that improves neural estimation and classification under label noise.

title: Estimating Instance-dependent Bayes-label Transition Matrix using a Deep Neural Network

abstract: Optimal transport is an important tool in machine learning, allowing to capture geometric properties of the data through a linear program on transport polytopes. We present a single-loop optimization algorithm for minimizing general convex objectives on these domains, utilizing the principles of Sinkhorn matrix scaling and mirror descent. The proposed algorithm is robust to noise, and can be used in an online setting. We provide theoretical guarantees for convex objectives and experimental results showcasing it effectiveness on both synthetic and real-world data.

We provide theoretical guarantees for convex objectives and experimental results showcasing it effectiveness on both synthetic and real-world data.

paragraphs: Optimal transport represents comparisons between data through an optimization problem over transport plans. The admissible plans form a transport polytope, a constrained domain that carries the structure of the problem. This paper considers minimizing general convex objectives over that domain, extending the optimization focus beyond the linear objective associated with standard optimal transport.

The proposed Mirror Sinkhorn algorithm combines principles from Sinkhorn matrix scaling and mirror descent in a single optimization loop. Matrix scaling supplies a connection to transport constraints, while mirror descent supplies the optimization perspective. Bringing these ideas together provides one procedure for working with convex objectives on transport polytopes, rather than restricting the objective to the standard linear case.

The authors state that the algorithm tolerates noise and can operate online, making it applicable when optimization proceeds as information arrives. They provide theoretical guarantees for convex objectives and demonstrate effectiveness on synthetic and real-world data. The result is a method whose stated scope includes both constrained transport geometry and learning settings with noisy or sequentially available information.
summary.tldr: Mirror Sinkhorn combines matrix scaling and mirror descent in a single-loop method for noisy and online convex optimization over transport polytopes.

title: Mirror Sinkhorn: Fast Online Optimization on Transport Polytopes

abstract: An abundance of recent impossibility results establish that regret minimization in Markov games with adversarial opponents is both statistically and computationally intractable. Nevertheless, none of these results preclude the possibility of regret minimization under the assumption that all parties adopt the same learning procedure. In this work, we present the first (to our knowledge) algorithm for learning in general-sum Markov games that provides sublinear regret guarantees when executed by all agents. The bounds we obtain are for $\textit{swap regret}$, and thus, along the way, imply convergence to a $\textit{correlated}$ equilibrium. Our algorithm is decentralized, computationally efficient, and does not require any communication between agents. Our key observation is that online learning via policy optimization in Markov games essentially reduces to a form of $\textit{weighted}$ regret minimization, with $\textit{unknown}$ weights determined by the path length of the agents’ policy sequence. Consequently, controlling the path length leads to weighted regret objectives for which sufficiently adaptive algorithms provide sublinear regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Learning against adversarial opponents in Markov games faces strong statistical and computational barriers. This paper studies a more structured situation: every agent follows the same learning procedure. That assumption leaves room for guarantees that adversarial-opponent impossibility results do not rule out.

The proposed algorithm achieves sublinear swap regret when all agents execute it, which also implies convergence to a correlated equilibrium. It is decentralized, computationally efficient, and requires no communication between agents. The guarantee therefore relies on a shared learning procedure while allowing agents to carry it out separately.

The key analysis connects policy optimization to weighted regret minimization. The relevant weights are unknown and depend on the path length of the agents' policy sequence, which captures how much their policies change over learning. Controlling that movement produces weighted objectives for which sufficiently adaptive algorithms achieve sublinear regret. This explains how coordinated choice of learning rule can support equilibrium convergence without communication, while preserving the essential condition that all participants use the proposed procedure.
summary.tldr: When all agents use its procedure, a decentralized Markov-game algorithm achieves sublinear swap regret and convergence to a correlated equilibrium.

title: Regret Minimization and Convergence to Equilibria in General-sum Markov Games

abstract: We study the accuracy of differentially private mechanisms in the continual release model. A continual release mechanism receives a sensitive dataset as a stream of $T$ inputs and produces, after receiving each input, an output that is accurate for all the inputs received so far. We provide the first strong lower bounds on the error of continual release mechanisms. In particular, for two fundamental problems that are closely related to empirical risk minimization and widely studied and used in the standard (batch) model, we prove that the worst case error of every continual release algorithm is $\tilde \Omega(T^{1/3})$ times larger than that of the best batch algorithm. Previous work shows only a $\Omega(\log T)$ gap between the worst case error achievable in these two models. We also formulate a model that allows for adaptively selected inputs, thus capturing dependencies that arise in many applications of continual release. Even though, in general, both privacy and accuracy are harder to attain in this model, we show that our lower bounds are matched by the error of simple algorithms that work even for adaptively selected inputs.

paragraphs: A continual-release system receives sensitive data over time and publishes an updated answer after every input. Each answer must describe everything received so far while preserving differential privacy. This paper studies how much accuracy that repeated-release requirement can cost compared with a batch algorithm that processes the dataset together.

For two fundamental problems closely connected to empirical risk minimization, the authors prove that every continual-release algorithm has worst-case error larger than that of the best batch algorithm by a factor scaling as T^(1/3), up to logarithmic factors. Earlier results established only a logarithmic gap. The new lower bounds therefore show a substantially greater accuracy cost for continual observation in these problems.

The paper also formalizes a setting where inputs can be chosen adaptively, capturing dependencies that arise during ongoing use. Although privacy and accuracy are generally harder in that setting, simple algorithms still match the new lower bounds. The combination of lower bounds and matching algorithms identifies both an unavoidable cost and an achievable level of accuracy, including when the input stream is adaptive.
summary.tldr: For two central problems, continual private release has a much larger worst-case error cost than batch release, with matching algorithms even for adaptive inputs.

title: The Price of Differential Privacy under Continual Observation

abstract: Denoising diffusion probabilistic models are becoming the leading generative modeling paradigm for many important data modalities. Being the most prevalent in the computer vision community, diffusion models have recently gained some attention in other domains, including speech, NLP, and graph-like data. In this work, we investigate if the framework of diffusion models can be advantageous for general tabular problems, where data points are typically represented by vectors of heterogeneous features. The inherent heterogeneity of tabular data makes it quite challenging for accurate modeling since the individual features can be of a completely different nature, i.e., some of them can be continuous and some can be discrete. To address such data types, we introduce TabDDPM — a diffusion model that can be universally applied to any tabular dataset and handles any feature types. We extensively evaluate TabDDPM on a wide set of benchmarks and demonstrate its superiority over existing GAN/VAE alternatives, which is consistent with the advantage of diffusion models in other fields.

paragraphs: Tabular data presents a different modeling problem from data whose components all have a similar form. A single row can mix continuous measurements with discrete categories, so a generative model must handle features of different kinds together. This paper investigates whether denoising diffusion models can provide an effective general approach to that heterogeneous setting.

The proposed model, TabDDPM, is designed to accommodate tabular datasets with any feature types. Its contribution is to bring the diffusion framework to data represented as mixed-feature vectors. Handling that mixture is central to the task: a model intended for general tables must represent the different feature types within the same generated record.

The authors evaluate TabDDPM on a broad set of benchmarks and report better performance than existing generative adversarial network and variational autoencoder alternatives. These findings extend the empirical case for diffusion beyond the domains where it had already attracted attention. The broad applicability claim concerns the kinds of tabular inputs the method can handle, while the reported superiority is evidence from the evaluated benchmarks.
summary.tldr: TabDDPM adapts diffusion modeling to tables with mixed feature types and outperforms GAN and VAE alternatives on the reported benchmarks.

title: TabDDPM: Modelling Tabular Data with Diffusion Models

abstract: Antibodies comprise the most versatile class of binding molecules, with numerous applications in biomedicine. Computational design of antibodies involves generating novel and diverse sequences, while maintaining structural consistency. Unique to antibodies, designing the complementarity-determining region (CDR), which determines the antigen binding affinity and specificity, creates its own unique challenges. Recent deep learning models have shown impressive results, however the limited number of known antibody sequence/structure pairs frequently leads to degraded performance, particularly lacking diversity in the generated sequences. In our work we address this challenge by leveraging Model Reprogramming (MR), which repurposes pretrained models on a source language to adapt to the tasks that are in a different language and have scarce data - where it may be difficult to train a high-performing model from scratch or effectively fine-tune an existing pre-trained model on the specific task. Specifically, we introduce ReprogBert in which a pretrained English language model is repurposed for protein sequence infilling - thus considers cross-language adaptation using less data. Results on antibody design benchmarks show that our model on low-resourced antibody sequence dataset provides highly diverse CDR sequences, up to more than a two-fold increase of diversity over the baselines, without losing structural integrity and naturalness. The generated sequences also demonstrate enhanced antigen binding specificity and virus neutralization ability. Code is available at https://github.com/IBM/ReprogBERT

paragraphs: Antibody design requires new sequences that are diverse while remaining structurally consistent. The complementarity-determining region is especially important because it influences binding affinity and specificity. Limited antibody sequence-and-structure data can constrain deep-learning methods, particularly their ability to generate a diverse collection of candidate sequences.

ReprogBert addresses this data constraint by repurposing a pretrained English language model for protein sequence infilling. The approach uses model reprogramming to adapt knowledge from a source language to a different sequence domain with scarce task data. Its central idea is to make an existing language model useful for filling antibody sequence regions when learning an effective model from the available antibody data is difficult.

On antibody-design benchmarks with limited sequence data, the model produces CDR sequences with diversity gains exceeding twofold over baselines in the reported results, while retaining structural integrity and naturalness. The generated sequences also show enhanced antigen-binding specificity and virus-neutralization ability. These findings support cross-language model adaptation as a useful approach to the examined antibody-design setting, with gains extending beyond diversity alone.
summary.tldr: ReprogBert repurposes an English language model for antibody infilling, reporting greater sequence diversity while retaining structural quality and improving functional properties.

title: Reprogramming Pretrained Language Models for Antibody Sequence Infilling

abstract: Invariant representations are transformations of the covariates such that the best model on top of the representation is invariant across training environments. In the context of linear Structural Equation Models (SEMs), invariant representations might allow us to learn models with out-of-distribution guarantees, i.e., models that are robust to interventions in the SEM. To address the invariant representation problem in a finite sample setting, we consider the notion of $\epsilon$-approximate invariance. We study the following question: If a representation is approximately invariant with respect to a given number of training interventions, will it continue to be approximately invariant on a larger collection of unseen intervened SEMs? Inspired by PAC learning, we obtain finite-sample out-of-distribution generalization guarantees for approximate invariance that holds probabilistically over a family of linear SEMs without faithfulness assumptions.

paragraphs: An invariant representation transforms input variables so that the best predictor built on it stays the same across training environments. Such representations might support prediction under changes to the system that generated the data. This paper studies that possibility for linear structural equation models, where different environments arise through interventions.

The authors focus on finite data, introducing approximate invariance with a tolerance called epsilon. Their central question is whether a representation that is approximately invariant across a given collection of training interventions will preserve that property across a larger collection of unseen interventions. This frames generalization around the stability of the representation’s predictive relationship across environments.

Drawing on probably approximately correct learning, the paper obtains finite-sample guarantees that hold probabilistically over a family of linear structural equation models. The results do not require faithfulness assumptions. Their significance lies in giving approximate invariance an out-of-distribution generalization framework with explicit statistical scope: the guarantee concerns a probability statement over the studied model family, rather than certainty for every possible intervention.
summary.tldr: The paper gives probabilistic finite-sample guarantees for approximate invariance across unseen interventions in linear structural equation models.

title: PAC Generalization via Invariant Representations

abstract: Collections of probability distributions arise in a variety of applications ranging from user activity pattern analysis to brain connectomics. In practice these distributions can be defined over diverse domain types including finite intervals, circles, cylinders, spheres, other manifolds, and graphs. This paper introduces an approach for detecting differences between two collections of distributions over such general domains. To this end, we propose the intrinsic slicing construction that yields a novel class of Wasserstein distances on manifolds and graphs. These distances are Hilbert embeddable, allowing us to reduce the distribution collection comparison problem to a more familiar mean testing problem in a Hilbert space. We provide two testing procedures one based on resampling and another on combining p-values from coordinate-wise tests. Our experiments in various synthetic and real data settings show that the resulting tests are powerful and the p-values are well-calibrated.
