paragraphs: Some datasets contain entire probability distributions as individual observations. Comparing two collections then requires accounting for where those distributions live, which might be an interval, a circle, a sphere, another manifold, or a graph. This paper develops a statistical approach that can handle these varied domains within a common construction.

The authors introduce intrinsic slicing to define a new class of Wasserstein distances on manifolds and graphs. These distances admit embeddings into a Hilbert space. That property lets the comparison of distribution collections become a more familiar test of means in the embedding space, connecting a geometric comparison problem to established statistical machinery.

The paper provides two testing procedures: one uses resampling, and the other combines p-values from tests on individual coordinates. Experiments on synthetic and real data report strong detection power and well-calibrated p-values. These findings indicate that the proposed tests can detect differences while producing meaningful statistical significance assessments in the evaluated settings, across domains where a single conventional representation would be restrictive.
summary.tldr: Intrinsic slicing turns comparisons of distribution collections on manifolds and graphs into mean tests in a Hilbert space.

title: Intrinsic Sliced Wasserstein Distances for Comparing Collections of Probability Distributions on Manifolds and Graphs

abstract: This paper develops an approximation to the (effective) $p$-resistance and applies it to multi-class clustering. Spectral methods based on the graph Laplacian and its generalization to the graph $p$-Laplacian have been a backbone of non-euclidean clustering techniques. The advantage of the $p$-Laplacian is that the parameter $p$ induces a controllable bias on cluster structure. The drawback of $p$-Laplacian eigenvector based methods is that the third and higher eigenvectors are difficult to compute. Thus, instead, we are motivated to use the $p$-resistance induced by the $p$-Laplacian for clustering. For $p$-resistance, small $p$ biases towards clusters with high internal connectivity while large $p$ biases towards clusters of small “extent,” that is a preference for smaller shortest-path distances between vertices in the cluster. However, the $p$-resistance is expensive to compute. We overcome this by developing an approximation to the $p$-resistance. We prove upper and lower bounds on this approximation and observe that it is exact when the graph is a tree. We also provide theoretical justification for the use of $p$-resistance for clustering. Finally, we provide experiments comparing our approximated $p$-resistance clustering to other $p$-Laplacian based methods.

paragraphs: Graph clustering groups vertices according to relationships encoded by edges. Methods based on the graph p-Laplacian offer a parameter that changes which cluster structures are favored, but computing their third and higher eigenvectors is difficult. This paper explores effective p-resistance as an alternative route to clustering a graph into multiple groups.

The parameter p gives this resistance measure an interpretable structural preference. Small values favor clusters with strong internal connectivity, while large values favor clusters with smaller extent, expressed through shorter paths between vertices. Exact p-resistance is expensive to compute, so the authors develop an approximation to make this approach more accessible computationally.

They prove upper and lower bounds for the approximation and establish that it is exact on trees. They also provide theoretical justification for using p-resistance in clustering and compare the resulting method with other p-Laplacian approaches experimentally. The contribution combines a controllable notion of cluster structure with a bounded approximation, avoiding reliance on the difficult higher-eigenvector calculations that motivated the work.
summary.tldr: An approximation to effective p-resistance supports graph clustering with tunable structural preferences and is exact for trees.

title: Multi-class Graph Clustering via Approximated Effective $p$-Resistance

abstract: To balance quality and cost, various domain areas of science and engineering run simulations at multiple levels of sophistication. Multi-fidelity active learning aims to learn a direct mapping from input parameters to simulation outputs at the highest fidelity by actively acquiring data from multiple fidelity levels. However, existing approaches based on Gaussian processes are hardly scalable to high-dimensional data. Deep learning-based methods often impose a hierarchical structure in hidden representations, which only supports passing information from low-fidelity to high-fidelity. These approaches can lead to the undesirable propagation of errors from low-fidelity representations to high-fidelity ones. We propose a novel framework called Disentangled Multi-fidelity Deep Bayesian Active Learning (D-MFDAL), which learns the surrogate models conditioned on the distribution of functions at multiple fidelities. On benchmark tasks of learning deep surrogates of partial differential equations including heat equation, Poisson’s equation and fluid simulations, our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art in prediction accuracy and sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Scientific simulations often offer several fidelity levels, trading computational cost against output quality. Multi-fidelity active learning seeks to predict the highest-fidelity outputs while choosing useful data from multiple levels. The challenge is to benefit from cheaper simulations without allowing their inaccuracies to dominate the more accurate prediction task.

The paper identifies two obstacles in existing approaches. Gaussian-process methods struggle to scale to high-dimensional data, while some deep methods organize hidden representations into a hierarchy that passes information only from lower to higher fidelity. That one-way structure can propagate errors from lower-fidelity representations into higher-fidelity ones.

Disentangled Multi-fidelity Deep Bayesian Active Learning, or D-MFDAL, instead learns surrogate models conditioned on distributions of functions at multiple fidelities. The proposal targets the restrictive information structure of earlier deep approaches while retaining the goal of selective data acquisition. On surrogate-learning benchmarks involving heat equations, Poisson's equation, and fluid simulations, the authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in both prediction accuracy and sample efficiency.
summary.tldr: D-MFDAL learns from multiple simulation fidelities and reports improved prediction accuracy and sample efficiency on PDE surrogate benchmarks.

title: Disentangled Multi-Fidelity Deep Bayesian Active Learning

abstract: This paper studies the online node classification problem under a transductive learning setting. Current methods either invert a graph kernel matrix with $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$ runtime and $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ space complexity or sample a large volume of random spanning trees, thus are difficult to scale to large graphs. In this work, we propose an improvement based on the online relaxation technique introduced by a series of works (Rakhlin et al., 2012; Rakhlin & Sridharan, 2015; 2017). We first prove an effective regret $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n^{1+\gamma}})$ when suitable parameterized graph kernels are chosen, then propose an approximate algorithm FastONL enjoying $\mathcal{O}(k\sqrt{n^{1+\gamma}})$ regret based on this relaxation. The key of FastONL is a generalized local push method that effectively approximates inverse matrix columns and applies to a series of popular kernels. Furthermore, the per-prediction cost is $\mathcal{O}(\operatorname{vol}{\mathcal{S}}\log 1/\epsilon)$ locally dependent on the graph with linear memory cost. Experiments show that our scalable method enjoys a better tradeoff between local and global consistency.

paragraphs: This paper studies online node classification in a transductive setting, where prediction takes place on a given graph. Existing approaches can require a costly graph-kernel matrix inverse or many sampled spanning trees. Those demands make very large graphs difficult to handle, motivating an algorithm that can make predictions using more localized computation.

The authors first analyze an online relaxation approach and establish a regret guarantee when suitable parameterized graph kernels are chosen. They then develop FastONL, an approximate algorithm with its own regret guarantee. Its central component is a generalized local push method that approximates columns of an inverse matrix and works with several popular graph kernels.

FastONL’s per-prediction cost depends on a local graph volume and logarithmically on inverse approximation tolerance, while its memory requirement is linear. This connects scalability to the graph region involved in a prediction. Experiments report a better trade-off between local and global consistency, showing how the approximation can support both efficient computation and useful graph-wide prediction behavior.
summary.tldr: FastONL approximates graph-kernel inverse columns locally to enable scalable online node labeling with theoretical regret guarantees.

title: Fast Online Node Labeling for Very Large Graphs

abstract: This paper tackles the challenge of detecting unreliable behavior in regression algorithms, which may arise from intrinsic variability (e.g., aleatoric uncertainty) or modeling errors (e.g., model uncertainty). First, we formally introduce the notion of unreliability in regression, i.e., when the output of the regressor exceeds a specified discrepancy (or error). Then, using powerful tools for probabilistic modeling, we estimate the discrepancy density, and we measure its statistical diversity using our proposed metric for statistical dissimilarity. In turn, this allows us to derive a data-driven score that expresses the uncertainty of the regression outcome. We show empirical improvements in error detection for multiple regression tasks, consistently outperforming popular baseline approaches, and contributing to the broader field of uncertainty quantification and safe machine learning systems.

paragraphs: Regression models predict numerical values, but a prediction alone does not indicate whether its error is likely to be unacceptable. Unreliability can arise from variability inherent in the data or from deficiencies in the model. This paper makes the target explicit by defining an unreliable regression outcome as one whose discrepancy exceeds a specified error threshold.

The method uses probabilistic modeling to estimate the distribution of prediction discrepancies. It then assesses the statistical diversity of that distribution with a proposed measure of statistical dissimilarity. These ingredients produce a data-driven uncertainty score for a regression outcome. The approach therefore uses information about possible errors to assess reliability, with the chosen discrepancy threshold defining what counts as a problematic prediction.

Across multiple regression tasks, the authors report improved error detection and consistent advantages over popular baseline approaches. The practical meaning is that the score can help identify predictions that warrant less confidence. The reported contribution concerns recognizing unreliable outcomes; its empirical support comes from better detection of errors across the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: The paper models prediction discrepancies to build an uncertainty score that improves detection of unreliable regression outputs in the reported experiments.

title: Beyond the Norms: Detecting Prediction Errors in Regression Models

abstract: Machine learning (ML) models in the real world typically do not exist in isolation. They are usually part of a complex system (e.g., healthcare systems, self-driving cars) containing multiple ML and black-box components. The problem of optimizing such systems, which we refer to as automated AI (AutoAI), requires us to jointly train all ML components together and presents a significant challenge because the number of system parameters is extremely high and the system has no analytical form. To circumvent this, we introduce a novel algorithm called A-BAD-BO which uses each ML component’s local loss as an auxiliary indicator for system performance. A-BAD-BO uses Bayesian optimization (BO) to optimize the local loss configuration of a system in a smaller dimensional space and exploits the differentiable structure of ML components to recover optimal system parameters from the optimized configuration. We show A-BAD-BO converges to optimal system parameters by showing that it is asymptotically no regret. We use A-BAD-BO to optimize several synthetic and real-world complex systems, including a prompt engineering pipeline for large language models containing millions of system parameters. Our results demonstrate that A-BAD-BO yields better system optimality than gradient-driven baselines and is more sample-efficient than pure BO algorithms.

paragraphs: Real machine learning systems often contain multiple trainable components alongside black-box operations. Optimizing the whole system is difficult because there may be millions of parameters and no analytical expression for overall behavior. This paper calls the joint optimization problem AutoAI and proposes A-BAD-BO to exploit the structure available inside individual components.

The method uses each component’s local loss as an auxiliary indicator of system performance. Bayesian optimization searches over a lower-dimensional configuration of these losses. The differentiable structure of the machine learning components then connects that optimized configuration back to system parameters, combining system-level search with component-level optimization.

The authors establish asymptotic no regret and use it to show convergence to optimal system parameters. They also evaluate synthetic and real-world systems, including a language-model prompt-engineering pipeline with millions of parameters. Reported results show better system optimality than gradient-driven baselines and greater sample efficiency than pure Bayesian optimization. The contribution is a way to coordinate many trainable parameters while reserving black-box search for a smaller space.
summary.tldr: A-BAD-BO combines Bayesian optimization over local-loss configurations with differentiable component training to optimize complex machine learning systems.

title: Towards AutoAI: Optimizing a Machine Learning System with Black-box and Differentiable Components

abstract: In this paper, we introduce and analyze a variant of the Thompson sampling (TS) algorithm for contextual bandits. At each round, traditional TS requires samples from the current posterior distribution, which is usually intractable. To circumvent this issue, approximate inference techniques can be used and provide samples with distribution close to the posteriors. However, current approximate techniques yield to either poor estimation (Laplace approximation) or can be computationally expensive (MCMC methods, Ensemble sampling...). In this paper, we propose a new algorithm, Varational Inference TS $\mathtt{VITS}$, based on Gaussian Variational Inference. This scheme provides powerful posterior approximations which are easy to sample from, and is computationally efficient, making it an ideal choice for TS. In addition, we show that $\mathtt{VITS}$ achieves a sub-linear regret bound of the same order in the dimension and number of round as traditional TS for linear contextual bandit. Finally, we demonstrate experimentally the effectiveness of $\mathtt{VITS}$ on both synthetic and real world datasets

paragraphs: Thompson sampling makes contextual-bandit decisions using samples from a posterior distribution that changes as observations arrive. Drawing those samples exactly is usually intractable. Approximate inference offers a route forward, but the paper identifies a tradeoff: some approximations estimate the posterior poorly, while others require expensive computation at each decision round.

VITS uses Gaussian variational inference to build a posterior approximation that is efficient to compute and easy to sample from. This makes approximate inference part of the decision-making algorithm itself. The approach aims to retain the benefits of posterior-based exploration without making each round depend on costly sampling procedures.

For linear contextual bandits, the authors prove a sublinear regret bound with the same order of dependence on dimension and number of rounds as traditional Thompson sampling. Sublinear regret means accumulated decision loss grows more slowly than the interaction horizon. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets further demonstrate effectiveness, combining a computationally practical approximation with a theoretical guarantee in the linear setting.
summary.tldr: VITS uses Gaussian variational inference for efficient Thompson sampling and matches its regret order for linear contextual bandits.

title: $\mathttVITS$ : Variational Inference Thompson Sampling for contextual bandits

abstract: Motivated by practical applications in clinical trials and online platforms, we study A/B testing with the aim of estimating a confidence interval (CI) for the average treatment effect (ATE) using the minimum expected sample size. This CI should have a width at most $\epsilon$ while ensuring that the probability of the CI not containing the true ATE is at most $\delta$. To answer this, we first establish a lower bound on the expected sample size needed for any adaptive policy which constructs a CI of ATE with desired properties. Specifically, we prove that the lower bound is based on the solution to a max-min non-convex optimization problem for small $\delta$. Tailoring the “plug-in” approach for the ATE problem, we construct an adaptive policy that is asymptotically optimal, i.e., matches the lower bound on the expected sample size for small $\delta$. Interestingly, we find that, for small $\epsilon$ and $\delta$, the asymptotically optimal fraction of treatment assignment for A and B is proportional to the standard deviation of the outcome distributions of treatments A and B, respectively. However, as the proposed approach can be computationally intensive, we propose an alternative adaptive policy. This new policy, informed by insights from our lower bound analysis, is computationally efficient while remaining asymptotically optimal for small values of $\epsilon$ and $\delta$. Numerical comparisons demonstrate that both policies perform similarly across practical values of $\epsilon$ and $\delta$, offering efficient solutions for A/B testing.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate the average difference between two treatments using as few samples as possible. The target is a confidence interval with a specified maximum width and a specified maximum probability of missing the true effect. Treatment assignments can adapt as observations accumulate, making allocation part of the estimation problem.

The authors first derive a lower bound on the expected sample size needed by any qualifying adaptive policy. For small error probabilities, that bound involves a non-convex optimization problem. They construct a plug-in policy that asymptotically matches it. When both the interval width and error probability are small, the optimal allocation proportions follow the treatments' outcome standard deviations.

Because the first policy can be computationally expensive, the authors develop an alternative informed by the lower-bound analysis. It remains asymptotically optimal when both requirements become stringent while being computationally efficient. Numerical comparisons show similar performance between the policies at practical parameter values, connecting the theoretical allocation result to a more tractable procedure.
summary.tldr: Adaptive A/B testing policies achieve asymptotically optimal sample use for treatment-effect confidence intervals, including a computationally efficient alternative.

title: Asymptotically Optimal and Computationally Efficient Average Treatment Effect Estimation in A/B testing

abstract: The multi-group learning model formalizes the learning scenario in which a single predictor must generalize well on multiple, possibly overlapping subgroups of interest. We extend the study of multi-group learning to the natural case where the groups are hierarchically structured. We design an algorithm for this setting that outputs an interpretable and deterministic decision tree predictor with near-optimal sample complexity. We then conduct an empirical evaluation of our algorithm and find that it achieves attractive generalization properties on real datasets with hierarchical group structure.

paragraphs: A single predictor may need to perform well for several subgroups, including groups that overlap. Multi-group learning formalizes that requirement instead of assessing the predictor only across the population as a whole. This paper studies the case where the groups have a hierarchical structure, making the relationships among groups part of the learning setting.

The authors design an algorithm that produces a deterministic decision tree predictor. The tree is interpretable, so the learned prediction rule has an explicit structure that can be examined. They establish near-optimal sample complexity, meaning the algorithm's data requirements are close to the best achievable for the setting addressed by their analysis.

The paper also evaluates the algorithm on real datasets with hierarchical groups and reports attractive generalization properties. The theoretical and empirical contributions address complementary questions: how efficiently the predictor can be learned, and how it behaves on real data. Together, they support hierarchical group structure as a useful basis for learning one interpretable predictor with multiple subgroup requirements.
summary.tldr: An algorithm for hierarchical multi-group learning produces interpretable decision trees with near-optimal sample complexity and promising empirical generalization.

title: Multi-group Learning for Hierarchical Groups

abstract: Bayesian few-shot classification has been a focal point in the field of few-shot learning. This paper seamlessly integrates mirror descent-based variational inference into Gaussian process-based few-shot classification, addressing the challenge of non-conjugate inference. By leveraging non-Euclidean geometry, mirror descent achieves accelerated convergence by providing the steepest descent direction along the corresponding manifold. It also exhibits the parameterization invariance property concerning the variational distribution. Experimental results demonstrate competitive classification accuracy, improved uncertainty quantification, and faster convergence compared to baseline models. Additionally, we investigate the impact of hyperparameters and components. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/keanson/MD-BSFC.

paragraphs: This paper studies Bayesian classification when only a few labeled examples are available. Its starting point is a Gaussian process approach, where making predictions requires reasoning about uncertainty. The computational challenge is non-conjugate inference: the relevant probability distributions do not combine into a conveniently solvable form, so the method must approximate the distribution needed for prediction.

The authors integrate variational inference based on mirror descent into this setting. Variational inference learns an approximate probability distribution, while mirror descent chooses updates using a non-Euclidean geometry. In the paper’s account, this geometry provides a steepest descent direction along the corresponding manifold and accelerates convergence. The approach also has parameterization invariance with respect to the variational distribution.

Experiments report competitive classification accuracy alongside improved uncertainty quantification and faster convergence relative to the evaluated baselines. The authors also investigate the influence of hyperparameters and components. Together, these results suggest that changing how the approximate distribution is optimized can improve computational behavior and uncertainty estimates while maintaining competitive predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Mirror descent improves convergence and uncertainty quantification in Gaussian process few-shot classification while retaining competitive accuracy.

title: Accelerating Convergence in Bayesian Few-Shot Classification

abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is key to aligning Large Language Models (LLMs), typically paired with the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm. While PPO is a powerful method designed for general reinforcement learning tasks, it is overly sophisticated for LLMs, leading to laborious hyper-parameter tuning and significant computation burdens. To make RLHF efficient, we present ReMax, which leverages 3 properties of RLHF: fast simulation, deterministic transitions, and trajectory-level rewards. These properties are not exploited in PPO, making it less suitable for RLHF. Building on the renowned REINFORCE algorithm, ReMax does not require training an additional value model as in PPO and is further enhanced with a new variance reduction technique. ReMax offers several benefits over PPO: it is simpler to implement, eliminates more than 4 hyper-parameters in PPO, reduces GPU memory usage, and shortens training time. ReMax can save about 46% GPU memory than PPO when training a 7B model and enables training on A800-80GB GPUs without the memory-saving offloading technique needed by PPO. Applying ReMax to a Mistral-7B model resulted in a 94.78% win rate on the AlpacaEval leaderboard and a 7.739 score on MT-bench, setting a new SOTA for open-source 7B models. These results show the effectiveness of ReMax while addressing the limitations of PPO in LLMs.

paragraphs: ReMax aims to simplify reinforcement learning from human feedback for language models. The paper argues that PPO brings unnecessary complexity to this setting because it does not exploit three relevant properties: fast simulation, deterministic transitions, and rewards assigned to complete trajectories. ReMax builds its training approach around those properties.

It avoids training the additional value model used by PPO, eliminates more than four PPO hyperparameters, and reduces memory use and training time. Together, the results support a simpler alignment-training procedure that retains strong measured performance while reducing the computational and tuning burdens associated with PPO.
summary.tldr: ReMax simplifies language-model RLHF with REINFORCE and variance reduction, avoiding a value model while reducing memory use and achieving strong reported results.

title: ReMax: A Simple, Effective, and Efficient Reinforcement Learning Method for Aligning Large Language Models

abstract: We investigate parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods that can provide good accuracy under limited computational and memory budgets in the context of large language models (LLMs). We present a new PEFT method called Robust Adaptation (RoSA) inspired by robust principal component analysis that jointly trains $\textit{low-rank}$ and highly-sparse components on top of a set of fixed pretrained weights to efficiently approximate the performance of a full-fine-tuning (FFT) solution. Across a series of challenging generative tasks such as grade-school math and SQL query generation, which require fine-tuning for good performance, we show that RoSA outperforms LoRA, pure sparse fine-tuning, and alternative hybrid methods at the same parameter budget, and can even recover the performance of FFT on some tasks. We provide system support for RoSA to complement the training algorithm, specifically in the form of sparse GPU kernels which enable memory- and computationally-efficient training, and show that it is also compatible with low-precision base weights, resulting in the first joint representation combining quantization, low-rank and sparse approximations. Our code is available at https://github.com/IST-DASLab/RoSA.

We present a new PEFT method called Robust Adaptation (RoSA) inspired by robust principal component analysis that jointly trains $\textit{low-rank}$ and highly-sparse components on top of a set of fixed pretrained weights to efficiently approximate the performance of a full-fine-tuning (FFT) solution. We provide system support for RoSA to complement the training algorithm, specifically in the form of sparse GPU kernels which enable memory- and computationally-efficient training, and show that it is also compatible with low-precision base weights, resulting in the first joint representation combining quantization, low-rank and sparse approximations. Our code is available at https://github.com/IST-DASLab/RoSA.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a large language model under limited memory and compute requires choosing which changes to learn. RoSA keeps pretrained weights fixed and jointly trains two additions: a low-rank component and a highly sparse component. Inspired by robust principal component analysis, this combination aims to approximate the performance of full fine-tuning with a smaller trainable parameter budget.

The authors evaluate RoSA on challenging generative tasks, including grade-school mathematics and SQL generation. At the same parameter budget, it outperforms LoRA, purely sparse fine-tuning, and other hybrid methods. On some tasks it recovers full-fine-tuning performance, showing that the combined representation can close that performance gap in the evaluated cases.

The paper also supplies sparse GPU kernels to make the training method efficient in memory and computation. RoSA is compatible with low-precision pretrained weights, combining quantization with low-rank and sparse approximations. This systems support matters because the proposal includes both a way to allocate trainable parameters and an implementation designed to make that allocation computationally useful.
summary.tldr: RoSA combines low-rank and sparse updates to improve parameter-efficient fine-tuning, matching full fine-tuning on some evaluated tasks.

title: RoSA: Accurate Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning via Robust Adaptation

abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides an efficient framework for transferring knowledge from a teacher model to a student model by aligning their predictive distributions. The existing KD methods adopt the same strategy as the teacher to formulate the student’s predictive distribution. However, employing the same distribution-modeling strategy typically causes sub-optimal knowledge transfer due to the discrepancy in model capacity between teacher and student models. Designing student-friendly teachers contributes to alleviating the capacity discrepancy, while it requires either complicated or student-specific training schemes. To cast off this dilemma, we propose to introduce an auxiliary variable to promote the ability of the student to model predictive distribution. The auxiliary variable is defined to be related to target variables, which will boost the model prediction. Specifically, we reformulate the predictive distribution with the auxiliary variable, deriving a novel objective function of KD. Theoretically, we provide insights to explain why the proposed objective function can outperform the existing KD methods. Experimentally, we demonstrate that the proposed objective function can considerably and consistently outperform existing KD methods.

Its experiments report considerable and consistent improvements over existing methods. Together, the analysis and evaluations support the auxiliary variable as a useful way to improve knowledge transfer. The key contribution is the reformulated learning objective, which addresses the teacher–student mismatch through the student’s predictive modeling.
summary.tldr: An auxiliary variable reshapes the student’s predictive distribution to improve knowledge distillation across teacher–student capacity differences.

title: Knowledge Distillation with Auxiliary Variable

abstract: Training autonomous agents that can learn new tasks from only a handful of demonstrations is a long-standing problem in machine learning. Recently, transformers have been shown to learn new language or vision tasks without any weight updates from only a few examples, also referred to as in-context learning. However, the sequential decision making setting poses additional challenges having a lower tolerance for errors since the environment’s stochasticity or the agent’s actions can lead to unseen, and sometimes unrecoverable, states. In this paper, we use an illustrative example to show that naively applying transformers to sequential decision making problems does not enable in-context learning of new tasks. We then demonstrate how training on sequences of trajectories with certain distributional properties leads to in-context learning of new sequential decision making tasks. We investigate different design choices and find that larger model and dataset sizes, as well as more task diversity, environment stochasticity, and trajectory burstiness, all result in better in-context learning of new out-of-distribution tasks. By training on large diverse offline datasets, our model is able to learn new MiniHack and Procgen tasks without any weight updates from just a handful of demonstrations.

The authors instead train on sequences of trajectories with particular distributional properties. They investigate which design choices improve adaptation without changing model weights. These findings make the organization and variety of training experience central to learning new tasks from context.

The results demonstrate in-context adaptation in those sequential environments and show that the training distribution matters substantially for obtaining it, beyond simply choosing a Transformer architecture.
summary.tldr: Training Transformers on suitably structured, diverse trajectories enables adaptation to new sequential tasks from a few demonstrations without weight updates.

title: Generalization to New Sequential Decision Making Tasks with In-Context Learning

abstract: Existing paradigms of pushing the state of the art require exponentially more training data in many fields. Coreset selection seeks to mitigate this growing demand by identifying the most efficient subset of training data. In this paper, we delve into geometry-based coreset methods and preliminarily link the geometry of data distribution with models’ generalization capability in theoretics. Leveraging these theoretical insights, we propose a novel coreset construction method by selecting training samples to reconstruct the decision boundary of a deep neural network learned on the full dataset. Extensive experiments across various popular benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our method over multiple competitors. For the first time, our method achieves a 50% data pruning rate on the ImageNet-1K dataset while sacrificing less than 1% in accuracy. Additionally, we showcase and analyze the remarkable cross-architecture transferability of the coresets derived from our approach.

paragraphs: Coreset selection tries to identify a smaller training subset that retains much of the usefulness of the full dataset. This paper approaches the problem through the geometry of the model’s decision boundary. The central question is which examples are needed to reconstruct the boundary learned by a deep network trained on all the data.

The authors first develop a preliminary theoretical connection between data geometry and generalization. They then use those insights to select training samples for boundary reconstruction. This gives subset selection a concrete target: preserve the structure that the full-data model uses to separate predictions, rather than choosing examples without reference to that learned structure.

Experiments across popular benchmarks report improvements over multiple competing selection methods. On ImageNet-1K, the method removes half the training data while losing less than 1% accuracy. The authors also demonstrate and analyze transfer of the selected coresets across architectures. These results support the usefulness of boundary-oriented selection, including situations where the subset is used with a different network architecture.
summary.tldr: Selecting examples to reconstruct a learned decision boundary removes half of ImageNet-1K training data with less than 1% accuracy loss.

title: Mind the Boundary: Coreset Selection via Reconstructing the Decision Boundary

abstract: The remarkable generalization of large-scale models has recently gained significant attention in multimodal research. However, deploying heterogeneous large-scale models with different modalities under Federated Learning (FL) to protect data privacy imposes tremendous challenges on clients’ limited computation and storage. In this work, we propose M$^2$FedSA to address the above issue. We realize modularized decomposition of large-scale models via Split Learning (SL) and only retain privacy-sensitive modules on clients, alleviating storage overhead. By freezing large-scale models and introducing two specialized lightweight adapters, the models can better focus on task-specific knowledge and enhance modality-specific knowledge, improving the model’s adaptability to different tasks while balancing efficiency. In addition, M$^2$FedSA further improves performance by transferring multimodal knowledge to unimodal clients at both the feature and decision levels, which leverages the complementarity of different modalities. Extensive experiments on various multimodal classification tasks validate the effectiveness of our proposed M$^2$FedSA. The code is made available publicly at https://github.com/M2FedSA/M-2FedSA.

paragraphs: Federated multimodal learning must accommodate clients with different types of data and limited computing resources. Large models make this difficult because storing and adapting them can exceed client capacity. M²FedSA addresses the problem through a combination of model partitioning, lightweight adaptation, and knowledge transfer between clients with different available modalities.

The framework uses split learning to divide large models into modules, retaining only privacy-sensitive modules on clients to reduce local storage demands. It freezes the large models and introduces two specialized lightweight adapters. These support task-specific learning and modality-specific knowledge, allowing adaptation without training the full large model. The design therefore addresses where model components reside as well as which components learn.

M²FedSA also transfers multimodal knowledge to clients that have only one modality, operating at both feature and decision levels. This allows those clients to benefit from complementary information represented by multiple modalities. Experiments on several multimodal classification tasks support the framework’s effectiveness. The overall contribution is a coordinated approach to reducing client resource demands while maintaining useful adaptation across heterogeneous data sources.
summary.tldr: M²FedSA combines split learning, lightweight adapters, and multimodal knowledge transfer to make large-model federated learning more resource efficient.

title: Enhancing Storage and Computational Efficiency in Federated Multimodal Learning for Large-Scale Models

abstract: Training Large Language Models (LLMs) presents significant memory challenges, predominantly due to the growing size of weights and optimizer states. Common memory-reduction approaches, such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA), add a trainable low-rank matrix to the frozen pre-trained weight in each layer, reducing trainable parameters and optimizer states. However, such approaches typically underperform training with full-rank weights in both pre-training and fine-tuning stages since they limit the parameter search to a low-rank subspace and alter the training dynamics, and further, may require full-rank warm start. In this work, we propose Gradient Low-Rank Projection (GaLore), a training strategy that allows full-parameter learning but is more memory-efficient than common low-rank adaptation methods such as LoRA. Our approach reduces memory usage by up to 65.5% in optimizer states while maintaining both efficiency and performance for pre-training on LLaMA 1B and 7B architectures with C4 dataset with up to 19.7B tokens, and on fine-tuning RoBERTa on GLUE tasks. Our 8-bit GaLore further reduces optimizer memory by up to 82.5% and total training memory by 63.3%, compared to a BF16 baseline. Notably, we demonstrate, for the first time, the feasibility of pre-training a 7B model on consumer GPUs with 24GB memory (e.g., NVIDIA RTX 4090) without model parallel, checkpointing, or offloading strategies.

summary.tldr: GaLore projects gradients into low-rank form to reduce training memory while retaining full-parameter learning, enabling demonstrated 7B pretraining on 24GB consumer GPUs.

title: GaLore: Memory-Efficient LLM Training by Gradient Low-Rank Projection

abstract: This paper introduces von Mises-Fisher exploration (vMF-exp), a scalable method for exploring large action sets in reinforcement learning problems where hyperspherical embedding vectors represent these actions. vMF-exp involves initially sampling a state embedding representation using a von Mises-Fisher distribution, then exploring this representation’s nearest neighbors, which scales to virtually unlimited numbers of candidate actions. We show that, under theoretical assumptions, vMF-exp asymptotically maintains the same probability of exploring each action as Boltzmann Exploration (B-exp), a popular alternative that, nonetheless, suffers from scalability issues as it requires computing softmax values for each action. Consequently, vMF-exp serves as a scalable alternative to B-exp for exploring large action sets with hyperspherical embeddings. Experiments on simulated data, real-world public data, and the successful large-scale deployment of vMF-exp on the recommender system of a global music streaming service empirically validate the key properties of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning systems must explore alternatives, but choosing among a very large action set can be expensive. Boltzmann exploration assigns probabilities through a softmax calculation over every action. This paper introduces a more scalable approach for settings where actions are represented by embedding vectors on a hypersphere.

The method, called vMF-exp, samples a state representation from a von Mises-Fisher distribution and explores nearby action embeddings using nearest-neighbor search. This replaces the need to compute a softmax value for every candidate with sampling and neighborhood retrieval. The construction is designed to support extremely large action collections while retaining a connection to a familiar exploration rule.

Under theoretical assumptions, the authors show that vMF-exp asymptotically gives each action the same exploration probability as Boltzmann exploration. This is a qualified limiting result, rather than a claim of exact equivalence in every finite setting. Simulations, public real-world datasets, and deployment in a global music streaming recommender provide empirical support for the method’s key properties and practical scalability.
summary.tldr: vMF-exp scales exploration through hyperspherical sampling and nearest neighbors, asymptotically matching Boltzmann exploration under theoretical assumptions.

title: Exploring Large Action Sets with Hyperspherical Embeddings using von Mises-Fisher Sampling

abstract: The proliferation of disinformation demands reliable and scalable fact-checking solutions. We present Dynamic Evidence-based FAct-checking with Multimodal Experts (DEFAME), a modular, zero-shot MLLM pipeline for open-domain, text-image claim verification. DEFAME operates in a six-stage process, dynamically selecting the tools and search depth to extract and evaluate textual and visual evidence. Unlike prior approaches that are text-only, lack explainability, or rely solely on parametric knowledge, DEFAME performs end-to-end verification, accounting for images in claims and evidence while generating structured, multimodal reports. Evaluation on the popular benchmarks VERITE, AVeriTeC, and MOCHEG shows that DEFAME surpasses all previous methods, establishing itself as the new general state-of-the-art fact-checking system for uni- and multimodal fact-checking. Moreover, we introduce a new multimodal benchmark, ClaimReview2024+, featuring claims after the knowledge cutoff of GPT-4o, avoiding data leakage. Here, DEFAME drastically outperforms the GPT-4o baselines, showing temporal generalizability and the potential for real-time fact-checking.

paragraphs: DEFAME is a modular pipeline for checking open-domain claims containing text and images. It uses multimodal language models in a zero-shot setting and gathers evidence as part of verification. The system treats images as relevant both within the claim being checked and within the material used to assess it.

Its six-stage process dynamically chooses tools and determines how deeply to search. It extracts and evaluates visual and textual evidence, then produces structured multimodal reports. This connects evidence collection, assessment, and explanation within one workflow, addressing the limitations of approaches that use only text or depend entirely on knowledge already stored in a model.

The authors report that DEFAME surpasses previous methods on VERITE, AVeriTeC, and MOCHEG. They also introduce ClaimReview2024+, whose claims occur after GPT-4o's knowledge cutoff to avoid data leakage from those claims. DEFAME substantially outperforms GPT-4o baselines on this benchmark. These findings support its ability to handle newer claims and indicate potential for real-time fact-checking, while the reported comparisons concern the evaluated benchmarks.
summary.tldr: DEFAME dynamically gathers text and image evidence to verify claims, reporting leading results across several fact-checking benchmarks.

title: DEFAME: Dynamic Evidence-based FAct-checking with Multimodal Experts

abstract: Addressing selection bias in latent variable causal discovery is important yet underexplored, largely due to a lack of suitable statistical tools: While various tools beyond basic conditional independencies have been developed to handle latent variables, none have been adapted for selection bias. We make an attempt by studying rank constraints, which, as a generalization to conditional independence constraints, exploits the ranks of covariance submatrices in linear Gaussian models. We show that although selection can significantly complicate the joint distribution, interestingly, the ranks in the biased covariance matrices still preserve meaningful information about both causal structures and selection mechanisms. We provide a graph-theoretic characterization of such rank constraints. Using this tool, we demonstrate that the one-factor model, a classical latent variable model, can be identified under selection bias. Simulations and real-world experiments confirm the effectiveness of using our rank constraints.

paragraphs: Discovering causal structure is difficult when some relevant variables are hidden, and selection bias adds another complication. The observed sample can have a different joint distribution from the population of interest. This paper investigates whether covariance information can still reveal causal structure when latent variables and selection bias occur together.

The analysis focuses on linear Gaussian models and rank constraints on covariance submatrices. These constraints generalize information provided by conditional independence. The authors show that selection can substantially change the distribution while leaving matrix ranks informative about both the causal graph and the selection mechanism. They provide a graph-based characterization of those surviving constraints.

Using this characterization, the paper demonstrates that a one-factor latent-variable model can be identified under selection bias. Simulations and real-world experiments support the effectiveness of the proposed rank constraints. The contribution is a statistical tool for a setting where standard latent-variable methods have lacked an adaptation to selection, together with a concrete identification result showing what that tool can recover.
summary.tldr: Covariance rank constraints retain useful causal information under selection bias and enable identification of a one-factor model in the studied setting.

title: Latent Variable Causal Discovery under Selection Bias

abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as CLIP excel at zero-shot classification due to large-scale pre-training but are vulnerable to adversarial examples. Adversarial fine-tuning robustifies zero-shot models by aligning prediction scores of individual adversaries with their clean counterparts, which typically overlooks intermediate adversarial samples along the adversarial trajectory crossing the decision boundary. Such intermediate adversaries and their vicinity produce informative representations capturing the decision boundary in detail. They can be improved by sampling adversarial candidates from simplices formed by joining two consecutive vertices on the adversarial trajectory and their clean counterpart. However, sampling simplices for adversaries is very costly. To train robust VLM, we overcome these limitations by Taylor expansion and formulating an upper-bound of alignment loss that depends on the Jacobian/Hessian obtained at clean samples. As regions between clean and intermediate adversarial samples capture a larger decision landscape, we robustify VLM by plausible adversaries from simplices by our closed-form formulation equivalent to infinite uniform sampling of the simplex. We obtain state-of-the-art robustness across 15 datasets and diverse vision-language tasks.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can classify unseen categories through text descriptions, but adversarial inputs can disrupt their predictions. Adversarial fine-tuning commonly aligns an attacked example’s prediction scores with those of its clean counterpart. This paper argues that intermediate examples along the attack trajectory contain valuable information about the decision boundary that this approach typically overlooks.

The authors consider simplices formed from a clean example and two consecutive points on the adversarial trajectory. Sampling within these regions would expose training to a broader local decision landscape, but doing so is expensive. They use a Taylor expansion to formulate an upper bound on alignment loss involving the Jacobian and Hessian at clean examples.

The resulting closed-form formulation is equivalent to infinite uniform sampling of the simplex within that formulation, avoiding explicit sampling of all those candidates. The method reports state-of-the-art robustness across 15 datasets and diverse vision-language tasks. Its central contribution is an efficient way to incorporate information from regions connecting clean inputs and intermediate adversarial examples.
summary.tldr: A closed-form alignment formulation uses regions along adversarial trajectories to improve zero-shot vision-language robustness without costly explicit simplex sampling.

title: Improving Zero-Shot Adversarial Robustness in Vision-Language Models by Closed-form Alignment of Adversarial Path Simplices

abstract: Off-dynamics reinforcement learning (RL), where training and deployment transition dynamics are different, can be formulated as learning in a robust Markov decision process (RMDP) where uncertainties in transition dynamics are imposed. Existing literature mostly assumes access to generative models allowing arbitrary state-action queries or pre-collected datasets with a good state coverage of the deployment environment, bypassing the challenge of exploration. In this work, we study a more realistic and challenging setting where the agent is limited to online interaction with the training environment. To capture the intrinsic difficulty of exploration in online RMDPs, we introduce the supremal visitation ratio, a novel quantity that measures the mismatch between the training dynamics and the deployment dynamics. We show that if this ratio is unbounded, online learning becomes exponentially hard. We propose the first computationally efficient algorithm that achieves sublinear regret in online RMDPs with $f$-divergence based transition uncertainties. We also establish matching regret lower bounds, demonstrating that our algorithm achieves optimal dependence on both the supremal visitation ratio and the number of interaction episodes. Finally, we validate our theoretical results through comprehensive numerical experiments.

paragraphs: Off-dynamics reinforcement learning studies agents trained under transition dynamics that differ from those encountered at deployment. This paper considers robust learning when an agent can gather experience only by interacting online with the training environment. That restriction makes exploration central: the learner cannot freely query arbitrary state-action pairs or rely on a dataset already covering deployment states.

The authors introduce the supremal visitation ratio to quantify mismatch between training and deployment dynamics. They show that an unbounded ratio makes online learning exponentially hard. This identifies a concrete source of difficulty arising from the relationship between the environment available for exploration and the environments against which robustness is required.

For transition uncertainty described using f-divergences, the paper proposes a computationally efficient algorithm with sublinear regret. Matching lower bounds establish optimal dependence on both the visitation ratio and the number of interaction episodes. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings. The contribution links exploration difficulty to a measurable mismatch quantity and characterizes achievable learning performance in this online setting.
summary.tldr: The paper quantifies exploration difficulty under changing dynamics and gives an efficient robust-learning algorithm with matching regret bounds on key factors.

title: Sample Complexity of Distributionally Robust Off-Dynamics Reinforcement Learning with Online Interaction

abstract: Neural Algorithmic Reasoning (NAR) trains neural networks to simulate classical algorithms, enabling structured and interpretable reasoning over complex data. While prior research has predominantly focused on learning exact algorithms for polynomial-time-solvable problems, extending NAR to harder problems remains an open challenge. In this work, we introduce a general NAR framework grounded in the primal-dual paradigm, a classical method for designing efficient approximation algorithms. By leveraging a bipartite representation between primal and dual variables, we establish an alignment between primal-dual algorithms and Graph Neural Networks. Furthermore, we incorporate optimal solutions from small instances to greatly enhance the model’s reasoning capabilities. Our empirical results demonstrate that our model not only simulates but also outperforms approximation algorithms for multiple tasks, exhibiting robust generalization to larger and out-of-distribution graphs. Moreover, we highlight the framework’s practical utility by integrating it with commercial solvers and applying it to real-world datasets.

This paper develops a framework for harder problems by drawing on the primal-dual paradigm used to construct efficient approximation algorithms.

These are empirical results: they support learning useful approximation behavior without asserting that the network becomes an exact solver for all harder problems.

title: Primal-Dual Neural Algorithmic Reasoning

abstract: Many applications in machine learning and decision-making rely on procedures to aggregate human preferences. In such tasks, individual express ordinal preferences over a set of items through votes, ratings, or pairwise comparisons. We then summarize their collective preferences as a ranking. Standard methods for preference aggregation are designed to return rankings that arbitrate individual disagreements in ways that are faithful and fair. In this work, we introduce a paradigm for selective aggregation, where we can avoid the need to arbitrate dissent by abstaining from comparison. We summarize collective preferences as a selective ranking – i.e., a partial order where we can only compare items where at least $100\cdot(1 - \tau)%$ of individuals agree. We develop algorithms to build selective rankings that achieve all possible trade-offs between comparability and disagreement, and derive formal guarantees on their safety and stability. We conduct an extensive set of experiments on real-world datasets to benchmark our approach and demonstrate its functionality. Our results show selective aggregation can promote transparency and robustness by revealing disagreement and abstaining from arbitration.

paragraphs: Combining people’s votes, ratings, or pairwise comparisons usually produces a ranking that resolves disagreements into a shared ordering. This paper proposes allowing the output to leave some comparisons undecided. Its selective rankings are partial orders, so they can express collective agreement without requiring every pair of items to be ranked.

A disagreement threshold controls which comparisons are permitted. Items can be compared only when at least 100 times one minus tau percent of individuals agree. This creates an explicit tradeoff: the desired level of agreement determines how much of the ranking can be resolved. Disputed comparisons can remain open rather than being settled by the aggregation procedure.

The authors develop algorithms covering all possible tradeoffs between comparability and disagreement, together with formal safety and stability guarantees. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate how the approach functions in practice. The reported benefit is greater transparency and robustness through making disagreement visible. A selective ranking communicates both the comparisons supported by sufficient agreement and the places where the group has not reached that standard.
summary.tldr: Selective aggregation produces partial rankings that compare items only when a specified share of people agree.

title: Selective Preference Aggregation

abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have significantly advanced the development of real-world image super-resolution (Real-ISR), but the computational cost of multi-step diffusion models limits their application. One-step diffusion models generate high-quality images in a one sampling step, greatly reducing computational overhead and inference latency. However, most existing one-step diffusion methods are constrained by the performance of the teacher model, where poor teacher performance results in image artifacts. To address this limitation, we propose FluxSR, a novel one-step diffusion Real-ISR technique based on flow matching models. We use the state-of-the-art diffusion model FLUX.1-dev as both the teacher model and the base model. First, we introduce Flow Trajectory Distillation (FTD) to distill a multi-step flow matching model into a one-step Real-ISR. Second, to improve image realism and address high-frequency artifact issues in generated images, we propose TV-LPIPS as a perceptual loss and introduce Attention Diversification Loss (ADL) as a regularization term to reduce token similarity in transformer, thereby eliminating high-frequency artifacts. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing one-step diffusion-based Real-ISR methods. The code and model will be released at https://github.com/JianzeLi-114/FluxSR.

paragraphs: Real-world image super-resolution uses generative models to produce higher-resolution images from degraded inputs. Multi-step diffusion can deliver strong results, but repeated sampling adds computation and latency. One-step methods reduce that burden, although their results can inherit weaknesses from the teacher model used during training, including visible artifacts.

FluxSR builds a one-step super-resolution method from the flow matching model FLUX.1-dev, using it as both teacher and base model. Flow Trajectory Distillation transfers a multi-step generation process into a single sampling step. The method also introduces TV-LPIPS, a perceptual loss intended to improve realism, and Attention Diversification Loss, which reduces token similarity inside the Transformer to address high-frequency artifacts.

The reported experiments show that FluxSR outperforms existing one-step diffusion-based methods for real-world super-resolution. The approach combines compression of the generation trajectory with objectives aimed at the visual problems that can remain after compression. Its findings support the usefulness of jointly addressing sampling efficiency, teacher quality, and artifact-related training behavior when building a fast super-resolution model.
summary.tldr: FluxSR distills a flow matching model into one-step super-resolution and adds losses that improve realism and suppress high-frequency artifacts.

title: One Diffusion Step to Real-World Super-Resolution via Flow Trajectory Distillation

abstract: Activation sparsity can reduce the computational overhead and memory transfers during the forward pass of Large Language Model (LLM) inference. Existing methods face limitations, either demanding time-consuming recovery training that hinders real-world adoption, or relying on empirical magnitude-based pruning, which causes fluctuating sparsity and unstable inference speed-up. This paper introduces LaRoSA (Layerwise Rotated Sparse Activation), a novel method for activation sparsification designed to improve LLM efficiency without requiring additional training or magnitude-based pruning. We leverage layerwise orthogonal rotations to transform input activations into rotated forms that are more suitable for sparsification. By employing a Top-K selection approach within the rotated activations, we achieve consistent model-level sparsity and reliable wall-clock time speed-up. LaRoSA is effective across various sizes and types of LLMs, demonstrating minimal performance degradation and robust inference acceleration. Specifically, for LLaMA2-7B at 40% sparsity, LaRoSA achieves a mere 0.17 perplexity gap with a consistent 1.30$\times$ wall-clock time speed-up, and reduces the accuracy gap in zero-shot tasks compared to the dense model to just 0.54%, while surpassing TEAL by 1.77% and CATS by 17.14%.

LaRoSA aims to obtain predictable sparsity and practical acceleration without an additional training stage.

Its central step is an orthogonal rotation of the input activations at each layer. This changes their representation into a form better suited to sparsification. The zero-shot accuracy gap from the dense model is 0.54%, with improvements over TEAL and CATS of 1.77% and 17.14%, respectively. These results demonstrate a measured efficiency-quality tradeoff at the reported setting.
summary.tldr: LaRoSA rotates activations before Top-K sparsification to deliver consistent language-model sparsity and measured inference speedups without additional training.

title: La RoSA: Enhancing LLM Efficiency via Layerwise Rotated Sparse Activation

abstract: Generating ultra-long sequences with large language models (LLMs) has become increasingly crucial but remains a highly time-intensive task, particularly for sequences up to 100K tokens. While traditional speculative decoding methods exist, simply extending their generation limits fails to accelerate the process and can be detrimental. Through an in-depth analysis, we identify three major challenges hindering efficient generation: frequent model reloading, dynamic key-value (KV) management and repetitive generation. To address these issues, we introduce TokenSwift, a novel framework designed to substantially accelerate the generation process of ultra-long sequences while maintaining the target model’s inherent quality. Experimental results demonstrate that TokenSwift achieves over $3 \times$ speedup across models of varying scales (1.5B, 7B, 8B, 14B) and architectures (MHA, GQA). This acceleration translates to hours of time savings for ultra-long sequence generation, establishing TokenSwift as a scalable and effective solution at unprecedented lengths.

paragraphs: Generating sequences as long as 100,000 tokens can take substantial time. This paper finds that simply extending the generation limits of traditional speculative decoding methods does not solve the problem and can make performance worse. It examines the obstacles that become important at these unusually long output lengths.

summary.tldr: TokenSwift addresses bottlenecks in ultra-long generation and reports over threefold speedups while preserving target-model quality.

title: TokenSwift: Lossless Acceleration of Ultra Long Sequence Generation

abstract: Turning the multi-round vanilla Federated Learning into one-shot FL (OFL) significantly reduces the communication burden and makes a big leap toward practical deployment. However, this work empirically and theoretically unravels that existing OFL falls into a garbage (inconsistent one-shot local models) in and garbage (degraded global model) out pitfall. The inconsistency manifests as divergent feature representations and sample predictions. This work presents a novel OFL framework FAFI that enhances the one-shot training on the client side to essentially overcome inferior local uploading. Specifically, unsupervised feature alignment and category-wise prototype learning are adopted for clients’ local training to be consistent in representing local samples. On this basis, FAFI uses informativeness-aware feature fusion and prototype aggregation for global inference. Extensive experiments on three datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of FAFI, which facilitates superior performance compared with 11 OFL baselines (+10.86% accuracy). Code available at https://github.com/zenghui9977/FAFI_ICML25

paragraphs: One-shot federated learning reduces communication by replacing repeated exchanges with a single round of local model uploads. The paper identifies a problem with that saving: independently trained client models can disagree in their feature representations and predictions. Its theoretical and empirical analysis links this inconsistency to degradation in the resulting global model.

FAFI addresses the issue during client training. It combines unsupervised feature alignment with category-wise prototype learning so that clients represent their local samples more consistently. Prototypes provide category-level representations, while feature alignment targets disagreement in the features themselves. The approach therefore tries to improve the compatibility of what clients upload before global inference takes place.

For global inference, FAFI fuses features according to their informativeness and aggregates the learned prototypes. Experiments on three datasets report better performance than 11 one-shot federated learning baselines, including a reported accuracy gain of 10.86%. The results support the paper's central argument that the quality and consistency of local training are important to making a single communication round effective.
summary.tldr: FAFI improves one-shot federated learning by aligning client representations before combining their features and category prototypes.

title: Does One-shot Give the Best Shot? Mitigating Model Inconsistency in One-shot Federated Learning

abstract: We analyze the hardmax limit of self-attention dynamics for token embeddings in the zero-temperature regime $(\beta \to +\infty)$ and relate it to finite-$\beta$ behavior. In this limit, the update rule can be viewed as a Frank-Wolfe step for a quadratic objective over the convex hull of the current tokens. When the key-query matrix is negative semidefinite, the dynamics converge with the standard sublinear rate $\mathcal{O}(t^{-1})$ on the quadratic energy, whereas in the positive semidefinite case, extending the hardmax rule to the convex hull induces a Voronoi structure: vertices are stationary, interior points remain in their initial cells, and each token moves along a straight line toward its cell’s vertex with exponential convergence under a step-size bounded away from zero. We additionally establish well-posedness of the associated ODE limit in this regime. For finite $\beta$, we model self-attention as a Markov chain and prove dynamic metastability: interior tokens reach near-vertex configurations in a constant number of steps and remain trapped for times exponential in $\beta$ with high probability, before eventual collapse to some point within the initial convex hull. Thus, hardmax dynamics accurately approximate the finite-$\beta$ process over exponentially long time horizons.

summary.tldr: Self-attention’s hardmax limit connects to Frank-Wolfe optimization and explains long-lived near-vertex behavior at finite temperature.

title: Attention’s forward pass and Frank-Wolfe

abstract: Hidden-action principal-agent problems model scenarios in which a principal induces an agent to take a costly and unobservable action through the provision of outcome-dependent payments. These problems find application in a variety of real-world settings, such as crowdsourcing, online labor platforms, and machine learning task delegation. Recently, much of the literature has focused on how to handle the principal’s uncertainty about the agent and the surrounding environment, which is often the main challenge in practice. One prominent approach is to adopt an online learning framework, where the principal repeatedly interacts with the agent to learn optimal payments from experience. However, existing learning algorithms, while achieving regret that scales sublinearly in the number of interaction rounds $T$, typically suffer from an exponential dependence on the size of the problem instance. In this paper, we show that this problematic exponential growth can be avoided by assuming that the principal has knowledge of a set of possible actions of the agent, while remaining unaware of which actions are actually available—an assumption that is reasonable in many real-world settings.

paragraphs: In a hidden-action contract problem, a principal offers payments tied to outcomes to motivate an agent whose costly action cannot be observed. The principal may also be uncertain about the agent and the environment. Repeated interaction provides a way to learn better payments from experience in settings such as crowdsourcing and task delegation.

Existing online approaches can achieve regret that grows sublinearly with the number of interactions, yet still depend exponentially on the size of the problem. This means favorable learning over time can coexist with poor scaling as the instance becomes larger. The paper focuses on removing that exponential dependence.

Its positive result assumes that the principal knows a set of possible agent actions while remaining uncertain about which are actually available. Under this knowledge assumption, the problematic exponential growth can be avoided. The contribution identifies a useful middle ground in the information available to the principal: knowing the candidate action set can make learning more tractable even when the agent’s actual capabilities remain unknown.
summary.tldr: Knowing a candidate set of agent actions can remove exponential problem-size dependence in online contract learning despite unknown action availability.

title: Online Contract Design With Unknown Technology

abstract: Generative Recommendation (GR) has emerged as a promising paradigm by formulating item recommendation as a sequence-to-sequence generation task over item identifiers. Recent studies have incorporated multimodal signals to provide richer token-level evidence for generation. However, existing approaches largely rely on alignment-centric fusion and underexplore synergistic information across modalities. In practice, synergistic information plays a critical role in capturing emergent item properties that cannot be inferred from any single modality alone. Such properties encode intrinsic item semantics and guide user preferences, enabling models to move beyond surface-level feature matching. To address this limitation, we propose SynGR, a synergistic generative recommendation framework that explicitly encourages the exploitation of cross-modal dependencies during generation. By constraining overreliance on dominant modalities, SynGR enables the model to capture emergent item semantics beyond shared or modality-specific signals. Extensive experiments across three benchmark datasets demonstrate that SynGR achieves superior performance.

paragraphs: Generative recommendation produces item identifiers as a sequence, using available signals to guide what should be recommended. Multimodal approaches provide richer evidence, but aligning modalities does not fully capture properties that emerge only when information from several modalities is considered together. SynGR focuses on this joint information.

The framework explicitly encourages the generator to use dependencies across modalities and constrains excessive reliance on a dominant modality. Its objective is to capture item semantics that are absent from any single modality alone. These emergent properties can reflect intrinsic item meaning and help explain user preferences beyond surface-level feature matches.

Experiments on three benchmark datasets report superior recommendation performance. The significance is that multimodal recommendation can benefit from learning how signals interact, alongside information that is shared across modalities or unique to one of them. SynGR makes those interactions an explicit part of generation, and the reported results support their usefulness for selecting items that match user preferences.
summary.tldr: SynGR improves generative recommendation by encouraging information that emerges jointly across modalities and limiting dependence on a dominant modality.

title: SynGR: Unleashing the Potential of Cross-Modal Synergy for Generative Recommendation

abstract: Multivariate time-series forecasting (MTSF) learns from high-dimensional covariates with strong temporal dependence, periodic structure, and cross-variable correlations. While modern pipelines often mitigate non-stationarity through instance-wise normalization and decomposition, these interventions operate at the data level and do not directly control dependence that can emerge among the parameters during training. We study MTSF optimization from a parameter-decorrelation viewpoint. Modeling stochastic optimization as a Markov chain in parameter space and leveraging its stochastic differential equation interpretation, we use the per-step transition-variance induced by gradient noise as a tractable signal for optimization-induced dependence and update uncertainty. This signal can empirically inflate during training; we theoretically show that such inflation can degrade generalization diagnostics. Motivated by this mechanism, we propose transition-variance alignment (TVA), an architecture-agnostic procedure that regulates transition-variance by smoothly gating the step size based on the mismatch between an estimated noise scale and a chosen target. TVA maintains effective transition-variance near a prescribed scale without architectural changes, incurs negligible overhead, and integrates seamlessly with diverse methods. Across real-world multivariate benchmarks, TVA consistently improves forecasting accuracy.

title: Parameter Decorrelation via Transition-Variance Alignment for Multivariate Time-series Forecasting

abstract: Time-series forecasting is critical in various scenarios, such as energy, transportation, and public health. However, most existing forecasters rely primarily on one-way inference, i.e., mapping history to target, and overlook the structural information provided by a revised natural chain (“history (model input) – target (ground-truth output) – post-target continuation”). The post-target continuation records how trajectories evolve after the target, which can help stabilize forecasting, but it is not observable at inference time. In this work, we aim to obtain an approximate proxy of the post-target continuation for the current input, providing structural knowledge for bidirectional forecasting. This idea is instantiated as KUP-BI (Knowledge Utilization Paradigm with Bidirectional Inspiration), a new time-series modeling paradigm that distills continuation-style knowledge (as an approximate post-target continuation proxy) from a train-only historical library and integrates it into standard forecasting backbones. The input stream and the continuation-proxy stream are fused via a lightweight feature-level gating module. This design does not introduce information beyond what is already contained in the training trajectories; instead, it provides a structured inductive bias that helps backbones exploit typical continuation patterns rather than relying solely on parametric extrapolation. Experimental results on six public datasets show that KUP-BI consistently improves the forecasting performance of state-of-the-art models, with small additional overhead.
