However, most existing forecasters rely primarily on one-way inference, i.e., mapping history to target, and overlook the structural information provided by a revised natural chain (“history (model input) – target (ground-truth output) – post-target continuation”). The post-target continuation records how trajectories evolve after the target, which can help stabilize forecasting, but it is not observable at inference time. In this work, we aim to obtain an approximate proxy of the post-target continuation for the current input, providing structural knowledge for bidirectional forecasting. This idea is instantiated as KUP-BI (Knowledge Utilization Paradigm with Bidirectional Inspiration), a new time-series modeling paradigm that distills continuation-style knowledge (as an approximate post-target continuation proxy) from a train-only historical library and integrates it into standard forecasting backbones. The input stream and the continuation-proxy stream are fused via a lightweight feature-level gating module. This design does not introduce information beyond what is already contained in the training trajectories; instead, it provides a structured inductive bias that helps backbones exploit typical continuation patterns rather than relying solely on parametric extrapolation. Experimental results on six public datasets show that KUP-BI consistently improves the forecasting performance of state-of-the-art models, with small additional overhead.

paragraphs: Most forecasting models map past observations directly to a future target interval. This paper considers a longer structure: the history, the target, and the trajectory after that target. That later continuation can provide useful structural information, but its actual values are unavailable when a forecast must be made. The approach therefore seeks an approximate continuation proxy.

KUP-BI obtains continuation-style knowledge from a historical library containing training trajectories only. It integrates this knowledge into standard forecasting models through two streams: one represents the current input, and the other represents the continuation proxy. A lightweight feature-level gate combines them, allowing the forecast to draw on typical continuation patterns represented in the training data.

The distinction between a proxy and the actual future is central to the method. KUP-BI adds no information beyond the training trajectories; it organizes existing information into a structural guide for forecasting. Across six public datasets, the authors report consistent improvements to state-of-the-art forecasting models with small additional overhead, supporting this use of historical continuation patterns.
summary.tldr: KUP-BI improves forecasting by combining current history with a continuation proxy derived exclusively from training trajectories.

title: Beyond Extrapolation: Knowledge Utilization Paradigm with Bidirectional Inspiration for Time Series Forecasting

abstract: We introduce LazyStack, a method for efficient model ensemble inference. The core idea is intuitive: after each model executes, we check whether accumulated evidence is sufficient to exit confidently. Sometimes one model suffices; other times we aggregate predictions from several models via trained meta-learners before reaching confidence. Two insights make this work. First, most inputs follow only 3 to 8 execution trajectories. This reduces the training problem from exponential to linear: we learn aggregators only for these common paths, not all possible model combinations. Second, we formulate trajectory selection as an MDP and use value iteration to compute the optimal routing policy, which reveals counterintuitive model orderings. On intrusion detection, starting with a moderately expensive model outperforms starting with the cheapest, because its higher confidence enables earlier overall exit. Across vision, text, tabular, and LLM tasks, we achieve up to 38x speedup at 97%+ accuracy retention compared to a complete ensemble. The result: ensemble-quality predictions at cascade-level cost. Code and a project page are available at https://ashwincolaco.github.io/lazystack.

paragraphs: An ensemble combines multiple models, but evaluating every model for every input can be expensive. LazyStack checks after each model whether the accumulated evidence supports a confident exit. When more evidence is needed, trained meta-learners combine predictions from additional models, joining early-exit routing with learned aggregation.

It trains aggregators for these common paths, reducing the training problem from exponential to linear. Across vision, text, tabular, and language-model tasks, LazyStack reports speedups of up to 38 times while retaining at least 97% of complete-ensemble accuracy. The findings emphasize total decision cost rather than the cost of an individual model.
summary.tldr: LazyStack learns how to combine and route ensemble models, reporting up to 38-fold speedups with at least 97% accuracy retention.

title: Unifying Stacking and Cascading for Efficient Ensemble Inference

abstract: Existing reinforcement learning approaches for Large Language Models typically perform policy optimization at the granularity of individual tokens or entire response sequences. However, such formulations often misalign with the natural step-wise structure of reasoning processes, leading to suboptimal credit assignment and unstable training in multi-modal reasoning tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose Segment-Aligned Policy Optimization (SAPO), a novel reinforcement learning paradigm that treats coherent reasoning steps, rather than tokens or full sequences as fundamental units of policy update. SAPO introduces a step-wise Markov decision process abstraction over reasoning segments, accompanied by segment-level value estimation, advantage computation, and importance sampling mechanisms that are semantically aligned with reasoning boundaries. Experiments on representative reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that SAPO consistently outperforms token-level and sequence-level policy optimization methods, achieving significant accuracy improvements while exhibiting better training stability and value estimation consistency. Our work underscores the importance of aligning reinforcement learning updates with the intrinsic structure of reasoning, paving the way for more efficient and semantically grounded policy optimization in complex reasoning tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/Graysonicc/SAPO.

The paper argues that these units can fit reasoning poorly, because a meaningful reasoning step may span several tokens while a full response contains many distinct steps. Segment-Aligned Policy Optimization treats coherent reasoning segments as the units of policy optimization. It formulates a step-wise Markov decision process over those segments, then aligns value estimates, advantage calculations, and importance sampling with their boundaries. The intention is for training signals to correspond more closely to the meaningful steps through which a model develops its answer.

Experiments on representative reasoning benchmarks report consistent improvements over token-level and sequence-level optimization methods. SAPO also shows better training stability and more consistent value estimation alongside significant accuracy gains. These findings support the idea that choosing an update unit aligned with reasoning structure can improve both the learning process and the resulting multimodal reasoning performance.
summary.tldr: SAPO improves multimodal reasoning training by aligning reinforcement-learning updates with coherent reasoning steps.

title: Segment-Aligned Policy Optimization for Multi-Modal Reasoning

abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are used to analyze embeddings, but their role and practical value are debated. We propose a new perspective on SAEs by demonstrating that they can be naturally understood as topic models. We propose a continuous topic model (CTM) inspired by Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) for embedding spaces and derive the SAE objective as a maximum a posteriori estimator under this model. This view implies SAE features are thematic components rather than steerable directions. To confirm our theoretical findings, we introduce SAE-TM, a topic modeling framework that: (1) trains an SAE to learn reusable topic atoms, (2) interprets them as word distributions on downstream data, and (3) merges them into any number of topics without retraining. SAE-TM yields more coherent topics than strong baselines on text and image datasets while maintaining diversity. Finally, we analyze thematic structure in image datasets and trace topic changes over time in Japanese woodblock prints. Our work positions SAEs as effective tools for large-scale thematic analysis across modalities. Code is available at https://github.com/ExplainableML/SAE-TM.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders break embeddings into a limited number of active features, but the interpretation and usefulness of those features remain debated. This paper develops a topic-modeling interpretation. It introduces a continuous topic model inspired by Latent Dirichlet Allocation and derives the sparse-autoencoder objective as maximum a posteriori estimation under that model.

Within this view, learned features represent thematic components rather than inherently steerable directions. The authors build SAE-TM around that interpretation: an autoencoder learns reusable topic atoms, downstream data gives those atoms word-distribution interpretations, and the atoms can be merged into different numbers of topics without retraining.

On text and image datasets, SAE-TM produces more coherent topics than strong baselines while maintaining diversity. Applications examine thematic structure in images and follow topic changes over time in Japanese woodblock prints. The theoretical connection therefore leads to a practical analysis workflow, where a single learned collection of atoms supports multiple topic granularities and thematic exploration across modalities.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic topic-model interpretation of sparse autoencoders supports reusable topic atoms and coherent thematic analysis across text and images.

title: Sparse Autoencoders are Topic Models

abstract: Tabular Language Models (TLMs) have been claimed to achieve strong generalization for tabular prediction. We conduct a systematic re-evaluation of Tabula-8B as a representative TLM, utilizing 165 datasets from the UniPredict benchmark. Our investigation reveals three findings. First, binary and categorical classification achieve near-zero median lift over majority-class baselines and strong aggregate performance is driven entirely by quartile classification tasks. Second, top-performing datasets exhibit pervasive contamination, including complete train-test overlap and task-level leakage that evades standard deduplication. Third, instruction-tuning without tabular exposure recovers 92.2% of standard classification performance and on quartile classification, format familiarity closes 71.3% of the gap with the residual attributable to contaminated datasets. These findings suggest claimed generalization likely reflects evaluation artifacts rather than learned tabular reasoning. We conclude with recommendations for strengthening TLM evaluation.

paragraphs: This paper re-evaluates claims that tabular language models generalize well to prediction tasks, studying Tabula-8B on 165 UniPredict datasets. It separates task types and examines contamination to understand what drives aggregate scores. That distinction matters because a strong combined result can conceal weak performance on major categories of tasks.

For binary and categorical classification, median improvement over majority-class baselines is near zero. Strong aggregate results come entirely from quartile classification tasks. The best-performing datasets also show pervasive contamination, including complete overlap between training and test data and task-level leakage that ordinary deduplication does not catch.

On quartile classification, familiarity with the format closes 71.3% of the gap, with the remaining difference attributed to contaminated datasets. Taken together, these findings suggest that the claimed generalization in this evaluation likely reflects artifacts rather than learned tabular reasoning. The study uses a representative model, so its evidence supports scrutiny of broader claims without establishing that every tabular language model behaves identically.
summary.tldr: A re-evaluation of Tabula-8B suggests its apparent tabular generalization largely reflects task mix, format familiarity, and contaminated evaluation data.

title: The Illusion of Generalization in Tabular Language Models

abstract: Large language models can express values in two main ways: (1) $\textit{intrinsic}$ expression, reflecting the model’s inherent values learned during training, and (2) $\textit{prompted}$ expression, elicited by explicit prompts. Given their widespread use in value alignment, it is paramount to clearly understand their underlying mechanisms, particularly whether they mostly overlap (as one might expect) or rely on distinct mechanisms. We analyze this largely understudied problem at the mechanistic level using two approaches: (1) $\textit{value vectors}$, feature directions representing value mechanisms extracted from the residual stream, and (2) $\textit{value neurons}$, MLP neurons that contribute to value vectors. We demonstrate that intrinsic and prompted value mechanisms partly share common components crucial for inducing value expression, generalizing across languages and reconstructing theoretical inter-value correlations in the model’s internal representations. Yet, each mechanism also possesses unique components that fulfill distinct roles. In particular, the intrinsic mechanism activates in more diverse value-related scenarios and promotes response diversity, whereas the prompted mechanism strengthens instruction compliance, taking effect even in distant tasks like jailbreaking.

paragraphs: A language model can express values through behavior learned during training or in response to an explicit instruction. This paper examines whether these two routes use the same internal machinery. The distinction matters for value alignment because eliciting a value through a prompt may engage mechanisms with different behavioral effects from those active without that instruction.

The authors study value vectors, which are directions in the model's residual representations, and value neurons, which are MLP neurons contributing to those directions. They find partial overlap between intrinsic and prompted mechanisms. Shared components help induce value expression, generalize across languages, and reproduce theoretical relationships among values within the model's internal representations.

Each route also has components with distinct roles. The intrinsic mechanism activates across a wider range of value-related situations and promotes more varied responses. The prompted mechanism strengthens instruction compliance, with effects extending to tasks such as jailbreaking. The findings describe a mixture of shared and specialized mechanisms, showing why prompted value expression cannot be understood solely by examining the components common to both routes.
summary.tldr: Intrinsic and prompted value expression share some internal components but also engage mechanisms with different behavioral roles.

title: Dual Mechanisms of Value Expression: Intrinsic vs. Prompted Values in Large Language Models

abstract: Large models recently are widely applied in machine learning, so efficient training of large models has received widespread attention. More recently, the useful Muon optimizer is specifically designed for matrix-structured parameters of large models. Although some works have begun to study the Muon optimizer, the existing Muon and its variants still suffer from high sample complexity or high memory for large models. To fill this gap, we propose a light and fast Muon (LiMuon) optimizer for training large models, which builds on the momentum-based variance reduced technique and randomized Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). In particular, our LiMuon simultaneously has a lower memory and lower sample complexity than the Muon and its variants. Moreover, we prove that our LiMuon with lower memory has a lower sample complexity of $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ for finding an $\epsilon$-stationary solution of non-convex stochastic optimization under the generalized smoothness condition. To further narrow practice and theory gap, we also prove that our LiMuon with Newton-Schulz steps has a lower sample complexity than the Muon with Newton-Schulz steps. Numerical experimental results on pre-training Mamba-130M, Qwen2.5-0.5B and ViT models demonstrate effectiveness of our LiMuon.

paragraphs: Muon is an optimizer designed for matrix-shaped parameters in large models, but its existing forms can require substantial memory or many stochastic samples. This paper introduces LiMuon to improve both requirements. The method combines a momentum-based variance reduction technique with randomized singular value decomposition.

The theoretical result concerns nonconvex stochastic optimization under a generalized smoothness condition. In that setting, the authors prove a sample complexity of O(ε⁻³) for reaching an ε-stationary solution while using less memory. Stationarity is the optimization target of the guarantee; the result does not assert that the algorithm finds a global minimum.

The authors also analyze a version using Newton–Schulz steps and establish better sample complexity than the corresponding Muon version. This connects their analysis to another implementation of the optimizer’s matrix operations. Pretraining experiments involving Mamba-130M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, and vision transformer models demonstrate LiMuon’s effectiveness. Together, the results present reduced memory and improved theoretical sampling requirements as compatible objectives in large-model optimization.
summary.tldr: LiMuon combines variance reduction and randomized matrix decomposition to reduce memory and improve Muon’s sample complexity under generalized smoothness.

title: LiMuon: Light and Fast Muon Optimizer for Large Models

abstract: Continual learning (CL) aims to train models sequentially over multiple domains without forgetting previously learned knowledge. However, existing CL methods optimize for in-domain performance and are therefore prone to learning spurious, domain-specific cues ("shortcut learning"), which limits generalization to unseen domains after deployment. In this paper, we address this limitation through continual learning of domain-invariant representation. We introduce a broad class of CL methods that sequentially learn representations capturing invariant structures across domains. Our methods are motivated by the observation that such invariant structures often preserve the underlying causal mechanisms, which can reduce the risk of overfitting to domain-specific cues and thus offer better out-of-domain generalization. Our proposed CL methods combine replay-based training with a tailored sequential invariance alignment to learn—and preserve—invariant structures over time. We evaluate our methods under a deployment-oriented protocol that measures performance on unseen target domains. Across six benchmark and real-world datasets spanning vision, medicine, manufacturing, and ecology, our methods consistently outperform existing CL baselines in terms of generalization to unseen target domains. As an ablation, we further show that naïve extensions of sequential training with existing domain-invariant representation learning (DIRL) methods provide only limited benefits. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to develop domain-invariant representation methods for CL.

paragraphs: Continual learning trains a model on domains encountered in sequence while trying to preserve earlier knowledge. This paper argues that avoiding forgetting is insufficient for deployment: a model can retain domain-specific shortcuts that fail on unfamiliar domains. The authors therefore target representations that capture structures shared across domains as learning proceeds.

Their methods combine replay-based training with a sequential alignment procedure tailored to preserving invariance. Replay brings earlier information back into training, while alignment encourages the representation to retain shared structure over time. The motivation is that invariant structures often preserve underlying causal mechanisms and can therefore reduce reliance on incidental domain cues; the paper does not equate all invariance with causality.

Ablations find only limited benefits from naïvely applying existing domain-invariant learning methods sequentially. The findings support designing invariance preservation specifically for continual learning.
summary.tldr: Combining replay with sequential invariance alignment improves continual learners’ generalization to unseen domains across six datasets.

title: Continual Learning of Domain-Invariant Representations

abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) achieve strong reasoning with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting but incur high sequential-generation cost, error accumulation, and limited self-correction. Diffusion Multimodal Large Language Models (dMLLMs) unmask tokens in an order-agnostic process, improving efficiency and enabling iterative refinement, yet their reasoning and how to enhance it remain underexplored. We propose a training-free method, Spatio-Temporal Token Veto (ST-Veto), which leverages the ability to observe all token positions at each diffusion step. Rather than relying only on current-step confidence, ST-Veto vetoes temporally unstable tokens via second-order Taylor prediction of confidence dynamics and filters weakly grounded tokens using image-attention mass, swapping them with safer candidates. Across multiple dMLLMs and multimodal reasoning benchmarks, ST-Veto consistently outperforms standard decoding policies and prior VLM reasoning methods, improving accuracy by up to 9% with no additional training or generation cost. Analyses show that ST-Veto steers generation toward higher-confidence, better-grounded paths.

paragraphs: Diffusion multimodal language models can fill token positions in flexible orders and revisit their outputs through iterative refinement. This gives them a different opportunity for controlling reasoning than sequential generation provides. ST-Veto uses the availability of information about all token positions at each diffusion step to improve which candidates are selected.

The method checks two kinds of evidence. A second-order Taylor prediction estimates how token confidence is evolving, allowing temporally unstable candidates to be vetoed. Image-attention mass provides a signal of visual grounding, filtering candidates with weak image support. The method then swaps rejected tokens for safer candidates instead of relying only on confidence at the current step.

Across multiple diffusion multimodal models and reasoning benchmarks, ST-Veto consistently outperforms standard decoding policies and the prior vision-language reasoning methods evaluated. Accuracy improvements reach up to 9%, with no additional training or generation cost reported. Analyses associate the gains with generation paths that have higher confidence and stronger visual grounding, supporting the value of combining temporal stability with evidence from the image.
summary.tldr: ST-Veto improves multimodal diffusion reasoning by rejecting tokens with unstable confidence or weak visual grounding.

title: ST-Veto: Spatio-Temporal Token Veto for Diffusion MLLMs via Taylor Prediction and Visual Grounding

abstract: High-quality data is a key input to modern machine learning models, leading to the emergence of platforms that facilitate the buying and selling of data. A central challenge in these platforms is how the data is priced to balance the interests of both buyers and sellers. Traditional market equilibrium notions, where demand meets supply are commonly used to price goods but do not extend naturally to data due to its non-rivalrous nature, whereby multiple buyers can simultaneously benefit from the same dataset. We therefore introduce a new notion of equilibrium for data pricing based on Nash equilibrium and study it in settings where data may be complementary or substitutable, focusing on the canonical utility models for each, namely Leontief and linear, respectively. We show that equilibrium prices fail to exist for linear utilities even with homogeneous buyers and two sellers, while establishing strong existence, efficiency, and polynomial-time computation guarantees for Leontief utilities in general markets with $n$ homogeneous buyers and $m$ sellers. We further examine the role of platform mediation and price discrimination in enabling optimal equilibrium outcomes efficiently. On the technical front, we develop a novel proof technique based on systematically reducing the space of candidate equilibria through the graph-of-deviations, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Data pricing differs from pricing ordinary goods because multiple buyers can benefit from the same dataset simultaneously. Standard supply-meets-demand reasoning therefore does not transfer directly. This paper introduces a data-pricing equilibrium based on Nash equilibrium and examines how the answer changes depending on whether datasets complement one another or can substitute for one another.

The authors study complementary data through Leontief utilities and substitutable data through linear utilities. The distinction has major consequences: equilibrium prices can fail to exist with linear utilities even for homogeneous buyers and only two sellers. For Leontief utilities, they establish existence, efficiency, and polynomial-time computation guarantees in general markets with homogeneous buyers and multiple sellers.

The paper also examines how platform mediation and price discrimination can enable optimal equilibrium outcomes to be computed efficiently. Its proof approach uses a graph of deviations to systematically narrow the set of candidate equilibria. Together, the results show that the structure of buyers’ preferences is central to whether a stable and efficiently computable data-pricing arrangement is available.
summary.tldr: A Nash-based data-pricing framework yields strong guarantees for complementary-data utilities, while equilibrium can fail for substitutable-data utilities.

title: How to Price Data: A Market Equilibrium Based Approach

abstract: Determining an effective data mixture is a key factor in Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training, where models must balance general competence with proficiency on hard tasks such as math and code. However, identifying an optimal mixture remains an open challenge, as existing approaches either rely on unreliable tiny-scale proxy experiments or require prohibitively expensive large-scale exploration. To address this, we propose Decouple Searching from Training Mix (DeMix), a novel framework that leverages model merging to predict optimal data ratios. Instead of training proxy models for every sampled mixture, DeMix trains component models on candidate datasets at scale and derives data mixture proxies via weighted model merging. This paradigm decouples search from training costs, enabling evaluation of unlimited sampled mixtures without extra training burden and thus facilitating better mixture discovery through more search trials. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DeMix breaks the trade-off between sufficiency, accuracy and efficiency, obtaining the optimal mixture with higher benchmark performance at lower search cost. Additionally, we release the DeMix Corpora, a comprehensive 22T-token dataset comprising high-quality pre-training data with validated mixtures to facilitate open research. Our code and DeMix Corpora is available at https://github.com/Lucius-lsr/DeMix.

This paradigm decouples search from training costs, enabling evaluation of unlimited sampled mixtures without extra training burden and thus facilitating better mixture discovery through more search trials. Additionally, we release the DeMix Corpora, a comprehensive 22T-token dataset comprising high-quality pre-training data with validated mixtures to facilitate open research. Our code and DeMix Corpora is available at https://github.com/Lucius-lsr/DeMix.

paragraphs: Language model pretraining requires choosing how much data to draw from different sources. That choice influences the balance between broad competence and difficult capabilities such as mathematics and coding. Testing many mixtures directly is expensive, while results from very small proxy models may not reliably guide larger training runs.

DeMix changes how candidate mixtures are evaluated. It first trains component models on candidate datasets at scale, then combines those models with different weights to produce proxies for different data ratios. Once the components exist, additional mixture candidates do not require separate proxy training runs. This separates the cost of training components from the number of mixtures explored.

The experiments report better benchmark performance and lower search cost when identifying an optimal mixture through this process. The benefit is a wider search supported by proxies built from models trained at scale; evaluating those proxies still remains part of the search. The authors also release DeMix Corpora, a 22-trillion-token collection of high-quality pretraining data with validated mixtures, supporting further research into data composition.
summary.tldr: DeMix searches pretraining data mixtures through weighted model merging, avoiding a new proxy training run for each candidate.

title: Decouple Searching from Training: Scaling Data Mixing via Model Merging for Large Language Model Pre-training

abstract: How do inference time and latent computations enable large language models (LLMs) to solve multi-step reasoning problems? We introduce AlgoTrace, a framework for tracing and steering algorithmic operations in the model latent space for multi-step reasoning. We operationalize primitives by clustering latent activations of the model when solving four benchmarks: Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP), 3SAT, AIME, and Graph Navigation. We annotate the clusters using their corresponding tokens in the reasoning trace. We then apply function vector methods to extract primitive vectors as reusable compositional building blocks of reasoning. We find that a) injecting a primitive vector into models (Phi, Qwen, Llama) elicits the associated algorithmic operation in the reasoning trace, b) injecting primitives can steer behavior across tasks, c) primitive vectors can be composed through algebraic operations, revealing a geometric logic in activation space, and d) a fine-tuned model exhibits improved composition of primitives (Phi-4-Reasoning vs. Phi-4). These findings demonstrate that LLM reasoning can be understood as a walk through algorithmic primitives in the latent space governed by compositional geometry. These primitives transfer across tasks, and reasoning finetuning strengthens algorithmic generalization and composition across domains.

The evidence connects reasoning fine-tuning with stronger composition and transfer across the studied domains.
summary.tldr: AlgoTrace identifies internal vectors associated with reasoning operations and shows that injecting and combining them can steer models across tasks.

title: AlgoTrace: Algorithmic Primitives and Compositional Geometry of Reasoning in Language Models

abstract: Evaluating the real-world capabilities of AI systems requires grounding benchmark performance in human-interpretable measures of task difficulty. Existing approaches that rely on direct human task completion time annotations are costly, noisy, and difficult to scale across benchmarks. In this work, we propose BRIDGE, a unified psychometric framework that learns the latent difficulty scale from model responses and anchors it to human task completion time. Using a two-parameter logistic Item Response Theory model, we jointly estimate latent task difficulty and model capability from model performance data across multiple benchmarks. We demonstrate that latent task difficulty varies linearly with the logarithm of human completion time, allowing human task completion time to be inferred for new benchmarks from model performance alone. Leveraging this alignment, we forecast frontier model capabilities in terms of human task length and independently reproduce METR’s exponential scaling results, with the 50% solvable task horizon doubling approximately every 6 months.

paragraphs: Benchmark scores can be difficult to interpret in terms of work people actually perform. Human completion time offers a more familiar measure of difficulty, but collecting those timings is expensive and noisy. BRIDGE estimates a shared difficulty scale from model responses and connects that scale to human task duration.

The framework uses a two-parameter logistic Item Response Theory model to jointly estimate task difficulty and model capability across benchmarks. The authors find a linear relationship between this latent difficulty and the logarithm of human completion time. The framework makes benchmark performance more interpretable through a common human-time reference.
summary.tldr: BRIDGE links model-derived task difficulty to human completion time, enabling capability comparisons in terms of human task length.

title: BRIDGE: Predicting Human Task Completion Time From Model Performance

abstract: Temporal graphs are ubiquitous in real-world applications and Temporal Graph Networks (TGNs) have achieved superior predictive accuracy. Understanding which historical events drive model predictions can enhance trustworthiness of TGNs. Existing explanation methods overlook the memory module, the core component that records and updates node histories, leaving the influence of past events unexplored. To address this, we attribute TGNs predictions through the topology attribution tree and memory backtracking tree. The topology attribution tree captures the influence of neighbors and their memory vectors, then the memory backtracking tree quantifies how historical events shape node memory vectors. We apply the LRP in TGNs, ensuring that the total contribution of events equals the model’s logits. Finally, top-k selection may be unfaithful due to the nonlinear mapping from logits to probabilities, we design optimization objectives to identify the important events. Experiments on nine temporal graph datasets, spanning node property prediction, link prediction tasks and graph classification tasks, show that our method provides faithful explanations and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/yazhengliu/MemExplainer.

paragraphs: Temporal Graph Networks retain information about earlier events in node memories, so explaining a prediction requires tracing how those memories were formed. The paper argues that existing explanation methods overlook this central mechanism. Its method connects the graph relationships used for a prediction with the historical events recorded inside node states.

A topology attribution tree first tracks the influence of neighboring nodes and their memory vectors. A memory backtracking tree then quantifies how past events contributed to those vectors. The authors apply layer-wise relevance propagation so that total event contributions equal the model's logits, the scores that precede conversion into prediction probabilities.

The paper also observes that simply choosing the highest-ranked events may produce unfaithful explanations because logits map nonlinearly to probabilities. It therefore introduces optimization objectives for selecting important events. Experiments on nine temporal graph datasets cover node property prediction, link prediction, and graph classification. The reported explanations are faithful and outperform state-of-the-art baselines, supporting explicit memory tracing as a way to explain predictions grounded in event history.
summary.tldr: The method explains Temporal Graph Network predictions by tracing both neighbor influence and the historical events embedded in node memory.

title: Towards the Explainability of Temporal Graph Networks via Memory Backtracking and Topological Attribution

abstract: Unified Multimodal models (UMMs) built on a single architecture have shown impressive performance in both understanding and generation. We identify a fundamental challenge lies in inductive biases induced by distinct supervision signals: generation branch prefers high-fidelity, fine-grained representations capable of reconstruction, while the understanding favours semantically discriminative embeddings that remain invariant to task-irrelevant factors. Consequently, optimizing these complementary but non-equivalent objectives within a monolithic backbone leads to mutual impairment instead of enhancement. In this paper, we first analyze the root cause of this interference in unified backbones and reveal a complementary structure in their internal representations. Motivated by the observation, we propose DIVA, a self-improved post-training framework that transforms the representation divergence into interior synergy. By explicitly factorizing the visual representation into shared and unique components based on two complementary information flow, DIVA enables both the understanding and generation branches to achieve beneficial transferring while preserving the integrity of unique information from cross-flow interference via mutual information estimation. Despite its generality, our method consistently achieves improvements across visual understanding (+7.82%) and generation (+8.46%). The official code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DIVA-D225.

paragraphs: A unified multimodal model may use one backbone for both understanding images and generating them, but these tasks reward different representations. Generation benefits from retaining fine visual details needed for reconstruction. Understanding favors features that distinguish meaning while ignoring irrelevant variation. The paper argues that optimizing both objectives together can make them interfere.

DIVA begins by analyzing this interference and identifying complementary structure inside the model’s representations. Its post-training framework separates visual information into shared components and components unique to each task. Two complementary information flows support transfer between understanding and generation, while mutual information estimation helps protect task-specific information from interference across those flows.

The purpose of this separation is to preserve the differences that each task needs while allowing useful information to pass between them. The authors report consistent improvements in both branches, with gains of 7.82% for visual understanding and 8.46% for generation. These findings support the approach of explicitly organizing representation differences as part of joint post-training, rather than assuming a shared backbone will automatically make the objectives mutually beneficial.
summary.tldr: DIVA separates shared and task-specific visual information to improve both understanding and generation in unified multimodal models.

title: DIVA: Harnessing the Representation Divergence in Unified Multimodal Models for Mutual Reinforcement

abstract: Optimizing pretraining data composition is pivotal for LLM generalization. While dynamic mixing outperforms static strategies by capturing evolving training dynamics, current methods fail to reconcile computational efficiency with sample efficiency and structural flexibility for diverse pipelines.We introduce Actor–Critic Online Data Mixing (AC-ODM), which approaches data mixing from a reinforcement learning perspective with a parameterized policy that we theoretically prove to act as a dynamic linear surrogate maximizing the constructive interference of gradients. To enhance practical flexibility, AC-ODM supports two operational modes: (i) a proxy mode for fixed, pre-prepared corpora, where a policy learned on a small model is transferred to a larger target; and (ii) a non-proxy mode for direct end-to-end training from scratch without priors. Empirically, AC-ODM significantly outperforms prior methods in convergence speed and downstream accuracy across various architectures. On Pythia-1B, it reaches optimal validation perplexity using up to 66% fewer training steps than competitive baselines, delivering a 27.5% relative improvement in MMLU accuracy and a 2.23$\times$ higher pass@1 on HumanEval, all while incurring a virtually negligible ($ $0.4%) per-step wall-clock increase and only 2% additional memory overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/DANG-ai/AC-ODM.

paragraphs: AC-ODM studies how to change the mixture of pretraining data as a language model learns. A fixed mixture cannot respond to changing training needs, but adapting that mixture can introduce extra computation. The paper treats data selection as a reinforcement learning problem, using an actor–critic policy to adjust the mix during training.

The theoretical analysis connects this policy to a dynamic linear surrogate that maximizes constructive interference between gradients. In plain language, it favors combinations of training signals that help each other. The framework supports two workflows: learning a policy on a small model and transferring it to a larger one for a prepared corpus, or learning the mixture directly during training from scratch without prior information.

Experiments report better convergence and downstream accuracy across architectures. On Pythia-1B, the method reaches optimal validation perplexity with up to 66% fewer steps, alongside a 27.5% relative MMLU accuracy improvement and 2.23 times higher HumanEval pass@1. The reported overhead is about 0.4% per training step and 2% additional memory, making the gains relevant to total training efficiency.
summary.tldr: AC-ODM learns to adjust pretraining data mixtures, improving reported training efficiency and downstream performance with small computational overhead.

title: AC-ODM: Actor–Critic Online Data Mixing for Sample-Efficient LLM Pretraining

abstract: KV-cache retrieval is essential for long-context LLM inference, yet existing methods struggle with distribution drift and high latency at scale. We introduce ParisKV, a drift-robust, GPU-native KV-cache retrieval framework based on collision-based candidate selection, followed by a quantized inner-product reranking estimator. For million-token contexts, ParisKV supports CPU-offloaded KV caches via Unified Virtual Addressing (UVA), enabling on-demand top-$k$ fetching with minimal overhead. ParisKV matches or outperforms full attention quality on both long-input and long-generation benchmarks. It achieves state-of-the-art long-context decoding efficiency: it matches or exceeds full-attention speed even at batch size 1 for long contexts, delivers up to 2.8$\times$ higher throughput within full attention’s runnable range, and scales to million-token contexts where full attention runs out of memory. At million-token scale, ParisKV reduces decode latency by 17$\times$ and 44$\times$ compared to MagicPIG and PQCache, respectively—two state-of-the-art KV-cache top-$k$ retrieval baselines; code is available at https://github.com/amy-77/ParisKV/tree/main.

paragraphs: Long-context language models must retrieve useful information from a large cache of attention keys and values. Existing retrieval approaches can suffer from high latency and distribution drift. ParisKV introduces a GPU-native retrieval framework designed to handle both problems, including contexts large enough that keeping the entire cache on the GPU becomes impractical.

The method first selects candidates using collisions and then reranks them with a quantized estimator of inner products. For million-token contexts, it supports caches offloaded to CPU memory through Unified Virtual Addressing. This allows the model to fetch the selected top-k entries on demand with minimal overhead.

On the reported long-input and long-generation benchmarks, ParisKV matches or exceeds full-attention quality. It matches or surpasses full-attention speed even at batch size one for long contexts and delivers up to 2.8 times higher throughput where full attention fits. At million-token scale, where full attention runs out of memory, decode latency is reduced by factors of 17 and 44 relative to MagicPIG and PQCache, respectively.
summary.tldr: ParisKV combines fast candidate retrieval, quantized reranking, and CPU cache offloading to scale decoding to million-token contexts.

title: ParisKV: Fast and Drift-Robust KV-Cache Retrieval for Long-Context LLMs

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a cornerstone for fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs), with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) serving as the de facto standard algorithm. Despite its ubiquity, we argue that the core ratio clipping mechanism in PPO is structurally ill-suited for the large vocabularies inherent to LLMs. PPO constrains policy updates based on the probability ratio of sampled tokens, which serves as a noisy single-sample Monte Carlo estimate of the true policy divergence. This creates a sub-optimal learning dynamic: updates to low-probability tokens are aggressively over-penalized, while potentially catastrophic shifts in high-probability tokens are under-constrained, leading to training inefficiency and instability. To address this, we propose Divergence Proximal Policy Optimization (DPPO), which substitutes heuristic clipping with a more principled constraint based on a direct estimate of policy divergence (e.g., Total Variation or KL). To avoid huge memory footprint, we introduce the efficient Binary and Top-K approximations to capture the essential divergence with negligible overhead. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that DPPO achieves superior stability and efficiency compared to existing methods, offering a more robust foundation for RL-based LLM fine-tuning. Our code is available at https://github.com/sail-sg/Stable-RL.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning fine-tuning needs to improve a language model without allowing destabilizing changes. PPO commonly controls updates by clipping probability ratios for sampled tokens. The paper argues that this is a noisy way to assess changes in a distribution over a large vocabulary, producing uneven constraints across tokens with different probabilities.

According to the authors’ analysis, clipping can penalize updates to unlikely tokens too strongly while insufficiently limiting large changes to likely tokens. Their alternative, Divergence Proximal Policy Optimization, constrains updates using a direct estimate of distributional divergence, such as Total Variation or KL. Binary and Top-K approximations are introduced to capture essential divergence information without the memory cost of a full calculation.

Empirical evaluations report better stability and efficiency than existing methods, with negligible overhead from the proposed approximations. The significance is the connection between how update size is measured and how reliably training proceeds. DPPO replaces a token-level proxy with an estimate aimed more directly at the policy distribution, and the reported experiments support that choice for language-model fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: DPPO replaces PPO’s sampled-token clipping with efficient divergence estimates, improving reported stability and efficiency in language-model reinforcement learning.

title: Rethinking the Trust Region in LLM Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Diffusion models for super-resolution (SR) produce high-quality visual results but require expensive computational costs. Despite the development of several methods to accelerate diffusion-based SR models, some (e.g., SinSR) fail to produce realistic perceptual details, while others (e.g., OSEDiff) may hallucinate non-existent structures. To overcome these issues, we present RSD, a new distillation method for ResShift. Our method is based on training the student network to produce images such that a new fake ResShift model trained on them will coincide with the teacher model. RSD achieves single-step restoration and outperforms the teacher by a noticeable margin in various perceptual metrics (LPIPS, CLIPIQA, MUSIQ). We show that our distillation method can surpass SinSR, the other distillation-based method for ResShift, making it on par with state-of-the-art diffusion SR distillation methods with limited computational costs in terms of perceptual quality. Compared to SR methods based on pre-trained text-to-image models, RSD produces competitive perceptual quality and requires fewer parameters, GPU memory, and training cost. We provide experimental results on various real-world and synthetic datasets, including RealSR, RealSet65, DRealSR, ImageNet, and DIV2K. We provide the code at https://github.com/Daniil-Selikhanovych/RSD.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based super-resolution can create visually strong images, but its computational demands motivate faster restoration methods. Existing acceleration approaches can struggle with realistic detail or introduce structures absent from the source. RSD addresses this setting by distilling the ResShift diffusion model into a student that restores an image in one step.

Its training criterion connects the student’s generated images back to the teacher. The student is trained so that a new ResShift model fitted to its outputs would coincide with the teacher model. This provides a route to single-step restoration, with the authors reporting that the student surpasses the teacher on the perceptual metrics LPIPS, CLIPIQA, and MUSIQ.

RSD outperforms SinSR and reaches perceptual quality comparable to state-of-the-art diffusion distillation methods. Relative to super-resolution methods built on pretrained text-to-image models, it offers competitive perceptual quality with fewer parameters, lower GPU memory requirements, and lower training cost. The reported gains concern perceptual quality and resource efficiency.
summary.tldr: RSD distills ResShift into single-step super-resolution, improving reported perceptual metrics while reducing resource demands relative to text-to-image-based methods.

title: One-Step Residual Shifting Diffusion for Image Super-Resolution via Distillation

abstract: We study the task of learning the structure of a $d$-sparse Gaussian graphical model on $n$ variables from a single trajectory of Glauber dynamics. Beyond algorithmic considerations, many applications present temporally correlated observations rather than i.i.d. samples. Moreover, in the classical i.i.d. setting, polynomial-time structure learning from a sublinear in $n$ number of samples is suspected to be computationally hard without additional assumptions on the precision matrix. Motivated in part by this, we design the first polynomial-time algorithm that recovers the conditional-independence graph from a single Glauber trajectory, with a trajectory-length guarantee that does not depend on the mixing time. Technically, our algorithm has three components. First, we estimate the conditional variances and rescale the trajectory to reduce to the unit-diagonal case, without changing the underlying graph. Second, we design a local edge test that extracts adjacency information from short update windows by isolating pairwise influence. Third, we aggregate these local statistics using a robust median-based estimator, and prove accuracy despite contamination and temporal dependence arising from a single trajectory.

paragraphs: This paper learns which variables are conditionally related in a sparse Gaussian graphical model from one temporally dependent sequence of observations. Specifically, the sequence follows Glauber dynamics. This setting matters because observations in applications may arrive as a correlated trajectory, rather than as independent samples, and their dependence changes what a learning algorithm can exploit.

The algorithm first estimates conditional variances and rescales the observations so the problem has a unit diagonal, while preserving the underlying graph. It then examines short windows of updates to isolate the influence of one variable on another. These local edge tests extract adjacency information directly from the dynamics of the observed sequence.

A robust median-based estimator combines the local statistics, with a proof of accuracy despite contamination and temporal dependence. The authors establish polynomial-time graph recovery with a trajectory-length guarantee that does not depend on mixing time, the time needed for the dynamics to approach equilibrium. This provides a way to recover structure without making the required observation length depend on that equilibration timescale.
summary.tldr: A polynomial-time algorithm recovers sparse Gaussian graph structure from one Glauber trajectory with an observation-length guarantee independent of mixing time.

title: Learning Gaussian Graphical Models from a Glauber Trajectory Without Mixing

abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) is the most widely used method for calculating molecular properties; however, its accuracy is often insufficient for quantitative predictions. Coupled cluster (CC) theory is the most successful method for achieving accuracy beyond DFT and predicting properties that closely align with experiment. It is known as the “gold standard” of quantum chemistry. Unfortunately, the high computational cost of CC limits its widespread applicability. In this work, we present the Molecular Orbital Learning Model (MoLe), an equivariant machine learning model that directly predicts CC’s core mathematical objects, the excitation amplitudes, from the mean-field Hartree-Fock molecular orbitals as inputs. We test various aspects of our model and demonstrate its very high data efficiency and remarkable out-of-distribution generalization to larger molecules and off-equilibrium geometries, despite being trained only on small equilibrium geometries. Finally, we also examine its ability to reduce the number of cycles required to converge CC calculations. MoLe can set the foundations for high-accuracy wavefunction-based ML architectures to accelerate molecular design and complement force-field approaches.

They also investigate whether MoLe can reduce the cycles needed for coupled cluster convergence. The findings position it as a possible foundation for accelerating molecular design with accurate wavefunction models and complementing force-field approaches.
summary.tldr: MoLe predicts coupled cluster excitation amplitudes from molecular orbitals and shows strong generalization beyond its small-molecule training geometries.

title: Coupled Cluster con MoLe: Molecular Orbital Learning for Neural Wavefunctions

abstract: Attribution methods reveal which input features a neural network uses for a prediction, adding transparency to their decisions. A common problem is that these attributions seem unspecific, highlighting both important and irrelevant features. We revisit the common attribution pipeline and observe that using logits as attribution target is a main cause of this phenomenon. We show that the solution is in plain sight: considering distributions of attributions over multiple classes using existing attribution methods yields specific and fine-grained attributions. On common benchmarks, including the grid-pointing game and randomization-based sanity checks, this improves the ability of 18 attribution methods across 7 architectures up to $2\times$, agnostic to model architecture.

This paper revisits the standard attribution pipeline and identifies a major contributor: using an individual class logit, or raw class score, as the quantity the explanation method tries to attribute.

The proposed change considers distributions of attributions across multiple classes using existing attribution methods. Looking across classes introduces class competition into the explanation, helping produce more specific and fine-grained maps. The contribution therefore lies in how attribution information is targeted and interpreted, allowing established explanation methods to benefit without requiring a new method for each model architecture.

On common benchmarks, including the grid-pointing game and randomization-based sanity checks, the change improves results for 18 attribution methods across seven architectures, with gains reaching up to twofold. That maximum describes the reported improvements, not a uniform doubling for every method. The results show that a shared pipeline choice can substantially affect explanation quality across otherwise different attribution techniques.
summary.tldr: Considering attribution across competing classes makes existing explanation methods more focused, with reported benchmark gains of up to twofold.

title: Hidden in Plain Sight – Class Competition Focuses Attribution Maps

abstract: Diffusion and flow models have become the dominant paradigm for generative modeling on Riemannian manifolds, with successful applications in protein backbone generation and DNA sequence design. However, these methods require tens to hundreds of neural network evaluations at inference time, which can become a computational bottleneck in large-scale scientific sampling workflows. We introduce Riemannian MeanFlow (RMF), a framework for learning flow maps directly on manifolds, enabling high-quality generations with as few as one forward pass. We derive three equivalent characterizations of the manifold average velocity (Eulerian, Lagrangian, and semigroup identities), and analyze parameterizations and stabilization techniques to improve training on high-dimensional manifolds. In promoter DNA design and protein backbone generation settings, RMF achieves comparable sample quality to prior methods while requiring up to 10$\times$ fewer function evaluations. Finally, we show that few-step flow maps enable efficient reward-guided design through reward look-ahead, where terminal states can be predicted from intermediate steps at minimal additional cost.

title: Riemannian MeanFlow

abstract: While current embodied policies exhibit remarkable manipulation skills, their execution remains unsatisfactorily slow as they inherit the tardy pacing of human demonstrations. Existing acceleration methods typically require policy retraining or costly online interactions, limiting their scalability for large-scale foundation models. In this paper, we propose Speedup Patch (SuP), a lightweight, policy-agnostic framework that enables plug-and-play acceleration using solely offline data. SuP introduces an external scheduler that adaptively downsamples action chunks provided by embodied policies to eliminate redundancies. Specifically, we formalize the optimization of our scheduler as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) aimed at maximizing efficiency without compromising task performance. Since direct success evaluation is infeasible in offline settings, SuP introduces World Model based state deviation as a surrogate metric to enforce safety constraints. By leveraging a learned world model as a virtual evaluator to predict counterfactual trajectories, the scheduler can be optimized via offline reinforcement learning. Empirical results on simulation benchmarks (Libero, Bigym) and real-world tasks validate that SuP achieves an overall $1.8\times$ execution speedup for diverse policies while maintaining their original success rates.

The authors formulate scheduling as a constrained decision problem: increase efficiency while preserving task performance. Offline data cannot directly reveal whether every proposed acceleration would succeed, so a learned world model predicts alternative trajectories. State deviation in these predicted trajectories serves as a surrogate constraint, giving offline reinforcement learning a way to evaluate changes in execution.

Experiments on Libero, Bigym, and real-world tasks report an overall 1.8-fold execution speedup across diverse policies while maintaining their original success rates. The preservation of success is an empirical finding in these evaluations, while training relies on world-model state deviation as its substitute for direct success evaluation.
summary.tldr: Speedup Patch learns an offline scheduler that accelerates robot policies by removing redundant actions, achieving a reported 1.8-fold overall speedup.

title: Speedup Patch: Learning a Plug-and-Play Policy to Accelerate Embodied Manipulation

abstract: Standard reward models typically predict scalar scores that fail to capture the multifaceted nature of response quality in non-verifiable domains, such as creative writing or open-ended instruction following. To address this limitation, we propose Rubric-ARM, a framework that jointly optimizes a rubric generator and a judge using reinforcement learning from preference feedback. Unlike existing methods that rely on static rubrics or disjoint training pipelines, our approach treats rubric generation as a latent action learned to maximize judgment accuracy. We introduce an alternating optimization strategy to mitigate the non-stationarity of simultaneous updates, providing theoretical analysis that demonstrates how this schedule reduces gradient variance during training. Extensive experiments show that Rubric-ARM achieves state-of-the-art performance among baselines on multiple benchmarks and significantly improves downstream policy alignment in both offline and online reinforcement learning settings.

These findings suggest that adapting evaluation criteria together with the evaluator can produce feedback that better guides subsequent model training.
summary.tldr: Rubric-ARM alternates training a rubric generator and a judge to improve preference judgments and downstream language-model alignment.

title: Alternating Reinforcement Learning for Rubric-Based Reward Modeling in Non-Verifiable LLM Post-Training

abstract: We aim to develop a multimodal research agent capable of explicit reasoning and planning, multi-tool invocation, and cross-modal information synthesis, enabling it to conduct deep research tasks. However, we observe three main challenges in developing such agents: (1) scarcity of search-intensive multimodal QA data, (2) lack of effective search trajectories, and (3) prohibitive cost of training with online search APIs. To tackle them, we first propose Hyper-Search, a hypergraph-based QA generation method that models and connects visual and textual nodes within and across modalities, enabling to generate search-intensive multimodal QA pairs that require invoking various search tools to solve. Second, we introduce DR-TTS, which first decomposes search-involved tasks into several categories according to search tool types, and respectively optimize specialized search tool experts for each tool. It then recomposes tool experts to jointly explore search trajectories via tree search, producing trajectories that successfully solve complex tasks using various search tools. Third, we build an offline search engine supporting multiple search tools, enabling agentic reinforcement learning without using costly online search APIs. With the three designs, we develop MM-DeepResearch, a powerful multimodal deep research agent, and extensive results shows its superiority across benchmarks.

paragraphs: MM-DeepResearch targets agents that must plan searches, invoke multiple tools, and combine visual and textual evidence. The authors identify three development obstacles: too few multimodal questions that genuinely require searching, insufficient examples of successful search sequences, and the expense of reinforcement learning through online search APIs. Their framework addresses each obstacle with a separate component.

These connections support questions requiring different search tools. DR-TTS then organizes tasks by tool type, optimizes specialized tool experts, and combines those experts through tree search to produce successful sequences of searches for complex tasks.

An offline search engine supplies multiple search tools during reinforcement learning without relying on costly online search APIs. Together, the data generation, trajectory construction, and offline training components produce the MM-DeepResearch agent. The paper reports superior results across benchmarks. Its contribution links the ability to learn multimodal research behavior with the availability of suitable questions, successful tool-use examples, and an affordable training environment.
summary.tldr: MM-DeepResearch combines multimodal question generation, tool-expert search trajectories, and offline search training to improve research-agent performance.

title: MM-DeepResearch: A Simple and Effective Multimodal Agentic Search Baseline

abstract: Visual Mamba models have recently emerged as alternatives to Vision Transformers (ViTs), which suffer from quadratic complexity. While the recurrent scanning mechanism of Mamba offers computational efficiency, it inherently limits non-causal interactions between image patches. Prior works have attempted to address this limitation through various multi-scan strategies; however, these approaches suffer from inefficiencies due to suboptimal scan designs and frequent data rearrangement. Moreover, Mamba exhibits relatively slow computational speed under short token lengths, commonly used in visual tasks. In pursuit of a truly efficient vision encoder, we rethink the scan operation for vision and the computational efficiency of Mamba. To this end, we propose SF-Mamba, a novel visual Mamba with two key proposals: auxiliary patch swapping for encoding bidirectional information flow under an unidirectional scan and batch folding with periodic state reset for advanced GPU parallelism. Extensive experiments on image classification, object detection, and instance and semantic segmentation consistently demonstrate that our proposed SF-Mamba significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines while improving throughput across different model sizes. The source code is available at: https://github.com/sony/SF-Mamba.

Existing approaches use multiple scans to broaden information flow, introducing inefficiencies from scan design and repeated data rearrangement. Mamba can also run relatively slowly on the short token sequences commonly used in visual tasks.

SF-Mamba addresses information flow and hardware utilization together. Auxiliary patch swapping allows a unidirectional scan to encode information flowing in both directions. Batch folding with periodic state resets improves GPU parallelism. These two changes target distinct sources of inefficiency: how image information travels through the model and how the computation is organized on the hardware.

Experiments cover image classification, object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation. Across these tasks and different model sizes, SF-Mamba significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines while increasing throughput. The reported findings show that reconsidering scan mechanics can improve both visual performance and practical processing speed, addressing the gap between an efficient recurrent formulation and its implementation for typical vision workloads.
summary.tldr: SF-Mamba combines patch swapping and batch folding to improve visual information flow, task performance, and GPU throughput.

title: SF-Mamba: Rethinking State Space Model for Vision

abstract: CauchyNet is a compact complex-valued network whose hidden units form products of shifted reciprocal features, motivated by Cauchy-type kernel representations. The design targets regression problems with sharp rational-like spikes and partially observed inputs, where standard real-valued networks often require large width. We prove that finite linear combinations of multivariate Cauchy kernels are dense in $C(M)$ on compact $M\subset\mathbb R^N$, and that CauchyNet can realize these kernel sums via its complex biases and output weights. In experiments, CauchyNet reaches lower error on near-singular and gap-filling benchmarks, often with substantially fewer trainable parameters in our settings; results on smooth and piecewise-affine targets are mixed and delineate the method’s intended regime.

The proposed alternative is a compact complex-valued network whose hidden units multiply shifted reciprocal features, giving its architecture a direct connection to Cauchy-type kernel representations.

The theoretical result establishes that finite sums of multivariate Cauchy kernels can approximate continuous functions arbitrarily closely on compact subsets of real-valued input space. The authors also show how CauchyNet can represent those sums through its complex biases and output weights. This connects the network’s construction to a broad approximation property, rather than relying solely on empirical performance.

In the reported experiments, CauchyNet achieves lower errors on near-singular functions and gap-filling tasks, often using substantially fewer trainable parameters. Results on smooth and piecewise-affine functions are mixed. That distinction helps identify the intended use case: the architecture is especially motivated by sharply varying rational-like behavior, while the experiments do not establish a uniform advantage across function types.
summary.tldr: CauchyNet uses complex reciprocal features to model sharp regression functions compactly, with mixed results on smoother target functions.

title: CauchyNet: Compact and Data-Efficient Learning using Holomorphic Activation Functions

abstract: The success of large language models (LLMs) in scientific domains has heightened safety concerns, prompting numerous benchmarks to evaluate their scientific safety. Existing benchmarks often suffer from limited risk coverage and a reliance on subjective evaluation. To address these problems, we introduce SafeSci, a comprehensive framework for safety evaluation and enhancement in scientific contexts. SafeSci comprises SafeSciBench, a multi-disciplinary benchmark with 0.25M samples, and SafeSciTrain, a large-scale dataset containing 1.5M samples for safety enhancement. SafeSciBench distinguishes between safety knowledge and risk to cover extensive scopes and employs objective metrics such as deterministically answerable questions to mitigate evaluation bias. We evaluate 24 advanced LLMs and reveal critical vulnerabilities. We also observe that LLMs exhibit varying degrees of excessive refusal behaviors on safety-related issues. For safety enhancement, we demonstrate that fine-tuning on SafeSciTrain significantly enhances the safety alignment of LLMs. Finally, we argue that determining the safety of a scientific question should depend on the specific context, rather than universally categorizing it as safe or unsafe.

Their framework includes SafeSciBench, with 250,000 samples across scientific disciplines, and SafeSciTrain, with 1.5 million samples for safety training.

This distinction matters because knowing about safety and responding safely to a potentially risky request are different evaluation concerns. The authors also emphasize context: the safety of a scientific question should depend on its particular use rather than a universal safe-or-unsafe label.

An evaluation of 24 advanced language models reveals critical vulnerabilities alongside varying levels of excessive refusal on safety-related topics. Fine-tuning with SafeSciTrain significantly improves safety alignment in the reported experiments. The framework therefore provides resources for both identifying unsafe behavior and studying improvement, while also drawing attention to unnecessary refusals.
summary.tldr: SafeSci introduces scientific safety evaluation and training datasets that expose vulnerabilities, measure excessive refusals, and improve safety alignment.

abstract: We consider spectral clustering and transductive inference for data with multiple views. A typical example is the web, which can be described by either the hyperlinks between web pages or the words occurring in web pages. When each view is represented as a graph, one may convexly combine the weight matrices or the discrete Laplacians for each graph, and then proceed with existing clustering or classification techniques. Such a solution might sound natural, but its underlying principle is not clear. Unlike this kind of methodology, we develop multiview spectral clustering via generalizing the normalized cut from a single view to multiple views. We further build multiview transductive inference on the basis of multiview spectral clustering. Our framework leads to a mixture of Markov chains defined on every graph. The experimental evaluation on real-world web classification demonstrates promising results that validate our method.

paragraphs: The same objects can have several useful representations. Web pages, for example, can be connected through hyperlinks or compared through their words. When each representation becomes a graph, combining them raises a modeling question: what shared clustering objective should the combined graph represent? Simply averaging graph weights or Laplacians does not, by itself, explain that objective.

This paper develops multiview spectral clustering by extending normalized cut from one graph to several. Normalized cut supplies a criterion for dividing a graph into groups, so its extension gives the combination of views an explicit organizing principle. The resulting framework has an interpretation as a mixture of Markov chains, with a chain defined on each graph.

The authors then build multiview transductive inference on the clustering framework, using the multiple representations for classification of the data under consideration. Experiments on real-world web classification produce promising results. The contribution is therefore both a principled basis for combining graph views and evidence that the resulting approach can be useful for web classification.
summary.tldr: Extending normalized cut to multiple graphs gives a principled multiview clustering and transductive learning framework with promising web-classification results.

title: Spectral clustering and transductive learning with multiple views

abstract: Many machine learning algorithms can be formulated as a generalized eigenvalue problem. One major limitation of such formulation is that the generalized eigenvalue problem is computationally expensive to solve especially for large-scale problems. In this paper, we show that under a mild condition, a class of generalized eigenvalue problems in machine learning can be formulated as a least squares problem. This class of problems include classical techniques such as Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA), Partial Least Squares (PLS), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), as well as Hypergraph Spectral Learning (HSL). As a result, various regularization techniques such as the 1-norm and 2-norm regularization can be readily incorporated into the formulation to improve model sparsity and generalization ability. In addition, the least squares formulation leads to efficient and scalable implementations based on the iterative conjugate gradient type algorithms. We report experimental results that confirm the established equivalence relationship. We also demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of the equivalent least squares formulations on large-scale problems. The presented analysis provides significant new insights into the relationship between the generalized eigenvalue and least squares problems in machine learning.

paragraphs: Several machine learning methods lead to generalized eigenvalue problems, whose computational cost can become a barrier on large datasets. This paper shows that a class of these problems can instead be written as least squares problems under a condition the authors describe as mild. The covered methods include canonical correlation analysis, partial least squares, linear discriminant analysis, and hypergraph spectral learning.

The reformulation matters because it opens these methods to tools already available for least squares optimization. In particular, penalties based on the 1-norm and 2-norm can be incorporated to support sparse models and improved generalization. Iterative algorithms of the conjugate gradient type also provide a route to efficient, scalable implementations.

Experiments confirm the stated equivalence and demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of the reformulations on large problems. The contribution is both computational and conceptual: apparently different optimization formulations can describe the same learning problem. That relationship remains conditional on the paper's stated assumption and applies to the identified class of problems.
summary.tldr: Under a mild condition, several generalized eigenvalue learning problems admit equivalent least squares formulations that support scalable optimization and regularization.

title: A least squares formulation for a class of generalized eigenvalue problems in machine learning

abstract: A learning problem might have several measures of complexity (e.g., norm and dimensionality) that affect the generalization error. What is the interaction between these complexities? Dimension-free learning theory bounds and parametric asymptotic analyses each provide a partial picture of the full learning curve. In this paper, we use high-dimensional asymptotics on two classical problems---mean estimation and linear regression---to explore the learning curve more completely. We show that these curves exhibit multiple regimes, where in each regime, the excess risk is controlled by a subset of the problem complexities.

The authors use high-dimensional asymptotic analysis to study two classical problems: mean estimation and linear regression. Studying these settings allows them to examine learning curves while accounting for multiple sources of complexity. The focus is on how the factors controlling error vary across regimes, rather than assigning the entire curve to a single complexity measure.

They show that the curves contain multiple regimes, each with excess risk controlled by a subset of the problem's complexities. This means the same complexity measures need not play equally prominent roles throughout learning. The contribution is a more complete theoretical picture for the two studied problems, explaining how different analyses can capture different portions of their behavior.
summary.tldr: High-dimensional analyses of mean estimation and linear regression reveal learning regimes governed by different subsets of complexity measures.

title: On the Interaction between Norm and Dimensionality: Multiple Regimes in Learning

abstract: A number of combinatorial optimization problems in machine learning can be described as the problem of minimizing a submodular function. It is known that the unconstrained submodular minimization problem can be solved in strongly polynomial time. However, additional constraints make the problem intractable in many settings. In this paper, we discuss the submodular minimization under a size constraint, which is NP-hard, and generalizes the densest subgraph problem and the uniform graph partitioning problem. Because of NP-hardness, it is difficult to compute an optimal solution even for a prescribed size constraint. In our approach, we do not give approximation algorithms. Instead, the proposed algorithm computes optimal solutions for some of possible size constraints in polynomial time. Our algorithm utilizes the basic polyhedral theory associated with submodular functions. Additionally, we evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm through computational experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies minimizing a submodular function when the chosen set must satisfy a size constraint. Without constraints, submodular minimization has strongly polynomial algorithms. Adding a size requirement changes the computational picture: the problem is NP-hard and includes the densest subgraph and uniform graph partitioning problems as special cases.

Rather than approximating an optimum for any requested size, the proposed algorithm computes exact optimal solutions for some of the possible size constraints. This is the central distinction in its guarantee. It does not promise to solve the problem optimally for an arbitrary size supplied in advance, which is precisely where the general computational difficulty remains.

The method uses the polyhedral theory associated with submodular functions and runs in polynomial time for its stated task. Computational experiments evaluate its performance. The contribution identifies a way to obtain exact answers within a difficult constrained problem by changing which size constraints the algorithm resolves, rather than weakening the quality of the solutions returned through an approximation guarantee.
summary.tldr: A polynomial-time algorithm finds exact submodular minima for some size constraints, without claiming to solve every prescribed size.

title: Size-constrained Submodular Minimization through Minimum Norm Base
